abstract: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) influences subsurface biogeochemistry yet controls on its composition in many tropical sub-Saharan aquifers remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated satellite-derived land-use/land-cover (LULC) data, terrain metrics, and inorganic tracers (NO3 −/Cl−, SO4 2−/Cl−) to evaluate how LULC patterns and terrain-driven hydrological convergence, expressed as topographic wetness index (TWI), influence bulk and fluorescent groundwater DOM (fDOM) across multiple spatial scales in Uganda. Groundwater DOM was dominated by weakly aromatic, highly processed material of mixed terrestrial and microbial origin (specific ultraviolet absorbance (SUVA) 0.5, β:α < 1, and fluorescence index (FI) ∼ 1.6). Total fluorescence (0.1 – 12.3 RU; median 0.3 RU) was dominated by fulvic-like (∼35 %) and tryptophan-like (∼29 %), followed by tyrosine-like (∼18 %) and humic-like (∼17 %) components. The combined influence of LULC and TWI was scale dependent, although LULC categories showed no significant associations with groundwater DOM, except surface-water cover. TWI was positively associated with dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and fDOM components consistent with potential lateral mobilisation and surface–groundwater interaction in hydrologically convergent zones. NO3 −/Cl− ratios were negatively correlated with DOC (Spearman ρ ∼ −0.56), and positively with SUVA (ρ ∼ 0.46), consistent with preferential depletion of relatively bioavailable DOM fractions and relative enrichment of more aromatic residual DOM under nitrate-enriched conditions. These results show that in the Victoria and Kyoga basins, hydrological convergence, rather than land use alone, likely influences groundwater DOM composition, highlighting surface waters and near-surface hyporheic zones as potential sources and transformation environments for organic matter entering aquifers.

title: REE and radioelement enrichment in heavy-mineral coastal placers: An integrated geophysical–geochemical synthesis from the eastern coast of India
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Shayantani Ghosal, Sudha Agrahari, Debashish Sengupta
abstract: This study presents a data integrated synthesis with new analytical results for mineral exploration along the eastern fringe of Peninsular India, focusing on heavy mineral rich coastal placer systems of Odisha. Rather than a standalone case study, the work combines previously published datasets with newly acquired field measurements and laboratory analyses to develop a unified understanding of the spatial distribution, subsurface architecture and geochemical characteristics of these placers. Non-invasive two-dimensional electrical resistivity imaging conducted along >40 km of coastline (including newly acquired profiles) delineates laterally continuous low-resistivity zones (0.1-1.1 Ω m) extending to depths of ∼20-25 m, interpreted as heavy mineral concentrations dominated by ilmenite and rutile. Near river mouths, these conductive zones occur as deeper, discontinuous pockets, reflecting localized depositional controls. Previously published radiometric datasets are integrated to the geoelectrical framework which enabled a robust multi-proxy comparison. The beach placers show elevated thorium and comparatively low uranium and potassium concentrations. Laboratory geochemical analyses, expanded through new datasets, indicate substantial enrichment of rare earth elements (REEs), with an average total REE concentration of 4243 ppm, approximately 29 times the upper continental crustal average (LREE > HREE). Inter-method comparison of REE concentrations obtained through ICP-MS and instrumental neutron activation analysis yields strong correlations (R2 = 0.6–0.8), confirming analytical robustness. A consistent positive relationship between thorium and total REE concentrations highlights the potential of thorium as an effective first-pass proxy for REE exploration. By explicitly integrating legacy datasets with new observations, this study establishes a process-based, multi-proxy exploration framework, advancing regional placer exploration models and providing an approach applicable to analogous coastal systems worldwide.

title: Transport and remobilization of Eu(III)-silicate colloids in a simulated fractured granite-groundwater system
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Daming Zhang, Yujia Zhang, Qicheng Yao, Wenbo Zhang, Qiang Jin, Zongyuan Chen, Zhijun Guo
abstract: The migration of actinides (An) in deep geological repositories is significantly influenced by colloid-facilitated transport, particularly via the formation of An-silicate colloids. This study investigates the transport and release behaviors of Eu(III)-silicate colloids (used as an analog for trivalent actinides) in a simulated water-saturated granite fracture system. Transport experiments were conducted in a laboratory-scale fracture flow system to evaluate the effects of pH (7.3-8.5), ionic strength (1-400 mM), and fulvic acid (FA, 2.0-10.0 mg/L) on colloid mobility, while retention-release experiments were performed to assess their remobilization potential. Mechanisms were elucidated using size-fractionated analysis, with consideration of colloidal heterogeneity, and DLVO theory. The results indicate that Eu(III)-silicate colloids exhibit high mobility under conditions of high pH (8.5) and low ionic strength (1 mM), achieving a recovery rate of 97.9%. This enhanced transport is driven by strong electrostatic repulsion and minimized hydrodynamic size. The presence of FA further promotes mobility through steric stabilization and the formation of soluble Eu(III)-FA complexes. The transport mechanism transitions from Langmuirian blocking to ripening when Eu(III)-silicate colloids become unstable and aggregate under elevated ionic strength (e.g., >200 mM NaCl at pH 8.5). Colloidal fractions with higher Si/Eu ratios demonstrated superior transport capability due to their smaller size and stronger surface charge, indicating that the heterogeneity of Eu(III)-silicate colloids plays an important role in their transport behavior. Furthermore, retained colloids at pH 8.0 and 300 mM NaCl can be remobilized by perturbations such as decreasing ionic strength, increasing pH, or increasing flow velocity. This release process is governed by a dual mechanism involving both direct detachment from the fracture surface and the disaggregation of larger aggregates. However, prolonged retention times were found to inhibit remobilization due to the aging effect, which strengthens adhesion and leads to a transition towards more stable attachment. These findings provide critical insights into the environmental fate of An (III)-silicate colloids and emphasize the potential risks associated with their remobilization in fractured granite environments.

title: Lead isotope studies of Precambrian basement in the midcontinent United States: Implications for metal sources in Mississippi Valley-type ores
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Mackenzie Moorhead, Adriana Potra, John R. Samuelsen, Gregory Dumond
abstract: Fifty-three basement samples from the Central Plains Orogen (1.65-1.8 Ga) and Southern Granite-Rhyolite Province (1.3-1.4 Ga) have been analyzed for Pb isotope ratios and for U, Th, and Pb concentrations to re-evaluate the possibility of a basement Pb source for Mississippi Valley-type (MVT) ores throughout the greater midcontinent region and to develop a schematic model pertaining to the ore-forming mechanisms. Current results for the Granite-Rhyolite Province basement rocks are all collinear with the array defined by published data and show higher Pb isotope ratios. This suggests mixing between a more depleted source, potentially a reservoir in the upper mantle, and a more enriched source that requires a crustal/sediment contribution. The Pb isotope ratios of the Central Plains Orogen rocks plot between those of the Granite-Rhyolite Province, indicating source(s) of intermediate enrichment. An important finding of this study is that several basement samples that yield highly radiogenic Pb isotope ratios (208Pb/204Pb between 40.534 and 45.810) originate from shallower depths (between around 650 m and 1050 m), and those that yield low Pb isotope ratios (208Pb/204Pb between 37.171 and 37.860) originate from deeper depths (between around 2200 m and 3800 m). While the current results agree with the description of the midcontinent basement being heterogeneous, there are likely specific, localized features (e.g., younger intrusion or a basement high) that impart certain rocks their unique, highly radiogenic Pb signatures. The samples that display the high Pb isotope ratios plot near the radiogenic end-member of the MVT ore array. The Pb isotope patterns noticed in basement rocks originating from various levels, together with available Pb isotopes and fluid inclusions data in the MVT ores, support the interpretation that metal-rich fluids emanating from local, shallower, more radiogenic basement rocks migrated along deep-seated faults directly to deposition zones, without mixing with basin-derived fluids (e.g., Northern Arkansas District). Other basement-derived fluids emanating from deeper, less radiogenic basement rocks might have migrated upward along deep-seated faults, then laterally, potentially mixing with basin-derived fluids enriched in radiogenic Pb and contributing to isotopic diversity (e.g., Tri-State and Southeast Missouri districts). The possible presence of unique features within the basement mentioned above may explain why the 1.05 Ga and 1.01 Ga model Pb source ages for midcontinent ores are younger than the ages of the Granite Rhyolite Province and the Central Plains Orogen.

title: Recognizing geochemical anomalies by locally selective combination of parallel autoencoders: Integrating AE, VAE, and AE-1SVM for robust metal exploration targeting
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Zeinab Soltani, Hossein Hassani, Ardeshir Hezarkhani, Saeid Esmaeiloghli
abstract: Deep learning (DL) models have become leading techniques for recognizing mineralization-related geochemical anomalies because they can learn deep feature representations of multi-element geochemical data arising from nonlinear Earth systems and complex statistical distributions. Among different DL techniques, autoencoder-backbone models are particularly attractive for geochemical exploration because they operate in an unsupervised manner and thus bypass the practical limitations of supervised strategies that require labeled training datasets. However, a critical challenge in geochemical anomaly detection is the model-based uncertainty imposed by the fact that different autoencoder-based detectors may generate inconsistent anomaly patterns within distinct geological architectures and highly complex frequency distributions. This issue may mislead metal exploration targeting when an anomaly map derived from a single model is used to delimit target areas. To address this model-based uncertainty, in this research, we propose the locally selective combination of parallel autoencoders (LSCPAE), which integrates three autoencoder-backbone anomaly detectors—autoencoder (AE), variational autoencoder (VAE), and autoencoder-based one-class support vector machine (AE-1SVM)—through the locally selective combination of parallel outlier ensembles (LSCP) strategy. The proposed workflow is applied to the stream sediment geochemical data pertaining to the Feizabad district, NE Iran, where anomaly scores from AE, VAE, AE-1SVM, and LSCPAE models are mapped to delineate spatial patterns favorable for gold-copper exploration. Performance appraisal through success rate curves indicates that the LSCPAE-derived anomaly map delivers a superior targeting performance than stand-alone autoencoder-backbone scenarios and soft voting technique (as a global ensemble strategy). The results suggest that the LSCPAE model can effectively reduce model-based uncertainty and provide lower-risk grounds for further metal exploration.

title: Historical fluxes and enrichment factors of trace elements in Lake Erie sediments
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Mahsa Tashakor, Anthony Chappaz
abstract: The Lake Erie watershed, the most densely populated of the Laurentian Great Lakes, has experienced significant trace element (TE) contamination over the past two centuries due to industrialization, agriculture, and urbanization. This study examines the sedimentary profiles of cadmium, chromium, copper, antimony, tungsten and zinc in a sediment core from the Central Basin of Lake Erie to reconstruct historical fluxes and enrichment factors for all these TEs in relation to anthropogenic impacts on the lake's watershed over the last century. Using 210Pb geochronology and 137Cs activity, sediment mass accumulation rates were determined, revealing that the Central Basin experienced the highest sediment loading among the Great Lakes during the second half of the 20th century. This coincides with increased TE inputs probably driven by industrial activities, fossil fuel combustion, and land-use changes. We identified four distinct periods of TE fluxes: (1) pre-1900, with minimal anthropogenic influence; (2) early to mid-1900s, characterized by rapid industrialization and a sharp rise in TE concentrations; (3) 1950s to 1990, marked by ongoing industrial and agricultural contamination; and (4) 1990–2014, when regulatory efforts contributed to a substantial decline in TE levels. Yet the levels of Sn and W in the top sediments remain concerning. Industrial processes were the primary source of TE contamination, and we present new evidence linking W contamination to historical tungsten production in the region. These findings underscore the lasting environmental impact of human activities on Lake Erie's sediments and emphasize the need for continued and improved monitoring and mitigation.

title: Environmental controls on methyl tert -butyl ether (MTBE) interphase redistribution in compacted low-permeability soils
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Meng Wang, Kangping Cui, Long Xu, Fusheng Zha, Qiao Wang, Jinkun Huang, Jingjing Liu
abstract: Methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a volatile and relatively water-soluble LNAPL compound, can partition into free, dissolved, vapor, and adsorbed states after release; however, quantitative evidence for how environmental controls drive redistribution in low-permeability soils remains limited. This study develops a sequential multi-phase NAPL extraction and analysis framework to quantify MTBE interphase distribution in compacted soils subjected to controlled thermal, hygroscopic, and compaction conditions. The method enables direct quantification of all four phase reservoirs, allowing phase-specific evaluation of environmental impacts on interphase redistribution. Across the full range of conditions tested, the vapor phase accounted for nearly all contaminant mass, whereas free phase accumulation was thermodynamically unfavorable under the tested conditions. Adsorbed and dissolved fractions acted as environmentally responsive reservoirs that were systematically displaced toward the vapor domain, indicating that vapor management governs mass reduction in compacted low-permeability matrices. Interphase redistribution showed strong directional responses, increasing temperature suppressed adsorbed and dissolved fractions through desorption, volatilization, and strengthened gas-water partitioning; rising relative humidity reduced sorption and expanded aqueous retention; and increasing dry density restricted pore water connectivity and favored gas-associated storage. Machine learning analysis confirmed temperature as the dominant driver of adsorbed phase behavior, while dissolved phase variability depended jointly on temperature, humidity, and dry density, revealing marked non-additive interactions. Molecular simulations corroborated weakened adsorption affinity, moisture-enhanced diffusion pathways, and confinement-regulated mobility, providing nanoscale evidence for desorption-controlled phase evolution. The combined experimental, modeling, and molecular results provide a mechanistic basis for designing MTBE remediation strategies in low-permeability source zones, especially those emphasizing vapor-phase removal and environmental regulation. Extension to other LNAPL compounds should consider compound-specific differences in volatility, aqueous solubility, and hydrophobicity.

title: Effect of clays on the formation kinetics of xonotlite
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): S. Mingione, F. Winnefeld, J. Mareels, P. Lopez, B. Lothenbach
abstract: Xonotlite (Ca6Si6O17(OH)2) formation is highly dependent on the reactivity of the raw materials used during hydrothermal synthesis. The raw materials, typically silica (SiO2) and lime (CaO), often contain secondary phases such as clay and Mg-bearing compounds which can further influence the synthesis of xonotlite. While small amounts of Mg stabilize xonotlite, the role of clay which may introduce Al, Fe and Si, remains poorly understood. This study investigates the impact of different quantities of clay during xonotlite synthesis. Xonotlite was obtained through hydrothermal synthesis carried out in an autoclave with stirring at 180 °C. The reaction kinetics was studied by stopping the synthesis at different time intervals and analyzing the obtained solids by XRD, TGA and FT-IR. Results indicate that the presence of aluminum from clay delays xonotlite formation and promotes instead the crystallization of (Al-)tobermorite, as confirmed by thermodynamic modelling. The effect increases with increasing quantities of clay or aluminum.

title: Cesium sorption onto clays from different deposits: experiments and modeling
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Irina R. Menshikova-Tonyan, Anna S. Semenkova, Ivan Mikheev, Andrey S. Toropov, Valentina S. Svitelman, Sergey V. Zakusin, Victoria V. Krupskaya, Anna Yu. Romanchuk, Stepan N. Kalmykov
abstract: Sorption properties of clays play a crucial role in the long-term safety of radioactive waste disposal. In this study, the sorption behavior of cesium on 11 different clay samples from various geological deposits was investigated under a broad range of experimental conditions, including varying cesium concentrations and pH levels. While smectite is the predominant mineral in all samples, sorption isotherms exhibit at least two types of sorption sites with different affinities. Experimental data were analyzed using previously published thermodynamic models and their modifications, with an automated heuristic optimization approach applied to adjust model parameters. The two-site ion-exchange model demonstrated a good fit to the experimental data, yet no clear correlation was observed between the number of exchange sites and sample properties such as mineral composition, specific surface area, cation exchange capacity determined by the Cu-trien method, or layer charge. Even highly smectitic bentonites required the introduction of highly selective sorption sites to adequately describe cesium sorption behavior. These findings highlight the complexity of cesium sorption mechanisms in clays and the necessity for further studies to refine predictive models for nuclear waste management applications.

title: Groundwater pH buffering in carbonate aquifers exposed to high-calcium ash backfill
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Madis Osjamets, Martin Liira, Riho Mõtlep
abstract: High-calcium ashes are known to produce highly alkaline leachates in laboratory settings, which has raised concerns regarding potential groundwater impacts when such ashes are used in mine backfills. In this study, we evaluated the effect of a high-calcium oil-shale ash backfill on groundwater pH in carbonate aquifers using an integrated approach combining geochemical modelling with a two-year field experiment. The backfill was injected into an abandoned mine drift in northeastern Estonia, and groundwater was monitored using continuous automatic sensors complemented by periodic sampling. Laboratory leaching tests confirmed the ash backfill has the potential to increase leachate pH values to above 12.5. However, geochemical modelling predicted rapid attenuation of alkalinity through buffering by bicarbonate in the carbonate aquifer, resulting in only minor pH changes restricted to the immediate vicinity of the backfill. Field observations corroborated the model predictions, showing no significant increase in pH in monitoring wells located 10 m from the backfill body. Instead of pH elevation, the most notable geochemical response in groundwater was an increase in sulphate concentrations. The results demonstrate that carbonate aquifers possess a strong natural buffering capacity that effectively mitigates the high alkalinity introduced by high-calcium ash backfill leachate. Although based on a single field site and therefore not directly generalisable to all carbonate mining settings, our results indicate that high-calcium industrial byproducts may be reused for mine reclamation with limited pH effects, while SO4 2− enrichment emerged as the dominant groundwater response. Future backfilling operations should account for the potential increase in dissolved SO4 2− in adjacent groundwater and incorporate sulphate-focused monitoring and mitigation measures into the design.

title: Hydrogeochemistry and dissolved organic matter as support tracers of recharge, flow paths, and discharge processes in hydrological systems
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): P.G. Schroeter, F. Bécher Quinodóz, E. Arbeloa, V. Lutri, M.C. Diéguez, P.E. García, S. Prámparo, Z. Fernández, M.T. Blarasin
abstract: This study evaluates the role of dissolved organic matter (DOM) as a tracer of hydrogeological processes in a fluvio–aeolian system of southern Córdoba, Argentina, integrating optical DOM properties with hydrochemistry. Groundwater from an unconfined aquifer, river water, and a shallow lagoon were analyzed to assess the relationships between water composition, DOM characteristics, and hydrological setting. Water mineralization is primarily controlled by water–sediment interactions, including silicate weathering, carbonate dissolution, and cation exchange. In contrast, DOM exhibits systematic variations related to source, degree of processing, and residence time. Groundwater contains moderately processed and variably humified DOM, reflecting transport within the aquifer under heterogeneous residence times, whereas river water is characterized by fresher, biologically influenced DOM associated with rapid renewal. Lagoon waters show highly humified and refractory DOM consistent with longer residence times and discharge conditions. Multivariate statistical analysis (PCA and HCA) reveals coherent patterns linking hydrochemical evolution and DOM composition, allowing differentiation of recharge, groundwater flow, and discharge sectors within the system. These results demonstrate that DOM provides complementary information to hydrochemistry and acts as a sensitive indicator of biogeochemical processing along flow paths in lowland environments.

title: Resolving barium matrix interferences in rare earth element analysis of seep barites: Implications for europium anomalies and fluid sources
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Tongtong Bai, Xudong Wang, Lanlan Zhang, Zhaoyang Wang, Zice Jia, Dong Feng
abstract: Barite is an important archive for tracing fluid-rock interactions in marine systems. However, accurate determination of rare earth elements (REEs) in barite by ICP-MS is strongly hindered by polyatomic ion interferences derived from high barium (Ba) matrix, particularly affecting europium (Eu) measurements. This analytical limitation has restricted the application of REE geochemistry in studies of barites from seeps (hereafter seep barites). Here we investigate barite-carbonate pairs from seeps in the Gulf of Mexico and develop a robust analytical protocol for reliable REE determination. The procedure integrates (1) selective removal of carbonate phases by mild acetic acid leaching, (2) complete digestion of the purified barite fraction using a mixed HNO3–HF–HClO4 acid system, and (3) efficient separation of Ba from REEs using DGA resin chromatography prior to ICP-MS analysis. Comparison of REE data before and after Ba removal demonstrates that extremely positive Eu anomalies observed in untreated samples (Eu/Eu∗ up to 122) may result from BaO+/BaOH+ interferences, highlighting the importance of careful matrix separation for reliable Eu determination. After matrix separation, the barite samples display moderate positive Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu∗ = 1.25–3.85), consistent negative Ce anomalies, and heavy REE-enriched patterns. These corrected REE signatures indicate precipitation from pore fluids interacting with surrounding sediments under suboxic to oxic conditions, rather than from high temperature hydrothermal fluids. Our results suggest that some previously reported extreme Eu anomalies in barite, particularly where Ba removal or interference correction was not documented, may warrant careful re-evaluation as potential analytical artifacts, and emphasize the necessity of matrix separation for reliable REE analysis in Ba-rich minerals.

title: Hydrochar-Amended bioreactors for passive treatment of acid mine drainage
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Aliching Marma, Natalie Kruse Daniels, Nigel Daniels
abstract: This study was based on a batch bioreactor experiment to investigate the effectiveness of using hydrochar as an amendment to promote the growth of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) in acid mine drainage (AMD) treatment, with a primary focus on Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn) and Cadmium (Cd) removal. This study evaluated the effect of hydrochar amendment in reducing bioreactors utilizing a mixture of organic substrates such as cow manure, maple woodchips, and cornflour acquired from a local granary, blended with hydrochar in triplicate, varying the amount of hydrochar: 0%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the total volume in the bioreactors. Bioreactors were operated for 98 days, and water quality parameters (pH, ORP, sulfate, total sulfur, metal concentration, COD) were analyzed periodically to determine the effect of variation in bioreactor substrate. Additionally, 16S rRNA sequencing was used to determine the presence of SRB in the bioreactors at the end of the tests. The results suggested that bioreactors without hydrochar content performed better in raising pH and removing metals, likely as metal sulfides, with removal percentages of Cu (89–100%), Zn (97–100%), Cd (100%), and sulfate (50–100%), following the removal trend of Cd > Zn > Cu. Statistical analysis results demonstrated no significant influence of hydrochar on metal removal (p > 0.05), but time had a significant effect (p < 0.05), indicating that removal effectiveness improved with time regardless of hydrochar quantity. The presence of SRB was confirmed in all bioreactors, although their relative abundance varied across treatments.

title: Can river chemistry in a karst region under human influences be used for catchment rock weathering estimation?
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Yan Liu, Y. Jun Xu, Xingxing Cao, Guangxi Long, Pan Wu, Zhangxing Liu
abstract: River chemistry is commonly used to estimate the weathering-induced carbon sink from rocks. However, the reliability of this approach in urbanized and agricultural watersheds remains unclear, particularly within fragile karst systems. This study examines the spatiotemporal variations in water chemistry of karst rivers across three catchments with different land use/land cover types in southwestern China. Our results reveal that rivers draining urban and agricultural catchments exhibit higher ionic loads of K+, Na+, and Cl− coupled with perturbed dissolved inorganic carbon dynamics, underscoring the influence of human activities on fluvial carbon fluxes. Especially, wastewater inputs substantially increase the concentrations of major ions (e.g., Na+, Cl−, NO3 −) and reduce ionic ratios such as Ca2+/Na+, Mg2+/Na+, and HCO3 −/Na+, shifting the river chemical signatures toward silicate weathering end-members, despite negligible actual silicate contribution, and the effect is modulated by rainfall. Such anthropogenic interference can bias assessments of natural weathering end-members and carbon source apportionment. Furthermore, nitrification in wastewater from urban and agricultural activities generates exogenous acids that participate in carbonate rock dissolution. Coupled with deviations in carbon source allocation, these processes affect the assessment of the rock weathering carbon sink. These findings highlight the need to account for anthropogenic inputs when evaluating karst carbon sink in urban and agricultural watersheds.

title: Microscopic and spectroscopic insights into uranium speciation and mobilization pathways associated with carnotite weathering in sediments
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Martina Wiejski-López, Gonzalo L. Bia, Eduardo D. Wannaz, Laura Borgnino
abstract: The speciation and mobility of uranium (U) in sediments are influenced by biogeochemical factors such as redox conditions, microbial activity, and the presence of organic matter (OM) and mineral phases. This study investigates the mechanisms controlling U behavior in sediments from the Punilla Valley (Córdoba, Argentina), using an integrated suite of analytical techniques including pXRF, XRD, SEM-EDS, XPS, and XAS. Field observations, together with geochemical and mineralogical analyses, indicate that U–V mineralization (i.e., carnotite) is heterogeneously distributed within reddish pelitic sediments and occurs as coatings on carbonates, micas, and plant roots. Grain-size and compositional data show U enrichment in fine sediment fractions, reflecting remobilization and secondary concentration under supergene conditions. Uranium redistribution appears to occur through the dissolution of carnotite, followed by interactions with plant roots and authigenic carbonates, as well as partial reduction to U(IV) mediated by Fe-bearing micas and dissolved organic matter. Synchrotron-based XAS analyses indicate that U(VI) is associated with calcite, whereas both U(IV) and U(VI) are associated with Fe-bearing micas, organic matter, and plant roots. These results demonstrate active U mobilization from carnotite, likely due to meteoric water infiltration, and highlight the important role of inorganic and organic sediment components as secondary sinks controlling U dynamics in sedimentary basins.

title: Crushed fines from basic rocks of the Serra Geral Group as the sole substrate for assessing bioweathering and nutrient release in elephant grass cultivation ( Cenchrus purpureus )
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Simone Zwirtes, Cassiana R.L. Michelin, Carlos Augusto Sommer, Andrea Sander, Carlos Augusto Posser Silveira
abstract: Tropical agriculture, generally developed on acid and leached soils, is highly dependent on soluble synthetic fertilizers (SSF), highlighting the need for local, economically viable, and more sustainable alternatives. Although intensive agriculture has increased global productivity through the use of these inputs, inadequate replacement of secondary nutrients and micronutrients has contributed to the progressive depletion of soil nutrients. In this context, agrogeology, particularly through the use of silicate agrominerals (SiA), emerges as a promising approach to assist developing countries in reducing their dependence on imported SSF by promoting the use of regional geological resources, such as crusher fines (CF) generated in the aggregate production chain for civil construction. This study evaluated nutrient release and plant uptake from CF derived from basic rocks of the Serra Geral Group (basalt and diabase), using an agronomic trial in which CF were used as the sole substrate, without soil addition. Elephant grass (cultivar BRS Kurumi) was grown with and without organic matter (OM) over 182 days in a greenhouse experiment arranged in a 2 × 2 factorial design, in addition to a control treatment.Reductions in Ca, Mg, K, and Si contents were observed in CF from plant treatments, more pronounced in the presence of OM, and were accompanied by substantial increases in nutrient uptake by elephant grass (up to 6.5-fold for basalt and 6-fold for diabase with OM) and in shoot dry matter (5.1 to 5.8-fold). The higher proportion of fine fractions in basalt CF favored nutrient release compared to diabase.The results indicate that bioweathering, driven by plant–OM interactions, intensified mineral dissolution and short-term release of K, Ca, Mg, Fe, and Si over months, supporting the use of CF from the studied lithologies as silicate agrominerals. The integration of SiA, plants, and OM increases biological activity, intensifies mineral dissolution in CF, and enhances agronomic efficiency, representing a viable strategy to reduce dependence on SSF in tropical agricultural systems.

title: Glucose promotes iron bi-directional redox transformation mediated by a single strain Comamonas sp. HJ-2
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Rong Peng, Rui Yang, Yuhang Liang, Haichuan Sun, Hui Liu
abstract: In anaerobic underground environments, the iron redox cycle is fundamentally driven by microbial activities, wherein the metabolic capacity of individual strains plays a pivotal role. This study investigated the regulatory mechanisms of three carbon sources — acetate, glucose, and lactate — on the iron redox cycle mediated by Comamonas sp. HJ-2 under neutral pH anaerobic conditions in Fe(III)–Fe(II) coexisting and Fe(III)-free systems. The results demonstrated that glucose enhanced Fe(II) bio-oxidation and Fe(III) bio-reduction by promoting energy metabolism. Glucose promoted sustained FMN accumulation, which is consistent with a potential contribution of the glycolysis-pentose phosphate pathway-riboflavin synthesis axis, which accumulated to a final concentration of approximately 0.40 μM. The accumulated FMN may function as an electron shuttle and thereby contribute to Fe(III) reduction. Mineralogical analyses further showed system-dependent effects of glucose. In ferrihydrite-containing systems, glucose inhibited the transformation of ferrihydrite toward more crystalline iron phases, whereas in ferrihydrite-free systems it shifted the product distribution toward a higher proportion of ferrihydrite and a lower proportion of lepidocrocite. Glucose also increased the content of surface-bound Fe(II) on minerals. In conclusion, glucose emerged as the most effective carbon source for optimizing the HJ-2-driven iron redox coupling process, likely due to its association with enhanced energy metabolism, FMN accumulation, and altered mineral phase transformation. This study elucidates the carbon source-dependent mechanisms governing microbial iron cycling in anaerobic environments and highlights the critical role of carbon source selection in enhancing iron biotransformation efficiency.

title: Fluid inclusion effects on boron isotope fractionation during halite crystallization
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Xuehai Ma, Huaide Cheng, Qingyu Hai, Wenhua Han, Haizhou Ma
abstract: Salt lakes are highly sensitive to climate fluctuations, making them valuable archives of past environmental changes. Among the various geochemical proxies used to reconstruct paleoclimate, the boron isotopic composition of evaporite minerals has emerged as a powerful tool for tracking brine salinity variations. Currently, carbonates in evaporites are the primary carriers for boron isotopic composition analysis due to their relatively high boron content. However, carbonates only exist during the initial stages of salt lake evaporation, occur in limited quantities, and are difficult to separate as single minerals, introducing significant uncertainties in reconstructing paleoclimate evolution. Given the presence of halite throughout nearly all stages of salt lake evolution, its boron isotopic record holds great potential for investigating global climate change. However, the exceptionally low partition coefficient of boron in halite has sparked ongoing debate regarding the incorporation mechanisms of boron in halite and the processes governing boron isotope fractionation between brine and halite. To address these uncertainties, this study examines the boron isotopic composition of halite precipitated from evaporation experiments using underground brine from the Wuyunbulake Salt Lake (Kumish Basin, Xinjiang) alongside experiments with pure sodium chloride solutions and simulated natural samples. Our results reveal that residual fluid trapped within halite plays a crucial role in boron isotope fractionation. When halite contains residual brine, the boron fractionation factor αhalite-brine approaches 1, indicating negligible fractionation. In contrast, when halite is free of residual brine, the fractionation factor falls below 1. These findings offer new insights into boron isotope behavior in evaporative systems and strengthen the application of halite as a paleoclimate proxy.

title: A Sobol-based ensemble framework for integrating multi-method geochemical anomaly detection
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Zohre Hoseinzade, Mobin Saremi, Moslem Fatehi, Amin Beiranvand Pour
abstract: In geochemical exploration, the geochemical anomalies identified by applying different methods within a study area often show considerable divergence and differences in terms of spatial distribution. Combining results from various methods across a region is challenging but crucial for producing reliable geochemical maps that help locate mineralized areas. To address this, the Sobol method was adopted to integrate the outputs of seven individual methods, including Isolation Forest (IF), Autoencoder (AE), Variational autoencoder (VAE), AE-one class support vector machine (AE1SVM), Deep One-Class Classification (Deep SVD), Cook's distance (CD), and Copula-based outlier detection (COPOD). To investigate the efficiency of the proposed approach, the Moalleman region located in NE Iran was selected as the real-case study. After that, the individual models were combined using a novel Sobol-based approach in which pseudo-random numbers were generated through quasi-Monte Carlo sampling. Then, a suitable statistical criterion was defined to identify and select the most stable weighted combination, and the final ensemble map was binarized using a percentile threshold. The identified anomalies through the Sobol approach show strong spatial correlation with known mineral occurrences (KMOs), major fault systems, and favorable lithological units. The proposed Sobol-based ensemble modeling framework effectively reduces model-related uncertainty and enhances the reliability of multi-element geochemical anomaly detection. Its demonstrated capacity to integrate diverse anomaly detection methods provides a robust decision-support tool for mineral exploration programs. The results underscore the approach's potential for delineating polymetallic mineralization targets and guiding future exploration in data-scarce or geologically complex regions.

title: Corrosion of borosilicate glass under unsaturated conditions: temperature-dependent evolution of secondary phases and surface alteration layer
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Yuhan Jiao, Xuan Wang, Wenxu Yin, Junjiang Zhu, Zhentao Zhang, Laurent Charlet, Qi Sun, Kaifeng Wang
abstract: Predicting the long-term performance of borosilicate glass for nuclear waste immobilization under unsaturated repository conditions requires a fundamental understanding of the evolution of the surface alteration layer (SAL) and secondary phases during corrosion. In this study, long-term static leaching experiments (up to 760 d, 50-90 °C) were conducted in pre-equilibrated solutions to investigate the corrosion behavior of borosilicate glass under unsaturated conditions. The evolution of aqueous chemistry, secondary phases, and the SAL was characterized using solution analysis combined with XRD, SEM, and STEM techniques. The results show that B release increases continuously with temperature and reaction time, whereas dissolved Si initially increases and subsequently exhibits slight variations associated with SAL evolution and secondary phase precipitation. XRD and SEM analyses reveal the progressive formation of secondary phases on the glass surface, including zeolites, analcime, calcium silicate, smectite, and barite. STEM-EDS observations further demonstrate that the SAL develops a multilayer structure consisting of a relatively dense inner alteration layer, a porous outer alteration region, and a compositional gradient region near the glass-SAL interface. These findings provide new insights into the coupled processes controlling borosilicate glass durability and improve the basis for performance assessment of vitrified nuclear waste in geological disposal environments.

title: Lead exposure in an urban population: isotopic evidence reveals contributions from dietary and inhalation pathways
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Shuhui Mu, Jin Wu, Jiaxin Ye, Jiemin Liu, Guangle Qiu, Xiaoyuan Lin, Xiangyang Bi
abstract: Environmental lead (Pb) exposure remains a persistent global public health concern. Dietary intake is widely recognized as the predominant exposure pathway, while the contribution of inhalation of Pb-containing particles to elevated blood lead levels (BLLs) has not been adequately explored. This study analyzed BLLs and lead isotopic fingerprints of residents in Guiyang, a typical city in Southwest China, and compared them with dietary samples, environmental media, and major lead emission sources to identify the primary sources and exposure pathways of lead in local residents. The results reveal strikingly elevated BLLs in both adults (57.8 μg/L) and children (44.0 μg/L), which are markedly higher than the U.S. national reference values (35 μg/L). A clear age-dependent trend was also observed, with BLLs generally increasing with age. The IsoSource model based on lead isotopic signatures revealed that lead in residents' blood primarily originated from lead-zinc smelting emissions (29.7%), historical vehicle emissions (29.5%), current traffic emissions (24.9%), and coal combustion emissions (15.9%). Furthermore, lead isotopic signatures showed that dietary intake and inhalation were the two major exposure pathways, with a binary mixing model estimating their relative contributions as 45.3% and 54.7%, respectively. This study demonstrates that lead isotope fingerprinting is a powerful tool for tracing environmental lead sources and human exposure routes, providing essential complementary insights to conventional exposure assessment models. These findings underscore the importance of integrated public health strategies that address both inhalation and dietary pathways to effectively mitigate lead exposure risks.

title: Disentangling the controls on fossil bone geochemistry using partial redundancy analysis
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Michał P. Surowski, Krzysztof Owocki, Bogusław Bagiński, David Chew, Foteini Drakou
abstract: Bones undergo severe diagenesis after burial, which leads to significant changes in their geochemistry during fossilization. There are many factors that influence the final composition of a fossilized bone, including the local burial conditions (further called the locality), cortical thickness, and skeletal part. In this study, we used partial redundancy analysis (pRDA) to investigate how these factors influence the geochemical composition of dinosaur bones from the Nemegt and Djadokhta Formations from the Gobi Desert (southern Mongolia). Four pRDA models were created to estimate the impact of these factors (locality, cortical thickness and skeletal part) on bone geochemistry. The results demonstrate that all of these factors exhibit statistically significant impact on bone geochemistry. The most significant factor is the locality. The elements most applicable for differentiating between localities are the medium to heavy rare earth elements (REE). Cortical thickness is a more significant factor than the skeletal part. Despite this, when cortical thickness and skeletal parts were analysed together, the thinnest bones and tibiae proved to have the largest impact on the model. Thinner bones are usually more enriched in REE and especially in heavy REE. This relationship becomes less clear with increasing thickness due to potential mechanical damage during diagenesis. The thicker bones tend to prefer Zn, Sr, Ba, and U over REE during diagenesis. The results also show that tibiae contain relatively more Ca than other bones, which may be related to their resistance to diagenetic processes.

title: A GIXAFS study of the Fe oxide precipitates on quartz surfaces
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Francesco Di Benedetto, Giordano Montegrossi, Francesco d’Acapito, Massimo Innocenti, Maurizio Romanelli
abstract: This study investigates the interaction between quartz surfaces and iron-bearing solutions through the precipitation of Fe oxide phases under controlled physicochemical conditions. Three differently oriented quartz crystal surfaces were exposed to buffered and unbuffered Fe(II) and Fe(III) solutions, and the resulting surface precipitates were analysed by GIXAFS spectroscopy. Due to the extremely low amount of deposited material, GIXAFS represented the only suitable technique capable of simultaneously probing iron oxidation state and local structural arrangement. The results demonstrate that Fe precipitates as nanoscale clusters rather than continuous surface coatings, independently of the crystallographic orientation of the quartz substrate. XANES, pre-edge, and EXAFS analyses reveal that the final Fe speciation frequently differs from the nominal redox state imposed by the starting solutions, with widespread occurrence of mixed Fe(II)–Fe(III) species and hematite-like local structures. Thermodynamic modelling performed with PHREEQC and Pourbaix diagrams successfully explains part of the observed behaviour, particularly the tendency toward Fe(III) oxide formation during evaporation and maturation of the precipitates. However, some experimental observations, including unexpected redox transformations, cannot be fully accounted for by bulk thermodynamics alone, suggesting an additional contribution from quartz surface effects or surface defects. These findings provide new insights into Fe oxide nucleation and redox evolution on silica surfaces, with potential implications for geochemical processes, environmental remediation, and the reactivity of crystalline silica in biological environments. In particular, the observed mixed-valence Fe precipitates may represent an additional contribution to the complex mechanistic framework linking crystalline silica exposure, persistent oxidative stress, and silica-related lung diseases.

title: Behaviour of 15 non-REE trace elements in Late Triassic vertebrate fossils: new insights into incorporation mechanisms and palaeoenvironmental proxy potentials
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Aishee Sanyal, Sanghamitra Ray
abstract: Trace elements, usually present in negligible amounts in natural systems and living organisms, often show elevated concentrations in fossil remains due to diagenetic uptake. Concentrations of 15 non-rare earth elements (REE) (Be, Sc, Co, Ga, Rb, Sr, Y, Zr, Nb, Cs, Ba, Hf, Pb, Th, and U) were analysed in fossil bones and associated host rocks from the Upper Triassic Tiki Formation, India to document for the first time measurable concentrations of elements such as Be and Ga. Overall trace element distribution patterns in the fossils and host rocks indicate comparable diagenetic conditions, though relatively higher concentrations in the former are interpreted to reflect enrichment primarily from diagenetic fluids rather than surrounding sediments. Enrichment factor (EF) calculations highlight significant enrichment of Sr, Y, Ba, and U in fossils (EF > 1), reflecting incorporation through Ca2+ substitution in apatite and adsorption into pore spaces during fluid-mediated diagenesis. In contrast, Be, Sc, Co, Ga, Rb, Zr, Nb, Cs, Hf, Pb, and Th yield EF values < 1, suggesting retention within detrital mineral phases. Several elements such as Co and Pb acted as redox indicators, with low Th/U ratios and modest U concentrations suggesting localised reducing microenvironments formed by organic matter decay. Principal Component Analysis further supports the dominating influence of fluid-mediated and lithogenic inputs on trace-element distribution in the Tiki bonebeds. Elevated Sr and Ba concentrations together with host rock Sr/Cu and Rb/Sr ratios suggest deposition under a seasonally variable semi-arid climatic regime. This study represents one of the first comprehensive investigations of non-REE trace elements in fossil bones, demonstrating their independent significance relative to REEs in reconstructing diagenetic palaeoenvironments, provenance, and palaeoclimatic conditions.

title: Effect of the temperature on the degradation of dissolved organic matter originated from different land use – an incubation experiment
description: Publication date: Available online 23 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Tibor Filep, Dóra Zacháry, Csilla Király, Gergely Jakab, Zoltán Szalai
abstract: The DOM cycle in terrestrial ecosystems is of particular interest in light of climate change, as DOM is one of the largest sources of available organic carbon for microorganisms and also has numerous other ecological functions. Therefore, this study investigated the effects of temperature on the composition, transformation, and decomposition of soil dissolved organic matter (DOM) originated from different land use areas (grassland, spruce, oak, arable) in a temperate region of Hungary using a 45-day laboratory incubation experiment. The chemical composition of DOM was evaluated using PARAFAC modelling, and the changes occurring during incubation were evaluated using two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy (2D COS). Significant differences were found in the chemical composition of DOM fractions in soils with different land uses. The PARAFAC model showed that although the relative amount of the low molecular weight compounds was similar in all four soils, the DOM fraction of arable soil also contained a large amount of the C2 component (high molecular weight, aromatic compounds). In contrast, the C5 component, identified as aromatic proteins/soluble microbial product (AP/SMP), was the smallest in the DOM fraction of arable soil. According to the 2D COS analysis, biogeochemical coupling was detected as negative correlations in the synchronous spectra, with correlations between the ∼320-258, 320-278, 385-258, and 350-280 nm regions at both temperatures indicating biogeochemical coupling between low molecular weight and higher molecular weight compounds. The decomposition of spruce soil DOM differed significantly for incubation at 25 and 35 °C: at the higher temperature, DOM shifted towards organic compounds with lower molecular weights than those observed at the lower temperature.

title: Mineralogy and geochemistry of beach sediments in the Gulf of Mexico and Mexican Pacific: Implication for provenance
description: Publication date: Available online 22 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Barbara Y. Pérez-Alvarado, John S. Armstrong-Altrin, Itzamna Z. Flores-Ocampo, Gloria D. Fernández-Guevara
abstract: This study assesses the geochemical characteristics and provenance of sediments from four beaches in the Gulf of Mexico (Barra Norte and Mocambo) and Mexican Pacific coast (Puerto Chiapas and Acapulco). Major, trace, and rare earth element (REE) concentrations with textural parameters were analysed to identify the sediment provenance and its associated geodynamic processes. Grain-size analysis revealed marked textural differences, with the domination of coarse-grained sediments in Acapulco, medium-grained sediments in Puerto Chiapas, and fine-grained sediments in Mocambo and Barra Norte beaches. Quartz dominates the mineral assemblages in all beaches, although Puerto Chiapas and Mocambo sediments contain higher proportions of mafic minerals, Acapulco and Barra Norte exhibit predominantly of felsic assemblages. Major-element geochemistry reveals strong compositional contrasts among three beaches. Puerto Chiapas sediments are enriched in Fe2O3, MgO, Cr, V, and Ni, indicating intermediate to mafic provenance, whereas Acapulco sediments exhibit high SiO2 contents (84.6-87.4 wt. %), consistent with felsic and compositionally mature sedimentary sources. In contrast, Barra Norte and Mocambo sediments are characterized by elevated CaO contents associated with carbonate input, as well as felsic and intermediate source rocks. The chondrite-normalized REE patterns show LREE enrichment in all samples. CIA and PIA values indicate overall low chemical weathering in the three beaches, with slightly higher alteration in Puerto Chiapas (CIA and PIA ≈ 57) compared to Acapulco, Mocambo, and Barra Norte beaches (CIA and PIA ≈ 41-49), reflecting the preservation of relatively unaltered feldspars. Elemental ratios like Al2O3/TiO2, Cr and Ni contents, and the size of the Eu anomaly suggest a felsic source for the Acapulco, and Barra Norte sediments, whereas Mocambo and Puerto Chiapas sediments reflect intermediate provenance with minor mafic contributions. The geoaccumulation index (Igeo) and enrichment factor (EF) indicate that the beach sediments are practically uncontaminated (Igeo < 0; EF < 2), except a moderate enrichment is observed for Co, Zn, and V in some Puerto Chiapas samples, collected near to the seaport. Principle Component Analysis (PCA) results indicate that major and trace elements variability is partly controlled by grain-size and heavy-minerals, while REE distributions are independent of grain size. The results of this study further indicate a diverse provenance, with contributions from mafic to intermediate source rocks for the Puerto Chiapas and Mocambo, and predominantly felsic source rocks for the Acapulco and Barra Norte beaches. These findings demonstrate that sediment geochemistry along the Mexican coastal areas is primarily controlled by source-rock lithology, regional tectonic setting, and hydrodynamic sorting.

title: Human activities as primary drivers of marine and inland groundwater salinization in the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system
description: Publication date: Available online 22 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Christian Narvaez-Montoya, Saugata Datta, Jürgen Mahlknecht, Miguel Rangel-Medina
abstract: Groundwater salinization is a major threat to coastal aquifers worldwide, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions subjected to intensive groundwater use. Understanding the behavior of individual coastal aquifer systems is therefore essential to support effective groundwater management. This study evaluates the spatiotemporal salinization patterns of the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system, located at the coastal margin of the Sonoran Desert, using 357 groundwater samples collected in 2009 and 2016, primarily from the most productive and shallow hydrogeological unit. Multivariate and hydrogeochemical analyses suggest that seawater intrusion is the dominant driver of total dissolved solids and chloride enrichment, strongly linked to long-term overexploitation. Inland, heterogeneous nitrate and sulfate distributions suggest the influence of anthropogenic inputs, including urban wastewater infiltration and irrigation return flow. Temporal comparisons indicate a decrease in nitrate concentrations, likely reflecting improved wastewater treatment, alongside a significant increase in sulfate, which may be associated with enhanced water-rock interaction processes previously linked to irrigation practices. 15% of samples exceed drinking water guideline limits, and 47% exhibit poor irrigation water quality, highlighting potential risks for human consumption, soil salinization, and agricultural productivity. This study provides one of the most comprehensive recent assessments of salinization processes in the Costa de Hermosillo aquifer system and emphasizes the need to reduce groundwater abstraction and strengthen wastewater and irrigation management to prevent further degradation of the aquifer. Because the interpretations are based on major ions and previous studies, future investigations incorporating more sensitive tracers are needed to better constrain the mechanisms responsible for groundwater salinization.

title: Investigating reservoir-scale heterogeneity in Li-enriched oil field brines of the Devonian Leduc and Nisku formations, Alberta Basin, Canada.
description: Publication date: Available online 10 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): M.R. Blake, K.L. Butler, L.A. Munk, D.F. Boutt, N. Morris, J. Kennedy, P. Saha, J. Serotta, H. Tompkins, G. Williams, A. Vengosh, J. Evaristo, D.E. Ibarra
abstract: Securing a North American lithium (Li) pipeline is pivotal to the clean energy transition and national security. The low-temperature sedimentary basin brines of the Devonian Alberta Basin, Canada are emerging as a promising unconventional domestic Li resource. This study integrates new and published geochemical and isotopic data from the Devonian Leduc and Nisku formation oil field brines to investigate brine origin, evolution, and Li enrichment mechanisms at the reservoir scale. Despite receiving considerably less attention than the Leduc Formation, the Nisku Formation brines display broadly similar geochemical and isotopic characteristics, suggesting common Li enrichment processes. Here we subdivide the Leduc and Nisku brines into geochemically distinct groups associated with four Devonian carbonate reef reservoirs (Redwater, Leduc, Chedderville, Bashaw) and evaluate the combined behavior of Li-B-radiogenic Sr-O-H isotope systems and major-element chemistry. Shallow reef complexes in hydraulic communication with surrounding formations contain low δ2H and δ18O values (avg. -78‰ and -3‰, respectively) and Li concentrations (avg. ∼32 mg/L), suggesting meteoric infiltration diluted the Li resource. Brines from structurally deeper reef complexes approaching the Rocky Mountain deformation front display high Li concentrations (avg. ∼67 mg/L), high δ18O (avg. 3.4‰) and radiogenic strontium values (avg. 0.70899), and low δ11B and δ7Li values (avg. 24‰ and 15‰, respectively), consistent with increased diagenetic interaction between brines and marine shales. Results suggest that Li enrichment and preservation are controlled by distinct but related processes, where shale-fluid interactions likely contributes Li to the basin brines while hydrologic isolation controls the preservation of elevated Li concentrations.

title: Source of Uranium (U) and Rare Earth Elements (REE) for Unconformity-Related U and REE Mineralization in the Athabasca Basin, Canada: Insights from Accessory Minerals in Sandstones
description: Publication date: Available online 25 June 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Goktug Harmanci, Guoxiang Chi, Jeremy Powell, Janina Czas, Victoria Tschirhart, Huimin Su, Yumeng Wang, Nahanni Danylczuk
abstract: The Athabasca Basin in Canada hosts the world’s largest and highest-grade unconformity-related uranium (URU) deposits, many of which are also enriched in rare earth elements (REE). There has been a long-lasting debate whether the U and REE were sourced from the basin or basement. This study investigates the potential contribution of detrital accessory minerals in the basin, particularly zircon and Ti-oxide (rutile), to U and REE mineralization. The textural and compositional characteristics of these detrital accessory minerals, as well as diagenetic minerals, including Ti-oxide (anatase), iron oxide/hydroxide (IOH) and aluminium phosphate sulfate (APS) minerals, were examined using multiple in-situ analytical methods. The results show that detrital zircon and rutile exhibit extensive dissolution and alteration features and large and irregular variations of U and REE concentrations within individual grains suggesting strong fluid-rock interactions. Large amounts of U and REE, especially heavy REE (HREE), were leached into the basinal brines, while some of them, especially light REE (LREE), were retained by diagenetic minerals. The resulting diagenetic basinal fluids are characterized by strong HREE enrichment, which broadly match the REE patterns of uraninite in the URU ores. Mass balance calculations suggest that 40 to 70 million tonnes of U and 80 to 330 million tonnes of REE, depending on the methods of calculation, could be leached from zircon and rutile. Despite the large variations and uncertainties, these estimations far exceed the amounts found in the URU deposits, implying significant potentials for further U and REE exploration. The results also highlight the vulnerability of zircon and rutile to hydrothermal alteration under certain conditions in sedimentary basins and its significance for large-scale U and REE mineralization.

title: In-situ Rb Sr dating of the crystalline basement beneath the Amadeus Basin, Australia: Implications for the radiogenic helium generation, migration and extreme 4 He accumulation
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Cecilia Loyola, Juraj Farkaš, Alan S. Collins, Jason Alexander Charlwood, Sarah E. Gilbert, Peter W. Haines
abstract: The crystalline basement beneath the Amadeus Basin (central Australia) hosts one of the world's highest recorded helium (He) concentrations (up to 9%) together with significant hydrogen (∼11%). The radiogenic 4He accumulated in the Neoproterozoic sedimentary succession of the Amadeus Basin was generated by alpha decay of U and Th in minerals of the underlying Proterozoic granitic basement. Initially retained within mineral lattices, He was later released through microfracturing. Constraining the timing of basement formation and subsequent fracturing is therefore critical to quantify long-term 4He production and migration. We applied in-situ RbSr dating using LA-ICP-MS/MS to primary K-rich igneous minerals (orthoclase, muscovite) and to secondary fine-grained micas and sericite hosted in microfractures from granitic basement beneath the Amadeus Basin, recovered from >2 km depth via the Jacko Bore 1 drillhole. Primary minerals yielded an age of 1100 ± 30 Ma, consistent with the timing of cooling following the Musgrave Orogeny. Secondary micas and sericite produced younger ages (642 ± 31 Ma to 517 ± 22 Ma), corresponding to deformation during the Ediacaran–Cambrian Petermann Orogeny. The concentrations of U and Th in basement rocks were determined by LA-ICP-MS and combined with Nuclear Emulsion Gel imaging to identify alpha-emitting and 4He producing domains. Integration of geochronology and trace element data enabled modelling of radiogenic 4He production from the Proterozoic to present. Modelled He isotope compositions agree with published 3He/4He ratios (0.031 Ra) from Jacko Bore 1 gas samples, demonstrating the utility of in-situ RbSr geochronology for evaluating radiogenic helium system.

title: Desert flashfloods recorded by Ba/Ca in benthic marine foraminifera ( Operculina ammonoides )
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Beverly Goodman-Tchernov, Shai Oron, Aleksey Sadekov, Gilad Antler, Timor Katz
abstract: River discharge proxies are essential for reconstructing terrestrial precipitation patterns and long-term climatic variability. Unfortunately, easily distinguishable direct proxies such as the presence of terrestrial muds in the sea are often missing after being winnowed and removed from the near-shore stratigraphy, or altered due to mixing and bioturbation. Barium, which is abundant in terrestrial sediments, is delivered to the sea via these runoff events in dissolved and particulate forms. Barium-to‑calcium (Ba/Ca) ratios in carbonate skeletons of marine organisms have proven to be an indicator of discharge events, though their application in benthic foraminifera remains under-studied. In particular, their capacity to resolve individual events in perennial systems where seasonal contrasts are often muted has not been explored. This study investigates Ba/Ca ratios in live benthic foraminifera (Operculina ammonoides) from the shallow marine shelf of the hyper-arid Gulf of Aqaba–Eilat. This setting provides a unique natural laboratory where ephemeral river (wadi) floods are rare and brief, potentially providing an isolated geochemical runoff signal. Our results demonstrate that foraminiferal chambers precipitated within five months of a flood event exhibit Ba/Ca ratios approximately double the background levels (∼8 versus ∼4 μmol/mol). Stable Mg/Ca ratios and historical water parameters negate temperature and pH as drivers of this enrichment. These findings suggest that Ba/Ca ratios in shallow-shelf benthic foraminifera are controlled by post-flood changes in the porewater, thereby successfully archiving desert flash floods. Consequently, and with added calibration this may provide a potent proxy for reconstructing high-resolution paleohydrology in arid coastal regions and offers a potential framework for developing paleo-environmental proxies in coastal settings generally.

title: The role of water in the generation of I-type barren granitic pegmatites
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): L.M. Fonseca Teixeira, M. Ackerson, O. Bachmann
abstract: Surging demand for critical elements highlights the need to understand how they concentrate in Earth's crust. Granitic pegmatites are key hosts of many rare metals, yet most pegmatites are unmineralized, prompting the question of what controls their fertility. Here, we challenge the traditional view of pegmatites as “residual granites” and propose that barren pegmatites share thermal histories with granitic parents. Using global geochemical datasets, we suggest that prior enrichment of the melt is unlikely to drive mineralization. Thermodynamic models and mineral chemistry from the I-type Bergell intrusion (Switzerland) show that silicic melts with high initial water content (i.e. H₂O > 6–8 wt% at the liquidus) trigger early fluid exsolution, forming chemically unfractionated pegmatites. Our Bergell data provide proof of concept, revealing pegmatites and granites with coeval cold crystallization at near and below the water-saturated haplogranitic solidus temperatures. We suggest that I-type granites are typically cold, wet, and ultimately host barren pegmatites, while drier S- and A-type granites host more mineralized pegmatites.

title: Citric acid redirects abiotic Mn(II) oxidation toward poorly crystalline hexagonal birnessite-like phases under circumneutral conditions
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Feng Zhang, Yanting Pan, Shuai Lan, Xiaoming Wang, Hui Yin, Zimeng Wang, Wenfeng Tan, Xionghan Feng
abstract: Abiotic oxidation of dissolved Mn(II) by O2 under circumneutral conditions commonly yields low-valence Mn oxides, whereas Mn(IV)-rich hexagonal birnessite is more often associated with microbial Mn(II) oxidation. Here we show that citric acid (CA) substantially alters this abiotic pathway by stabilizing filter-passing oxidized Mn species and redirecting mineral formation toward poorly crystalline hexagonal birnessite-like phase. Time-resolved kinetic experiments show that CA eliminates the initial lag phase and accelerates early accumulation of filter-passing oxidized Mn, but suppresses the later autocatalytic oxidation on Mn oxide surfaces. The reaction therefore evolves through three concentration-dependent stages: rapid accumulation of soluble/colloidal oxidized Mn, a plateau marked by dynamic balance between oxidation and decomposition of oxidized intermediates, and a later stage of inhibited heterogeneous Mn(II) oxidation and precipitation. Spectroscopic and microscopic analyses show that, in the absence of CA, oxidation produces a well-crystalline assemblage dominated by feitknechtite and triclinic birnessite, whereas low to moderate CA concentrations favor poorly crystalline hexagonal birnessite-like products and higher Mn average oxidation states. At higher CA concentrations, this trend weakens and lower-valence phases such as bixbyite and rhodochrosite become more abundant. These observations are consistent with a pathway in which CA stabilizes filter-passing oxidized Mn species, likely including Mn(III)-ligand species and colloidal Mn oxides, thereby redirecting precipitation toward hexagonal birnessite-like products. These results identify a ligand-mediated abiotic pathway by which organic complexation can control Mn redox kinetics, oxidized Mn mobility, and birnessite-like polytype selection under circumneutral conditions.

title: Evolution of reactive Fe minerals in paddy soils: constraints from Fe isotopes and spectroscopy
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Zhao Wang, Xiaodong Song, Huayong Wu, Zhen Zeng, Wei Li, Ganlin Zhang
abstract: Reactive Fe minerals are highly dynamic phases that play a critical role in regulating elemental cycling in soils, yet their formation and transformation under sustained redox oscillations in field settings remain poorly constrained. Here we investigate the evolution of reactive Fe oxides along a paddy soil chronosequence developed on Quaternary red clays by combining Fe stable isotope analysis, chemical extractions, EXAFS and 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy. Spectroscopic characterizations and extractions show that paddy cultivation redistributes Fe from crystalline Fe oxides into reactive Fe phases, increasing the reactive Fe fraction in both short- and long-term paddy surface horizons and in deep horizons of the long-term paddy profile. Across the long-term profile, bulk soils are systematically heavier than porewaters, yielding positive Δ56Fesolid–porewater offsets (0.45–0.98‰). These offsets are integrated contrasts between post-cycle solid Fe and mobile Fe under natural flood–drain cycling and are consistent with cumulative Fe mobilization and formation of reactive Fe phases. Operationally-defined porewater isotopes further suggest depth-dependent differences in Fe cycling, with potentially stronger colloid−/ligand-associated influence near the surface and relatively greater importance of aqueous Fe at depth. Comparison with published soil datasets shows an exploratory inverse correlation between Δ56Fesolid–porewater and reactive Fe abundance across systems. These results demonstrate that Fe isotope systematics, especially coupled with spectroscopic and extraction-based approaches, may provide a useful tracer of reactive Fe evolution in redox-dynamic soils.

title: Tellurium in volcanic and sedimentary systems – from outgassing to sequestration
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): N.B. Baumann, M. Regelous, T. Adatte, R.L. Rudnick, K. Chen, B. Schoene, G. Keller, N. Sharma, K.M. Haase
abstract: We describe a method for rapid and precise analysis of Te in geological materials using a conventional single-quadrupole ICP-MS coupled with a commercially available desolvating nebulizer. Unlike previous methods, this method allows analyses of other trace elements in the same sample solutions. A single step ion-exchange preconcentration extends the method to samples containing less than 0.5 ng/g of Te. Combining this method with new S-Cd-In-Tl data, we derive an updated estimate of the average Te concentration of the upper continental crust of 36.7 ± 1.6 ng/g based on the analyses of glacial diamictite composites. Analyses of basaltic lavas from the Deccan continental flood basalt province indicate that Te was not fractionated into sulfides but is largely degassed from lavas. This is supported by the high Te content of paleosol horizons interbedded with basaltic lava flows. Leaching experiments carried out on Early Eocene ashes and interbedded sediments, deposited during flood basalt volcanism in the North Atlantic, indicate that volcanic Te is tightly bound to the sediment matrix and silicate particulates and not readily mobilized after deposition. Our results confirm that Te concentrations in sedimentary rocks may be a useful proxy for past volcanism.

title: Dual-isotopic (δ 34 S and δ 18 O) evidence for net CO 2 release from the northwestern Himalayan catchments
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Rakesh Kumar Rout, Gyana Ranjan Tripathy, Satyabrata Das, Achyuth Venugopal, Nitish Kumar, Santosh Kumar Rai, Abhayanand Singh Maurya
abstract: The plausible linkage between Himalaya weathering and Cenozoic cooling often overlooks the CO2 release during sulfide oxidation (S-oxidation), which (unlike silicate weathering) has a positive climatic effect. In this study, dissolved sulfur (δ34SSO4) and oxygen (δ18OSO4) isotopic compositions for the Indus headwater basin have been investigated to evaluate the spatial distribution and rate of S-oxidation within the basin. The δ34SSO4 of these samples varies between −11 and 5‰ (n = 50), with lower values being observed for the mainstream samples (−4 ± 2‰; n = 12). Inverse modelling of major ions and δ34SSO4 data estimates the fraction of silicate-derived cations (0.12 ± 0.09) and sulfide-derived sulfates (f pyr ; 0.68 ± 0.28). The fraction of molecular O2 (f O2 ) involved in oxidation exhibits a negative correlation with the δ18OSO4/δ18OH2O ratio for a given f pyr value. Calculations involving δ18OSO4 and f pyr values show significant f O2 variations (<0.83), with higher values being observed for carbonate-dominated sub-basins. The CO2 uptake (1.4 × 105 mol/km2/yr) and release (4.4 × 105 mol/km2/yr) rates for the basin exceed the global riverine averages, and indicate a net CO2 release from the basin. The silicate weathering in the basin is mainly controlled by temperature, whereas intense S-oxidation is consistent with the basin lithology and extensive glacial cover. Modelling of present and compiled datasets for the entire basin confirms net CO2 release from the upper Indus basin and CO2 consumption in the floodplain regions. This underscores the dominant role of mountain erosion in driving pyrite oxidation in river basins, and hence, in the global carbon cycle.

title: Iron migration and isotope fractionation during estuarine sedimentary processes: Responses to monsoon intensity and climate events
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Jiarong Liu, Jinlong Ma, Guanhong Zhu, Kai Luo, Feng Ye, Fang Luo, Gangjian Wei
abstract: Iron (Fe) isotopes serve as a sensitive tracer of Fe biogeochemical cycles. However, their fractionation mechanisms during sedimentation and responses to the paleoenvironment remain inadequately constrained. Here, we analyze the Fe concentrations and isotopic compositions (δ56Fe) in bulk sediments and chemical extracts of a ∼ 2000-year-old sediment core from the Pearl River Estuary. Bulk sediments exhibit δ56Fe values (0.10–0.26‰) similar to those of riverine particulates, but with higher Fe/Al ratios. This indicates substantial Fe transformation during the sedimentary processes, which is not recorded by bulk δ56Fe values. Sequential extraction reveals that Fe (hydro) oxides (60.7–70.5% of total Fe) carry low δ56Fe values (0.06–0.17‰), and there is a positive correlation between δ56Fe and Fe/Mn, indicating the preferential incorporation of heavy isotopes during oxidation. The residue phase (19.9–30.0%) exhibits higher δ56Fe values (0.32–0.48‰), and a negative correlation between δ56Fe and chlorite suggests the preferential release of light isotopes during weathering. The organic phase is a minor Fe host (5.28–8.94%) with the lowest δ56Fe values (−0.20‰ to 0.02‰), indicating the preferential complexation of light Fe isotopes. Interestingly, the δ56Fe values of both the Fe (hydro) oxides and the residue phases respond to climatic events (e.g., Late Antique Little Ice Age, Medieval Warm Period, and Little Ice Age). Furthermore, the δ56Fe values of the Fe (hydro) oxides record redox conditions driven by climate change. The δ56Fe values of the residue phase exhibit consistent variation with the East Asian Winter Monsoon intensity proxy (foraminifera δ18O), indicating that the Fe isotopic compositions may record the monsoon intensity. Bulk δ56Fe integrates signals from multiple Fe pools, obscuring direct climatic interpretation. Therefore, the analysis of individual phases is necessary to provide new insights for reconstructing monsoon intensity and paleoclimate.

title: Local structure of trace elements in basaltic glass up to Earth's lower mantle pressures with implications for melt densification and element partitioning
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Georgii Kovalskii, Angelika D. Rosa, Olivier Mathon, Wolfgang Morgenroth, Guillaume Morard, Lea Pennacchioni, João Elias Figueiredo Soares Rodrigues, Max Wilke
abstract: This study investigates pressure-induced local structural changes of strontium (Sr2+) and yttrium (Y3+) in basaltic silicate glasses up to 130 GPa. To monitor local structural changes of these minor elements we conducted X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) experiments combined with the diamond anvil cell technique at room temperature. Both elements exhibit a two-stage reorganization of the local structure: in the first stage (up to ∼20 GPa), the average cation‑oxygen distance and cation's coordination number increase (for Sr from 6 to 8, for Y from 6 to 7); in the second stage, above 20–30 GPa, a progressive shortening of cation‑oxygen distance is observed, associated to the compression of coordination polyhedra. The two-stage compression scheme differs from that of network-forming cations, such as Si and Al.
