Those change from a corner-shared tetrahedral network to the closer packing of edge-sharing octahedra starting at 20–30 GPa. Due to the similarity of structural changes of Sr and Y to those around Ca and Mg, we conclude that their behavior reflects a universal trend for large cations in silicate melts during compression to conditions of the lower mantle. We used bond valence theory to validate the pressure-evolution of cation‑oxygen distances and compared them with data of crystalline counterparts. We expanded the bond valence theory by adding an additional pressure correction to ensure applicability at extreme pressure. The presented data improve our knowledge on local structural changes in basaltic melts across Earth's mantle pressures. We qualitatively assess the consequences for element partitioning between minerals and melt under core-mantle boundary conditions.

title: Titanium isotope fractionation in hydrous and oxidized large igneous provinces
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Sheng-Zhu Zhu, Xiao-Long Huang, Peng-Li He, Fan Yang, Jin-Long Ma, Yang Yu, Xin-Yue He, Le Zhang, Gang-Jian Wei
abstract: Titanium (Ti) isotopes have been utilized as tracers to determine the affinity of felsic rocks with either plumes or arcs, given that greater Ti isotope fractionation occurs in plume-related magmatism. However, it is essential to investigate whether this conclusion is universally applicable in hydrous and oxidized large igneous provinces (LIPs), as previous studies have primarily focused on water-poor and reduced plume-related rocks. This study presents the Ti isotope compositions of whole-rock samples and mineral separates from early Permian ultramafic–mafic–felsic rocks in the Wajilitag area of the hydrous and oxidized Tarim LIP (TLIP). The Wajilitag igneous rocks display Ti isotope fractionation (δ49Ti = −0.332‰ to +0.803‰), which is more pronounced than that in arc-related rocks, yet less significant compared to other plume-related rocks. Clinopyroxene, hornblende, biotite, and feldspar are slightly enriched in heavier Ti isotopes compared with their host rocks, whereas ilmenite and titanite are enriched in lighter Ti isotopes. Magnetite exhibits a wide range of Ti isotope compositions (δ49Ti = −0.120‰ to +2.247‰), with δ49Ti values increasing as TiO2 content decreases, heavier than equilibrium ilmenite. The mineral Ti isotopes indicate that primary magma TiO2, water contents (H2O), and oxygen fugacities (fO2) were the main factors controlling Ti isotope fractionation during magmatism. The primary magma of the TLIP has high TiO2 contents, as well as high H2O and fO2, which account for its medium Ti isotope fractionation between arc and plume magmatism. The interaction between plumes and subducted slab materials in the upper mantle is a key mechanism for the formation of hydrous and oxidized LIPs, resulting in deviations in Ti isotopes from typical plume magmas.

title: Heavy sulfur isotope of arc ultramafic cumulates revealed by S-rich apatite from the Dongwanzi intrusion, North China
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Huan Jennifer Chang, Mei-Fu Zhou, Wen-Jun Hu, Shengbiao Yang, Jian-Feng Gao
abstract: Arc magmas generally have higher sulfur (S) contents and higher δ34S values than mid-ocean ridge basalts. However, it remains debated whether the enrichment of S is due to crustal processes or mantle metasomatism. We present elemental and S-Sr isotopic compositions of apatite from the Early Permian Dongwanzi ultramafic intrusion, northern margin of the North China Craton. This arc intrusion is composed of clinopyroxenite and hornblendite based on textural relationships. Clinopyroxenites contains interstitial apatite and euhedral cumulus apatite. Interstitial apatite grains have high Cl (0.36–1.10 wt%), and Th (16.1–130 ppm), and La/Yb ratios (52.1–112), high 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.70370–0.70391), and low δ34SV-CDT values (−10.5 to +4.44 ‰), consistent with crystallization from late-stage trapped melts. In contrast, euhedral cumulus apatite grains have low Cl (0.23–0.71 wt%), high δ34SV-CDT values (∼ + 7.9 ‰), and La/Yb ratios (33.4–64.6), and low initial 87Sr/86Sr ratios (∼0.70337), indicative of growth from a relatively primitive magma. Compared to cumulus apatite in clinopyroxenites, cumulus apatite grains in hornblendites contain high F (1.45–2.69 wt%) and total REE + Y (1510–9830 ppm), and high 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.70333–0.70351), but slightly low Cl (0.01–0.50 wt%) and δ34SV-CDT (7.06 ‰ to 8.25 ‰), which were attributed to progressive fractional crystallization coupled with limited wall-rock contamination from clinopyroxenite to hornblendite. As a result, the consistently high δ34S values of cumulus apatite indicate that crustal contamination only caused a limited S isotope variation (∼1 ‰) during the formation of the Dongwanzi intrusion. Using S isotopic compositions of cumulus apatite in clinopyroxenite, the parental magma has δ34S values of ∼ + 7.9 ‰. Such high δ34S values are best explained by sub-arc mantle metasomatism rather than by crustal contamination. Collectively, our study highlights that S isotopic composition of apatite can be used to track the S isotope evolution and to constrain S sources in arc mafic-ultramafic cumulates.

title: Coupled δ 18 O–δ 13 C covariation and depositional architecture diagnose hydrologic state in barrage-cascade tufa systems
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Khalil Azennoud, Yassine Ait Brahim, Franziska Lechleitner, Hai Cheng, Radouan El Bamiki, Abdennasser Baali, Mohammed Hssaisoune, Hicham El Asmi, Xiaodong Jiang, Heather Stoll
abstract: Tufa carbonates are widely distributed terrestrial archives, yet lamina-scale geochemistry and system-scale depositional architecture have traditionally been studied in isolation: the former as a climate proxy, the latter as a geomorphic question. Here we show that these two scales are coupled, and that their coupling provides a direct diagnostic of hydrologic state in barrage-cascade systems. Combining U-Th chronology, petrography, stable isotope geochemistry, and geomorphic observations from a groundwater-fed barrage-cascade system in northern Morocco, we resolve six independent depositional intervals from the Middle Pleistocene to the Late Holocene, each preserving laminated microbialites and most retaining well-developed buttress architectures. Across these intervals, the magnitude of microbialite δ18Oc–δ13Cc covariation tracks upstream pool confinement and water residence time, defining a continuum from hydrologically open to evaporatively restricted configurations. These geochemical states correspond systematically to differences in buttress size, relief, and stacking geometry, providing an independent architectural validation of the proxy. This dual-scale approach helps reduce the ambiguity of single-proxy interpretations in continental carbonate archives. Comparison with modeled precipitation and regional context suggests that hydrologic state is better explained by temperature-modulated carbonate productivity and barrage-growth feedbacks than precipitation-driven discharge alone. These results establish a process-based framework that resolves barrage-cascade tufa systems as integrated geochemical–architectural archives of Earth-surface hydrology.

title: New evidence for normal seawater dolomitization in the middle Permian
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Heting Gao, Jiakai Hou, Manfei Chen, Xi Li, Sheng Li, Jianing Wang, Guangyou Zhu
abstract: Whether normal seawater drives platform-scale dolomitization remains debated. The viability of conventional evaporative brine or hydrothermal models is questioned by new studies favoring normal or slightly modified seawater. This study presents an example from the Middle Permian Maokou Formation (Sichuan, China) while, some evidence suggest dolomite formed in association with evaporative or hydrothermal fluid, re-evaluation from new data sets suggest dolomitization by normal seawater. The Maokou Formation comprises three main petrographic types of dolomites (micro-, fine-, and medium-coarse crystalline), that lack evaporites, exhibit dull-red cathodoluminescence, near-ideal cation ordering (0.56–1.0), and are cross-cut by fitted fabric microstylolites, which was interpreted to have formed penecontemporaneously into the early burial diagenetic realm. Their relatively constant δ13C values (2.79–6.03‰), 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.70737–0.70768), negative Ce and no positive Eu anomalies match coeval seawater. Negative δ18O values and few samples with Mn/Sr ratios <2 reflect closed-system recrystallization. Restored primary temperatures (27.9°C to 56.3°C), corrected for solid-state reordering via forward Δ47 modeling, and δ18Ofluid values (−0.8 to +1.2‰ VSMOW) are within the normal seawater range. U-Pb dating gives ages of 254.2±3.9 Ma (D1), 250.7±5.1 Ma (D2), and 249.2±2.5 Ma (D3), indistinguishable from each other but significantly older than saddle dolomite (244.8±1.5 Ma). This analysis strongly suggests that the dolomite was replaced by Permian normal seawater and subsequently experienced closed-system recrystallization during burial stage. The vertical variation of C-O isotopes and elemental data correlate with high-frequency sea-level fluctuations, confirming sea-level-driven sustained seawater circulation and cyclic reflux recharge as the driving mechanism for dolomitization. This study has revealed that the normal-seawater dolomitization could also proceed in a shallow-water platform, providing insights for coeval reservoirs in the Yangtze Block and similar settings worldwide.

title: Biomass-burning smoke water-soluble organic matter reverses ferrihydrite colloid-inhibited mobility of Cd 2+ through saturated porous media via interface fractionation and selective binding
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Bin Wang, Nan Yang, Kunyu Wen, ZhiWei Chen, Boyun Zheng, Yanbin Ma, Li Zhang, Zhichong Qi
abstract: Biomass burning events release large amounts of pyrogenic dissolved organic matter (BBS-WSOM) into terrestrial ecosystems, where it interacts with iron oxides and trace metals. However, how the molecular heterogeneity of BBS-WSOM governs colloid-facilitated metal transport remains poorly constrained. Here, we combined column transport experiments with multispectral analysis to elucidate how BBS-WSOM modulates the co-mobility of ferrihydrite (Fh) colloids and Cd2+ in saturated porous media. We found that humic-like components with higher aromaticity and hydrophobicity were preferentially retained on sand surfaces, whereas protein-like components remained largely in the aqueous phase. Protein-like components were the primary agents responsible for Cd2+ complexation, thus facilitating Cd2+ mobility. Although Fh colloids alone suppressed Cd2+ transport, the presence of BBS-WSOM not only neutralized this suppression but further enhanced Cd2+ mobility in the ternary system (Cd2+ + Fh + WSOMs) compared to the binary system (Cd2+ + WSOMs). This counterintuitive enhancement arose from molecular fractionation at the Fh-water interface: Fh preferentially adsorbed humic-like components, enriching the aqueous phase with protein-like components that bound Cd2+ more effectively. These findings reveal that the trade-off between humic-like and protein-like components within pyrogenic DOM critically controls the direction and magnitude of colloid-mediated metal transport. Our study provides mechanistic insights into how wildfire-derived or burning-derived DOM alters subsurface Cd geochemistry, with implications for the coupled cycling of carbon, iron, and trace metals in fire-impacted terrestrial environments.

title: Mechanisms of iodate reduction by sediment siderite and its contribution to iodide enrichment in groundwater
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Shilin Zhao, Junxia Li, Yinchun Su, Daolian Deng, Wenyi Zhang, Qian Liao, Xianjun Xie, Yanxin Wang
abstract: The enrichment of iodine in groundwater poses serious health risks worldwide, yet the abiotic mechanisms driving iodine mobilization in anoxic aquifers remain incompletely understood. Siderite, a ubiquitous Fe(II)-bearing mineral in reducing environments, may play an important role in iodine speciation; however, its reactivity toward iodine species transformation remains largely unexplored. Herein, we investigated the reduction of iodate (IO3 −) by siderite and the subsequent mechanisms of iodine release using both synthetic minerals and natural sediments from the Hetao Basin with varying Fe(II)‑carbonate contents. Batch kinetic experiments demonstrated that structural Fe(II) in siderite rapidly reduced IO3 − to highly mobile iodide (I−) within 20 min. The reduction kinetics and mineral transformation pathways were strongly controlled by the initial Fe(II)siderite:IO3 − molar ratio: excess IO3 − promoted the oxidation of siderite to goethite (FeOOH), whereas excess Fe(II)siderite favored the formation of magnetite (Fe3O4). Incubation experiments with natural sediments further revealed the critical role of intrinsic Fe(II)‑carbonate content in determining the IO3 − reduction capacity of sediments. Deep sediments enriched in siderite rapidly reduced IO3 − to I−, whereas shallow, siderite-depleted sediments exhibited negligible reduction. In addition, amendment of these shallow sediments with exogenous siderite induced the release of intrinsic sediment-bound iodine into the aqueous phase as I−. Overall, this study highlights the importance of siderite in iodine species transformation and provides new mechanistic insights into iodine enrichment in reducing groundwater systems.

title: Carboxyl-Fe and phosphonate-Fe interactions control the redistribution of organic phosphate during ferrihydrite transformation
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Xiaofan Pan, Zhenzhen Zhao, Xin Huang, Ning Deng
abstract: Transformation of poorly crystalline ferrihydrite (Fh) into crystalline phases is a critical process controlling mineral stability and element cycling. However, the molecular mechanisms by which organic phosphorus (OP) compounds influence Fh transformation remain unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of three representative OPs with distinct functional groups—triethyl phosphate (TEP), 2-phosphonobutane-1,2,4-tricarboxylic acid (PBTC), and 1-hydroxyethylidene-1,1-diphosphonic acid (HEDP)—on Fh transformation. Results showed that TEP, containing only a phosphate group, showed negligible adsorption and minimal effect, whereas PBTC and HEDP strongly bound to Fh via carboxyl and phosphonate groups, respectively, significantly slowing transformation. Synchrotron-based FTIR indicated that PBTC predominantly bound to Fh through strong Fe-carboxyl interactions, while HEDP mainly formed Fe-phosphonate complexes on Fh surfaces. The stronger carboxyl-mediated surface complexation of PBTC resulted in persistent association with the solid phase throughout the transformation process. In contrast, HEDP exhibited dynamic redistribution during Fh transformation, characterized by initial release followed by re-immobilization. Geochemical modeling showed that the complexation of HEDP with aqueous Fe3+ favored the incorporation of Fe3+-HEDP complexes into growing secondary mineral phases, leading to HEDP refixation. These results reveal that OP functional groups govern both Fe mineral stability and OPs fate, providing mechanistic insights into organic ligand-mediated Fe mineral evolution.

title: Subseafloor processes in ultramafic-influenced volcanic-hosted hydrothermal systems: An insight from the Gnitahei massive sulfide mineralization, Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridges
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Sabina Strmić Palinkaš, Marie Wold, Rolf Birger Pedersen, Håvard Hallås Stubseid, Fredrik Sahlström, Lahaye Yann, Leif-Erik Rydland Pedersen, Jorge E. Spangenberg
abstract: The extinct Gnitahei seafloor massive sulfide (SMS) deposit was discovered in 2019 on the ultraslow spreading Mohns Ridge (Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridge System, 72.8°N, 3.81°E, 3022–2760 mbsl). It provides a unique opportunity to study subseafloor hydrothermal processes without drilling, as tectonic uplift and ongoing mass wasting expose the deeper parts of the hydrothermal system. The deposit is hosted by hydrothermally altered basalts within the footwall of a NE–SW striking normal fault, in proximity to the active Fåvne Vent Field. Driven by extensional tectonics and facilitated by the thin oceanic crust along the ultraslow-spreading Mohns Ridge, hydrothermal circulation likely extends deep into the serpentinized upper mantle. Hydrothermal alteration exhibits vertical zonation. Chloritization accompanied by remobilization of silica, LILEs, and REEs dominate the deeper parts of the system. In contrast, silicification associated with an enrichment in LILEs and REEs characterizes the upper part of the Gnitahei SMS deposit. The paleosurface is clearly marked by a layer of red jasper. The sulfide mineralization is dominated by pyrite and marcasite, with euhedral pyrite prevailing in deeper zones and colloform pyrite being more abundant near the paleosurface. Native gold occurs mostly as inclusions in pyrite. Trace-element data obtained from pyrite, including elevated Ni and Co concentrations and a high Au/Ag ratios, are consistent with fluid interaction with underlying ultramafic rocks. Sulfur isotope composition of pyrite reveals a strong 34S enrichment (bulk δ34SVCDT = 11.1–15.9‰; in-situ δ34SVCDT = 10.8–17.3‰), indicating a significant contribution of reduced seawater sulfate, which constitutes ∼50% of the total sulfur according to a two-component mixing model. The high influx of reduced sulfate is attributed to reducing conditions driven by serpentinization of ultramafic lithologies. Under these conditions, seawater sulfate can be reduced prior to anhydrite deposition, allowing isotopically heavy sulfur to infiltrate the hydrothermal system. Depth-dependent decreases in δ34S values likely reflect greater contributions of reduced seawater sulfate in shallower zones and/or enhanced fractionation at lower temperatures.

title: A first principles critique of the back calculation method: Understanding and assessing the alteration of atmospheric gases trapped in ancient fluid inclusions
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Justin G. Park, Morgan F. Schaller
abstract: The extraction of atmospheric gases from fluid inclusions has emerged as an extremely promising approach for directly constraining the composition of Earth's ancient atmosphere. However, the veracity of data obtained from these inclusions critically depends on how well one can account for the effects of physical chemistry and post-depositional alteration. The Back Calculation Method (BCM) attempts to discern unaltered atmospheric compositions from variably modified inclusion gases, primarily O2 and CO2, but fails to account for the effects of gas solubility. Moreover, the method lacks an explicit mathematical formulation, and limited articulation of its implicit assumptions and limitations has introduced ambiguity in the interpretation of reconstructed atmospheric compositions. From first principles, we derive the formulation underlying the BCM and use it to formally evaluate the limitations of the method. We expand this framework to include the variable effects of gas solubility and incorporate recent techniques to partition inclusion volatiles trapped in the gaseous and aqueous phases. Re-examination of modern inclusion gases reveals evidence of heterogeneous entrapment of gas and brine, as well as post-entrapment alteration of O2 and CO2, with distinct stoichiometric relationships observed between samples. These observations violate the core assumptions of the BCM, suggesting the technique has been applied inappropriately to ancient samples and that their interpreted atmospheric compositions require thorough reevaluation. We conclude by demonstrating carbon isotope measurements of inclusion CO2 can be incorporated to assess the extent of gas alteration and provide an outline for future work intending to reconstruct atmospheric compositions from these inclusions.

title: The influence of coral nutritional status on its skeletal carbon isotope fractionation and δ 13 C values
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Shendong Xu, Jie Gao, Zhinan Zhang, Kefu Yu, Yiqi Zhao, Biao Chen
abstract: Almost all scleractinian corals are mixotrophic organisms and their skeleton stable carbon isotopes (δ13Cs) were widely used for environmental and climatic records. However, the interpretation of coral δ13Cs is still complicated and controversial. In particular, the impact of nutritional status (i.e. relative intensity of autotrophic photosynthetic and heterotrophic predation) and related photosynthesis/respiration ratio (P/R) on the coral δ13Cs was not well understood. In this study, coral samples (Favia palauensis) were collected from three coral reefs of different latitudes in the South China Sea (SCS), Weizhou (∼21°N), Xisha (∼16°N) and Nansha (∼9°N) Islands. Different types of physiological and geochemical parameters, including symbiodiniaceae (i.e. symbiotic zooxanthellae) density, tissue biomass, δ13C of zooxanthellae (δ13Cz), host tissue (δ13Ch), skeleton (δ13Cs) were measured. We also collected environmental and ambient seawater parameters, including ‌Sea Surface Temperature, ‌Sea Surface Salinity, Photosynthetically Active Radiation, Rainfall and Seawater δ18O and δ13CDIC. The P/R ratio was calculated based on these parameters. We conducted this study to analysis the spatial distribution characteristics of coral nutritional status, and then explore the potential impacts of coral's nutritional status on their P/R ratios and skeletal δ13C in the SCS. Our results show that corals have relatively high autotrophic photosynthesis intensity and P/R ratios in Weizhou reef. On the contrary, corals in relatively low latitude Xisha and Nansha reefs are more dependent on heterotrophic predation and have lower P/R ratios. Correspondingly, coral δ13Cs is more positive in Weizhou than that in Xisha and Nansha. In particular, there are high correlations between δ13Cs and δ13Cz of corals in Weizhou, but not in Xisha and Nansha. Overall, the corals in all three reef areas showed a positive correlation between P/R and δ13Cs values (p<0.05). These results indicate that different coral nutritional status and related P/R have different effects on δ13Cs. This maybe one of the important factors leading to the spatial variation of skeletal δ13C in the SCS. We suggest that special attention should be paid to this case when using coral skeletal δ13C for paleoclimate reconstruction, especially when conducting comparative analysis of climate in different regions of the world based on coral skeletal δ13C.

title: Selenium isotope fractionation during pyrite oxidation and acid mine drainage formation: Combined field and experimental constraints
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): José Luis Guerrero, Stephan König, Rafael Pérez-López, Carolina Rosca, Carlos J. Garrido, José Miguel Nieto
abstract: Selenium (Se) is a redox-sensitive chalcophile element whose isotopes provide valuable constraints on oxidative processes at the Earth's surface. This study presents a combined field and experimental investigation of Se isotope fractionation (δ82/76Se) during pyrite (FeS2) oxidation under acid mine drainage (AMD) conditions, integrating field observations, column experiments, geochemical modeling, and mineralogical characterization. Field leachates from the Tharsis mining district (Iberian Pyrite Belt) exhibit extreme acidity (pH ≈ 1–2), elevated Eh values (> 600 mV) consistent with ongoing pyrite oxidation, elevated Se concentrations (up to 1.3 × 103 μg/L), and significant isotopic variability, with δ82/76Se values ranging from −4.1 ± 0.53‰ at the waste dump outflow to +1.19 ± 0.07‰ in a receiving pond. Column experiments reproduce and extend this trend, with early leachates showing slightly negative values (≈ −1‰) attributed to rapid flushing of isotopically light, labile Se pools, followed by a progressive increase to a stable plateau of +12 ± 1‰. Speciation modeling indicates that dissolved Se occurs predominantly as Se(IV), excluding redox partitioning between aqueous oxidation states as the main control on Se isotope fractionation. Rayleigh-type calculations show that adsorption alone cannot account for the observed >10‰ isotopic shift. Instead, the isotopic evolution reflects open-system processes involving continuous Se release from sulfide oxidation, surface interactions with Fe(III) phases, and localized redox transformations. The agreement between field and experimental trends defines a coherent framework for Se isotope behavior during sulfide weathering. These results demonstrate the high mobility of Se under AMD conditions and highlight the potential of δ82/76Se as a tracer of oxidative release and attenuation processes in natural and mining-impacted environments.

title: Experimental insights into chlorine and bromine isotope fractionation during evaporation and mineral precipitation in multicomponent brines
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Yon-Gyung Ryuh, Randy L. Stotler, Shaun K. Frape
abstract: Chloride and bromide are commonly used as tracers in various aqueous geochemistry fields as a result of their well-known conservative behaviors. However, the behavior of their stable isotopes during evaporation and mineral precipitation remains poorly constrained. This study investigates how chlorine and bromine isotopes fractionate during evaporation of seawater. Synthetic seawater was evaporated under controlled conditions, and the isotopic compositions of chlorine and bromine were measured in brine, solids, and gas phase throughout sequential mineral precipitation. The results show that chlorine and bromine isotopes respond to distinct processes that vary with mineralogy and evaporation stage. Bromine isotopes fractionate during early calcium-phase precipitation through lattice substitution into aragonite, but mineralogical shifts with increasing salinity result in Br incorporation into precipitates through physical brine entrapment limiting further fractionation. In contrast, during halite precipitation, chlorine isotopes exhibit systematic lattice-controlled fractionation behavior broadly consistent with near-equilibrium fractionation, while bromine isotopes exhibit more complex behavior. Bromine isotope evolution during this stage is interpreted to reflect a combination of inefficient lattice incorporation and selective loss of isotopically light bromine to the gas phase. These findings suggest that chlorine and bromine isotopes may respond differently due to mineral-specific and process-dependent mechanisms, highlighting processes that may influence halogen isotope signatures in natural evaporite and saline systems.

title: Organic carbon enrichment in carbonate concretions of the Rincon Shale, California, USA: Implications for organic matter preservation in concretions
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Sean J. Loyd, Melonie D. Reyes, Natasha Kuhn, Adam D. Woods, Allyson M. Fry-Petit, Ashley E. Godoy
abstract: Carbonate concretions often form as a byproduct of the degradation of organic matter and/or methane in sediments. Despite these origins, concretions may subsequently protect sedimentary organic matter from degradation after precipitation. The degree to which concretions preferentially preserve organic material is poorly characterized, as are the degradation processes/environments against which they are most effective. Here, concretions and host sediment of the Miocene Rincon Shale are compared geochemically to assess the preservation capacity of concretions. Magnesian calcite and dolomite concretions of the Rincon Shale express carbonate carbon isotope compositions (δ13Ccarb) consistent with formation via microbial oxidative reactions and methanogenesis, respectively. Host shale laminae deflection around the concretions and high cement contents suggest that concretions formed at relatively shallow sediment depths during early diagenesis. Concretions contain higher concentrations of total carbonate-free organic carbon (TOCCF), iron, and manganese than neighboring host shales. When considered collectively, host shale and concretion Oxygen Index (OI) data correlate with TOCCF contents, consistent with oxidative weathering. However, most concretions express lower OI compositions than neighboring shales. Combined lower OI and higher TOCCF, iron, and manganese in concretions suggest that concretions protect organic matter and metal sulfides from oxidative weathering in outcrop. This preferential preservation indicates that concretions 1) represent a better target for outcrop-based study using organic archives and 2) may delay the weathering of sedimentary organic matter and impact carbon cycling.

title: 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology, Sr Nd isotopes and melting conditions of the Dahongshan alkaline basalts: Constraints on mantle modification beneath the northern Yangtze Craton
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Yue Song, Xuan-Ce Wang, Simon A. Wilde, Xiang-Zhong Li, Chong-Jin Pang, Si-Yu Hu, Yang Luo, Jia-Xu Tang, Si-Zhe Fu
abstract: We present new groundmass 40Ar/39Ar ages, whole-rock major and trace element data, SrNd isotopic compositions, and P–T estimates for the Dahongshan alkaline basalts in the northern Yangtze Craton, China. Integrating these data with regional records demonstrates that Late Cretaceous mafic magmatism in the northern Yangtze Craton records a transition from subduction-modified lithospheric mantle to increasingly asthenosphere-influenced melting. Four representative samples yield concordant plateau-like weighted mean 40Ar/39Ar ages of 83.4–84.1 Ma (2σ), constraining the eruption of Dahongshan magmas to ca. 84 Ma. The basalts have intraplate, OIB-like trace element patterns, elevated LREE/HREE ratios, and a narrow range of SrNd isotopic compositions ((87Sr/86Sr)ᵢ = 0.704358–0.704800; εNd(t) = −0.80 to +1.35), indicating derivation from a moderately enriched, pyroxenite-influenced mantle source with a mafic component and only limited syn-ascent crustal assimilation. Low Ce/Pb and Nb/U ratios, together with pronounced positive Pb anomalies, are interpreted as source-inherited features rather than evidence for significant crustal assimilation. Primary melt reconstruction and complementary whole-rock major element modelling yield low- to moderate-pressure P–T estimates of 1.4–2.1 GPa and 1252–1356 °C, interpreted to record final melt–mantle equilibration or segregation during ascent rather than the depth of melt initiation. In contrast, REE systematics indicate a garnet-influenced melting signal, suggesting that melt generation was initiated deeper, probably near the garnet–spinel transition, before undergoing re-equilibration at shallower lithospheric levels. Regional comparisons support a temporal shift from Early Cretaceous lithosphere-derived arc-like magmatism to Late Cretaceous increasingly asthenosphere-influenced volcanism, followed by Cenozoic deeper-sourced alkaline basalts consistent with garnet-facies melting during post-extension thermal adjustment.

title: Mineralogical and geochemical fingerprints for quantifying modern glacial and paleo-weathering sediments in the Amundsen Sea, West Antarctica
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Hebin Shao, Yong Yu, Shouye Yang, Jianfeng He, Yulong Guo, Di Cai, Guangfu Luo, Yingchun Cui, Li Wu, Hao Zhang
abstract: Silicate weathering regulates Earth's carbon cycle and climate, yet paleo-weathering products in Antarctic marine sediments obscure primary weathering signatures, a major challenge in polar carbon cycle studies. The Amundsen Sea, a key marginal sea of West Antarctica, contains abundant paleo-weathering products (i.e. materials sourced from Pre-Oligocene sedimentary rocks and reworked into modern sediments), but quantitative constraints on their contributions to sediment provenance remain lacking. We analyzed 12 clay-sized surface sediment samples from the western Amundsen Sea via mineralogical, elemental geochemical, and Sr-Nd-Li-Mg isotopic analyses. Results show clear spatial heterogeneity: samples from the east side of this area show higher kaolinite, chemical index of alteration (CIA) and δ26Mg, along with lower δ7Li. The proxies reveal intense chemical weathering of the source bedrock in the pre-glacial warm interval. By contrast, samples from the west side are dominated by chlorite and illite, with lower CIA and δ26Mg but higher δ7Li, reflecting limited chemical weathering of the source bedrock. Mineralogical and geochemical indices effectively distinguish three sediment provenance endmembers (Post-Oligocene igneous rocks, Pre-Oligocene igneous rocks, and Pre-Oligocene sedimentary rocks), and a mass balance model based on εNd and δ26Mg isotopes was established to quantify their relative contributions to shelf sediment provenance. This model shows that paleo-weathering sediments account for up to 60% of clay-sized sediments from the eastern side of the western Amundsen Sea, with contributions of 30%–50% in coastal areas via ocean current transport, while clay-sized sediments from the west side are dominated by modern glacial weathering products of Post-Oligocene volcanic rocks (up to 64%). Our findings establish a multi-proxy mineralogical and geochemical fingerprint framework for distinguishing and quantifying modern glacial and paleo-weathering sediments in West Antarctica, and provide critical insights for paleoclimatic reconstruction and understanding the impact of glacial erosion on marine carbon cycle dynamics in Antarctica.

title: Alteration kinetics of basaltic glass in acidic conditions: The effect of temperature and pH on glass dissolution and alteration layer formation
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Arpad Pusztai, Bastien Wild, Samuel Tardif, Zijie Liu, François Guyot, Imene Esteve, Alejandro Fernandez-Martinez, Damien Daval
abstract: Quantifying basaltic glass alteration kinetics is essential for modelling carbon sequestration and global biogeochemical cycles. However, current literature rates diverge by up to two orders of magnitude due to surface area normalization uncertainties (BET vs. geometric) and conflicting reports on the pH-dependence of activation energies (E a ). In this study, we resolve these inconsistencies by combining Vertical Scanning Interferometry (VSI) and in situ synchrotron X-ray Reflectivity (XRR) to decouple glass network dissolution from Amorphous Silica-rich Surface Layer (ASSL) growth between 5 and 60 °C and pH 2–5. Our results demonstrate that both dissolution and ASSL growth proceed linearly over time, following a surface-reaction-controlled regime. We show that the surface retreat method (VSI) provides a robust, normalization-independent proxy for network breakdown, yielding rates consistent with Si release. Furthermore, XRR data reveal that steady-state ASSL densities decrease with increasing growth rates, suggesting the formation of more porous structures at low pH. Contrary to common assumptions in long-term field rates, we find no evidence of surface passivation: ASSLs remain permeable and do not act as diffusion barriers over weeks-long experiments, accounting for up to 80% of the total altered volume. The temperature dependence of the dissolution rate (r) is best described by a pH-dependent Arrhenius law: r = A pH . exp − E a , pH RT a H + n where A pH is the pH-dependent preexponential factor, R is the gas constant, a H+ is the activity of protons, n the reaction order with respect to protons, which is close to 1 on the investigated temperature range, and where the apparent E a decreases from 62.9 ± 2.0 kJ/mol at pH 2 to values near zero (< 20 kJ/mol) as the pH approaches the point of zero charge of the glass. By providing quantitatively decoupled kinetics for substrate dissolution and layer formation, this work offers a high-resolution framework to refine predictive models of basalt weathering in both natural and engineered acidic environments.

title: Beyond evaporites: Assessing hypersalinity using boron-based salinity proxies
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Mariano N. Remírez, Geoffrey J. Gilleaudeau, Swapan K. Sahoo, Lucía Guerra, Chelsea Pederson, Eduardo Piovano, Alan J. Kaufman, Adrian Immenhauser, Stephen W. Lokier, Thomas J. Algeo
abstract: Boron-based paleosalinity proxies have been developed for both siliciclastic and carbonate sediments and sedimentary rocks, but to date modern analogs have been tested only over the salinity range from freshwater to normal-marine conditions (∼0–38 psu, or practical salinity units), with little attention given to hypersaline depositional systems (>38 psu). Here, we analyze boron and gallium concentrations in a known modern hypersaline facies (Abu Dhabi Lagoon) for comparison with an inferred ancient hypersaline facies (Devonian-Carboniferous Bakken Formation, Williston Basin, North America) to assess the applicability of the boron/gallium (B/Ga) and excess boron (Bxs) salinity proxies to hypersaline depositional systems. Our results show that B/Ga and Bxs effectively track salinity variation in the hypersalinity range for both siliciclastic and carbonate sediments. Although the precise thresholds between marine and hypersaline facies are tentative, the available data indicate ‘fuzzy thresholds’ of 10–12 for B/Ga and 70–100 ppm for Bxs in siliciclastic facies, with B/Ga > 12 and Bxs > 100 ppm unambiguously associated with hypersaline depositional conditions. In carbonate facies, B/Ga ratios can become artificially high as Ga concentrations approach zero, making the B/Ga proxy unreliable, although the Bxs proxy works well, with estimated proxy ranges of 40 ppm for hypersaline facies. These findings robustly establish the validity of boron-based salinity proxies for recognition of ancient hypersaline facies.

title: Corrigendum to “Calcium isotopic signatures of mid-ocean ridge basalts from the eastern Galápagos Spreading Center that influenced by plume-ridge interaction” [Chemical Geology 715 (2026) 123478]
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Yujie Shan, Renqiang Liao, Peijun Lin, Jianghong Deng, Long Du, Xin Li, Hongli Zhu, Zhaofeng Zhang, Weidong Sun

title: Scale-dependent responses of karst soil mineralization to climate: Evidence from 19 years of cave drip water monitoring
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Xiuli Li, Fanfan Yang, Ying Zhu, Linghan Zeng, MengYu Yang, Huan Yang, Jin Liao, Chaoyong Hu
abstract: Understanding soil organic matter (SOM) mineralization responses to hydroclimatic changes is critical for carbon modeling in fragile karst ecosystems, yet cross-scale climatic drivers and nonlinear hydrological responses remain unclear. Using a 19-year (2004–2023) hydrochemical and dual-isotope ( δ 15 N- NO 3 − and δ 18 O- NO 3 − ) dataset from Heshang Cave, Central China, we validate dripwater nitrate ( N O 3 − ) as a robust proxy for SOM mineralization (∼95% derived from soil nitrification). Generalized Additive Models reveal scale-dependent climatic controls: seasonal mineralization is dominated by drip rate (explaining 50% of variance), whereas interannual dynamics are driven by annual precipitation (48%). We identify distinct nonlinear “optimal windows” (monthly drip rate: 2.65–5 mL/min; annual precipitation: 910–1470 mm) where balanced soil air-water conditions maximize microbial activity. Mineralization rates decrease when precipitation is either below its minimum threshold (water limitation) or above its maximum threshold (anaerobic conditions and hydrological bypassing). Furthermore, extreme dry-wet alternations (e.g., 2019–2020) impair mineralization recovery via soil damage and substrate depletion. These long-term observations elucidate the nonlinear hydrological thresholds and scale-dependent controls on karst SOM mineralization, providing crucial parameters to refine global carbon cycle models.

title: The preservation of francolite-associated sulfate in lingulid brachiopods
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Jordan P. Todes, Jocelyn A. Richardson, Liisa Lang, Kalle Kirsimäe, Roger N. Bryant
abstract: Lingulid brachiopods – the namesake “living fossils” of Darwin – have a continuous record from the Cambrian to the present and possess phosphatic valves, rendering them largely unique among extant invertebrates. Due to their poorly understood vital effects and susceptibility to taphonomic breakdown, they have not been widely adopted as geochemical archives. However, inorganic sulfate is abundant in lingulid bioapatite, which may be more resistant to diagenetic alteration than carbonate-based minerals. As such, it is possible that lingulid shells may provide an alternative, independent archive of Phanerozoic sulfate seawater chemistry, provided that the distribution and preservation of sulfur within lingulid shells can be identified. Here, we leverage sulfur K-edge micro X-ray Fluorescence (μ-XRF) imaging, X-ray Absorption Near Edge Structure (XANES) spectroscopy, and petrography to characterize sulfur speciation and distribution within extant and fossil lingulid brachiopods. In modern Lingula anatina, inorganic sulfate is dominant along francolite-rich laminae, whereas organic sulfur species are mostly observed in non-mineralized laminae and the periostracum. In the Cambrian fossil Ungula ingrica, inorganic sulfate is generally dominant in regions with the lowest sulfur abundances, with higher sulfate abundances along compact laminae than on baculate laminae. In contrast, the distribution of diagenetic pyrite is heterogenous, although largely concentrated along shell edges and particular laminae. Notably, the XANES spectrum of francolite-associated sulfate is characterized by a unique post-edge feature at 2494.0 eV. Collectively, these results suggest that carefully selected lingulid specimens – and from intra-valve laminae with minimal diagenetic phases – have the potential to be insightful for reconstructing Phanerozoic sulfate seawater chemistry.

title: Thallium isotopic records of the Cambrian SPICE event reveal widespread deoxygenation and unique Mn-oxide cycling dynamics in early Paleozoic oceans
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Matthew A. LeRoy, Benjamin C. Gill, Sean M. Newby, Theodore R. Them, Jeremy D. Owens
abstract: Changes in the redox state of the oceans have exerted a powerful influence on the biological and chemical evolution of marine environments throughout Earth history. A relatively new proxy used to reconstruct this redox history is the analysis of the thallium isotopic composition (ε205Tl) of fine-grained clastic rocks. Its utility stems from the central role and large fractionation that redox-sensitive Mn-oxides impart on the ε205Tl of seawater in the modern ocean. Importantly, lower oxygenation levels of the ocean-atmosphere system earlier in Earth history may have fostered different Mn cycling dynamics and Tl isotope behavior. Here we explore this idea by examining a putative early Paleozoic interval of expanding marine deoxygenation, the Cambrian SPICE event (494.5 to 492.5 Ma). Our ε205Tl records from two SPICE localities: the Alum Shale of Sweden and the Stockingford Shale Group of England suggest a rapid reduction of Mn-oxide sedimentation accompanied the initiation of the SPICE, consistent with expanding anoxia at this time. However, while both locations show broadly similar ε205Tl patterns, to each other and to previous Tl investigations of anoxic events, we observe several differences that may reflect how Mn was cycled differently under lower oxygen levels. We note that most Mn-oxide sedimentation was likely localized in shallower environments creating more dynamic cycling of Mn and Tl than observed today. This view may have implications not only for the interpretation of Tl isotope data, but also for other isotopic systems influenced by Mn-oxides before the oxygenation of oceans reached modern levels.

title: Effects of ionic strength and pH on 18 O enrichment kinetics in aqueous carbonate and bicarbonate solutions
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Andrea Billarent-Cedillo, Oliver Plümper, Helen E. King
abstract: Oxygen isotopic composition plays a crucial role in the study of Earth's past climate conditions as well as understanding fluid-mineral reactions. Geochemical models commonly assume oxygen isotopic equilibrium between oxyanions and water. However, this may not be valid if the fluid-mineral reactions proceed more rapidly than isotopic enrichment in solution, where the enrichment rate can be influenced by pH and ionic strength. In this study, we used in-situ Raman spectroscopy to investigate the 18O enrichment kinetics into carbonate and bicarbonate oxyanions using solutions with 18O-enriched water containing different concentrations of NaCl. We report species-specific rates of 18O enrichment as a function of pH and ionic strength. The observed trends reflect expected dissolved CO2 behavior under different chemical conditions indicating that the experiments are following an incorporation reaction during the formation of different dissolved inorganic carbon species. In the carbonate system, increasing ionic strength significantly slows isotope incorporation. In contrast, the bicarbonate system shows a stronger dependence on pH, with minimal ionic strength effect. These findings highlight the distinct roles of pH and ionic strength in governing isotope incorporation kinetics across different dissolved inorganic carbon species. Our results refine the understanding of oxygen isotope behavior in aqueous, inorganic carbon systems, particularly with regards to environmental conditions with fluctuating pH and salinity.

title: Metal cations regulate microbial U(VI) biomineralization with calcium driving a pathway switch
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Yuqi Guo, Hong Tu, Junyuan Gong, Hui Li, Feize Li, Ning Liu, Jiali Liao
abstract: Microbial U(VI) biomineralization into phosphate minerals is a promising strategy for radionuclide immobilization, while the governing influence of coexisting metal cations on mineralization pathways remains elusive. This study proves that Ca2+ acts as a molecular switch, fundamentally redirecting U(VI) biomineralization induced by Bacillus sp. dwc-2 and enhancing uranium capture stability through wet chemistry and spectral data analysis. In the system without any additional metal ions, U(VI) precipitates as crystalline U(VI)–phosphate phases. However, increasing Ca2+ concentrations progressively suppress this crystallization, favoring a shift toward U(VI) adsorption on CaP phases. Crucially, this pathway shift significantly reduces the fraction of carbonate–extractable uranium, indicating that the Ca–mediated amorphous phases provide a more secure long-term sink than their crystalline counterparts. In contrast, Fe3+ exhibits pH–dependent dual effects, generally inhibiting U(VI)– phosphate biomineralization and forming Fe–P–U phases under acidic and neutral conditions, while allowing partial mineralization at pH 8.5, albeit less effectively than the Fe3–free control. Na+, K+, and Mg2+ show no obvious impacts on the mineralization process, although Na+ is incorporated into the interlayer of (UO₂PO₄)ⁿ− under neutral and alkaline conditions to form Na–autunite–like phases. These findings underscore the dominant and mechanism–altering role of Ca2+ in microbial U(VI) immobilization, providing crucial insights into uranium biogeochemistry and informing the development of targeted bioremediation strategies for uranium-contaminated environments.

title: Early cements in ammonites as seawater U Pb and 87 Sr/ 86 Sr archives to constrain oceanic anoxic events in Earth's history
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Sharon Y. Gamarra-Caicedo, Diego A. Sierra-Bermúdez, Cesar E. Herrera-Quintero, Marius N. Müller, Marcel Guillong, Rolando E. Clavijo-Arcos
abstract: Accurate dating of oceanic anoxic events (OAEs) is essential for paleoceanographic and paleoclimatic reconstructions of Earth's history, contributing to our knowledge of major shifts in global carbon cycling. Although OAEs have been widely studied, direct age constraints on the biostratigraphy associated with these events are limited. Attempts to establish absolute ages of OAEs have relied on UPb zircon dating of ash layers and ReOs geochronology in organic-rich sediments. However, UPb zircon ages are inherently limited by the spatially-restricted character of ash layers in carbonate successions, whereas ReOs systematics are affected by variability in initial Os values (e.g., bioturbation or inherited organic sources), collectively hindering robust global paleoenvironmental correlations and reliable reconstructions of seawater 87Sr/86Sr records from marine carbonates. Here, we demonstrate the feasibility of using early marine fibrous cements from ammonite chambers, retrieved from marine black shales of the OAE-3 as absolute radiometric archives to reconstruct minimum depositional ages by UPb dating via Laser Ablation Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS). The UPb age of early ammonite cements from OAE-3 sediments is estimated at 86.65 ± 2.35 Ma and validated against 87Sr/86Sr isotopic ratios (i.e., 0.707406 ± 0.000161) using Laser Ablation Multi-Collector Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (LA-MC-ICP-MS), confirming the local biostratigraphic framework of the OAE-3 record of northeastern South America. Our results demonstrate that early fibrous calcite cements preserved within ammonite chambers can serve as reliable UPb geochronometers and archives for the Sr isotopic composition of seawater, providing an integrated geochronological, petrographic and biostratigraphic tool for refining our understanding of Cretaceous oceanic anoxic events.

title: Sequential input of dissolved organic matter and phosphate alters their competitive adsorption at ferrihydrite-water interfaces
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Zezhen Ren, Shiwen Hu, Yuzhen Liang, Zhenqing Shi, Rong Li
abstract: Phosphate (P) and dissolved organic matter (DOM) commonly coexist in subsurface environments such as soils, sediments, and groundwater, where their adsorption behavior on iron (Fe) oxyhydroxides plays a crucial role in regulating carbon‑phosphorus biogeochemical cycling. However, the molecular mechanisms governing their competitive adsorption under different input sequences remain poorly understood. Here, sequential batch experiments were integrated with Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) depth profiling, and Charge Distribution MUltisite Ion Complexation (CD-MUSIC) surface complexation modeling to decipher these interfacial processes. Results demonstrate that the addition sequence significantly regulates the final adsorption equilibrium and molecular fractionation of DOM. Specifically, when DOM was pre-adsorbed, subsequent phosphate addition altered the molecular composition of dissolved organic matter in the aqueous phase, resulting in a relative enrichment of highly aromatic compounds such as condensed hydrocarbons, tannins, and lignin. In contrast, phosphate pre-adsorption strongly inhibited subsequent DOM binding due to its stronger site competition and more uniform depth distribution within ferrihydrite aggregates, as confirmed by XPS normalized center-of-mass depth (NCOMD) analysis. Our study demonstrates that the timing and sequence of phosphate input can significantly influence the fractionation and stabilization efficiency of DOM by ferrihydrite. These findings advance the understanding of DOM adsorptive fractionation and stability regulation in natural environments, providing theoretical support for carbon‑phosphorus cycling at mineral-water interfaces.

title: Position-specific carbon isotope fractionation in humic and fulvic acids: A density functional theory study using the cutoff calculation
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Pingjiao Xie, Jixi Zhang, Lanlan Wu, Jiajia Lu
abstract: Humic acid (HA) and fulvic acid (FA), the principal components of humus, are high-molecular-weight organic acids with diverse functional groups and non-equivalent carbon sites. To date, carbon isotope studies of HA and FA have primarily focused on bulk isotopic measurements. Natural HA and FA contain numerous equivalent and non-equivalent carbon sites whose position-specific δ13C values may provide isotopic information beyond that obtainable from bulk measurements. The cutoff calculation method provides an effective approach for simplifying molecules such as HA and FA, which possess complex structures and high molecular weights. In this study, eight molecular models containing 47–122 atoms were selected, and position-specific carbon isotope fractionation in HA and FA was investigated at the molecular level. Cutoff calculation was performed to validate seven of the molecular models. The results showed that, relative to whole-molecule calculation, cutoff calculation produces negligible changes in molecular volume before and after structural optimization (0.00–2.33 Å) and minor deviations in 103lnβ values (0.00‰-6.92‰). This supports the accuracy of the cutoff calculation for studying isotope fractionation in large molecules. Furthermore, our results indicate that the inductive effects of electron-donating groups (-OH and -NH2) and electron-withdrawing groups (-COOH and -CHO) influence the isotopic fractionation of adjacent carbon sites. Position-specific isotope fractionation also suggests that oxygen-containing functional groups are more prone to heavy isotope enrichment and that the 103lnβ values for sp2-hybridized carbon are higher than those for sp3-hybridized carbon. Overall, the cutoff calculation is an efficient and reliable method for studying position-specific isotope fractionation in complex organic macromolecules. This provides an insight for a comprehensive understanding of carbon isotope geochemical processes in HA and FA, as well as HA/FA–metal complexation mechanisms.

title: Kinetic control of Mn incorporation during CaCO 3 precipitation in Ca–carbonate systems
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Shigeshi Fuchida, Seiya Kato
abstract: Dissolved divalent manganese (Mn(II) aq ) is widely distributed in natural and anthropogenically impacted aqueous systems, sometimes at high concentrations. In carbonate-rich water, Mn(II) aq immobilization could proceed by the formation of carbonate compounds rather than through the formation of Mn oxides and oxyhydroxides, owing to the extremely slow abiotic oxidation rate of Mn(II) aq to Mn(III) by dissolved oxygen. In this study, the kinetic roles of calcium (Ca2+) and bicarbonate (HCO3 −) ions in controlling Mn(II) aq precipitation at pHs 6–10 were elucidated under unsteady-state conditions for 60–180 min. The Mn(II) aq was immobilized at pH 9 through the formations of Mn oxidized and rhodochrosite (MnCO3), whereas at pH 8.5 in the copresence of HCO3 − and Ca2+, it was incorporated into the Ca carbonate (CaCO3) phase. This coprecipitation with CaCO3 resulted in markedly faster Mn(II) aq removal than discrete MnCO3 formation, with the removal rate being directly proportional to the CaCO3 precipitation rate. Combined field-emission scanning transmission electron microscopy (FE-STEM) and Mn K-edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) analyses demonstrated that Mn(II) was immobilized through heterogeneous substitution into the CaCO3 lattice, forming a solid solution, initiated by Mn-rich nuclei and followed by the rapid growth of Ca-rich carbonate phases. This process was initiated by Mn-rich nuclei followed by the rapid growth of Ca-rich carbonate phases, without distinct phase transformation during the 60–180 min period. These findings highlight that Mn immobilization in HCO3 −- and Ca2+-rich aqueous systems is governed by kinetic coupling between CaCO3 precipitation and Mn incorporation, rather than by thermodynamic stability alone.

title: Revisiting the formation and differentiation of Neoproterozoic continental arc crust in the western Yangtze Block, South China
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Yu Zhu, Xiao-ping Xia, Feng Guo, Yan-jie Tang, Xin Zhu, Chang-xin Yin, M.P. Manu Prasanth, Ren-zhi Zhu, Min Liu, Zhuang Guo, Jiang-feng Qin, Fang-yi Zhang, Hang Yang, Shao-cong Lai
abstract: Neoproterozoic continental arc magmatism in the western Yangtze Block (South China) provides critical insights into early crust-mantle evolution during circum-Rodinia subduction-accretionary orogenesis. However, the specific processes of Neoproterozoic continental crustal growth and stratification remain unclear. Herein, we present a comprehensive synthesis of mineral chemistry, zircon U–Pb–Hf isotopes, whole-rock major and trace elements as well as SrNd isotopes from representative Neoproterozoic Igneous Intrusive Complexes (NIICs) in the western Yangtze Block, including the Tianquan (TIC; ca. 833–825 Ma) and Shimian complexes (SIC; ca. 781–779 Ma) in this study, alongside the previously reported Nanba (NIC; ca. 796–790 Ma) and Luding complexes (LIC; ca. 783–779 Ma). The NIICs comprise mafic gabbros through intermediate diorites to highly fractionated silica-rich granitoids, suggesting a coherent calc-alkaline differentiation trend. They exhibit variable but predominantly depleted whole-rock SrNd (e.g., TIC: εNd(t) = −0.08 ∼ +4.55; NIC: εNd(t) = −0.60 ∼ +1.91; LIC: εNd(t) = +2.35 ∼ +5.10; SIC: εNd(t) = +0.50 ∼ +6.07) and zircon Hf isotopes (TIC: mean εHf(t) = +7.75 ∼ +11.89; NIC: mean εHf(t) = +4.33 ∼ +5.66; LIC: εHf(t) = +4.03 ∼ +7.69; SIC: εHf(t) = +5.69 ∼ +9.81), indicating a heterogeneous mantle source metasomatized by subducted components. Combined with “crust-like” trace element signatures, systematic whole-rock compositional variations, and hornblende P-T estimates, the NIICs represent middle–upper crustal sections, which underscore a three-stage evolution for Neoproterozoic continental arc crustal growth and fractionation: (1) the generation of primary basaltic melts from heterogeneous metasomatized mantle source infiltrated by subducted components; (2) the long-lived supply of metasomatized mantle-derived melts, magma mixing, and polybaric crystallization-driven differentiation within a trans-crustal magmatic system; and (3) extraction of high-silica melts in a shallow mush reservoir. Integrated with previous studies, our findings demonstrate that this complex array of petrogenetic processes—alongside the partial melting of diverse crustal sources—ultimately governed the maturation and vertical stratification of the Neoproterozoic continental arc crust in the western Yangtze Block.

title: A body mass-based approach to inverse modeling of seasonality through enamel isotopes of Bovidae
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Alexandra L. Norwood, Daniel R. Green, J. Tyler Faith
abstract: Serial sampling of tooth enamel generates a record of changes in the food and water consumed by an animal on seasonal timescales. In the fossil record, these data provide insight into paleoseasonality, animal behavior, and ecology over sub-annual temporal scales that strongly influence longer-term trends in species distribution and dietary evolution. However, enamel mineralization varies in speed and internal geometry during tooth growth, warping the isotopic input it records. Growth rates and geometry also vary between taxa. Therefore, to recover more accurate estimates of input dietary and environmental signals, models must be built to account for the complexities of enamel mineralization in a specific taxon of interest and the way that mineral content with differing isotopic compositions is incorporated through time. Here, we present a set of models to recover input isotope time series from serial enamel isotope data in the Bovidae. Enamel mineralization is modeled based on conserved features of dental histology and scaled to body mass and tooth crown height. These mineralization models are then incorporated into an inverse modeling process. This approach allows a specified taxon to be modeled without detailed histological data, facilitating the recovery of seasonal environmental signals from serial enamel profiles from many bovid taxa across diverse modern and fossil contexts. Through sensitivity testing and a real-world application to waterbuck (Kobus ellipsiprymnus) from Queen Elizabeth National Park in Uganda, we show that these models recover an accurate seasonality signal from preserved enamel, particularly in larger-bodied animals and higher-crowned teeth, and over longer seasons.

title: Control of the water masses, aeolian and fluvial particulates and deoxygenation on the dissolved neodymium and its isotope composition in the Arabian Sea
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Damodararao Karri, Sunil Kumar Singh
abstract: This study presents high-resolution dissolved neodymium (Nd) concentrations and isotopic compositions (εNd) in the Arabian Sea (AS) water column along a 68°E meridional section (0∘ to 21∘N). The primary objectives were to identify and quantify regional water masses, assess the impact of particle-water interactions—driven by significant aeolian and fluvial sediment inputs—and evaluate the influence of water column deoxygenation on Nd isotope systematics. Dissolved Nd concentrations and ϵNd exhibit significant variability across the basin, ranging from 7.8 to 48.6 pmol kg−1 and − 14.37 to −5.57, respectively. Specifically, less radiogenic values characterise the northern and south-eastern AS, while moderately radiogenic signatures are found in deep and bottom waters. In contrast, the surface waters of the central AS (4°N–16°N) exhibit more radiogenic εNd signatures. Our results demonstrate a substantial presence of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) and Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) in the deep and bottom layers of the Arabian Sea. At intermediate depths (200–1000 m), Persian Gulf and Red Sea waters dominate between 4°N and 16°N. The less radiogenic signatures in the northern and south-eastern sectors are attributed to lithogenic inputs (εNd ≈ −15 to −17) from the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra river systems. Conversely, the radiogenic surface waters in the central AS are influenced by the dissolution of aeolian mineral dust. Based on Nd excesses and isotopic compositions, we estimate a mineral dust flux of 1.8 ± 1.4 g m−2 y−1 over the central Arabian Sea. This value is lower than previous estimates, suggesting significant temporal or seasonal variations in dust deposition. Ultimately, these results highlight that the Nd budget in the Arabian Sea is governed by a combination of water mass advection and dominant boundary exchange processes. This suggests that the use of εNd as a pure water-mass proxy is restricted in regions with high suspended particle loads, such as the northern and south-eastern Arabian Sea.

title: Zircon–apatite geochemistry and isotope constraints on VMS fertility in a late cretaceous back-arc basin, Eastern Sakarya Zone, Türkiye
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Hadi Shafaii Moghadam, Wenjiao Xiao, Orhan Karsli, Faruk Aydin, Massimo Chiaradia, William L. Griffin, Simge Oğuz-Saka
abstract: Volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) deposits are common in submarine back-arc environments, yet mineralization is unevenly distributed even among volcanic successions formed within the same tectonomagmatic system. Here we investigate felsic volcanic sequences associated with the Murgul VMS district and stratigraphically equivalent barren successions from the Hatila Valley in the Eastern Sakarya Zone, northeastern Türkiye, to evaluate how magma evolution and crustal magma transfer varied between fertile and barren domains within a single Late Cretaceous back-arc basin. Mafic rocks from both domains display comparable juvenile Nd-Hf isotope compositions, with εNd(t) = +1.3 to +3.7 and εHf(t) = +6.8 to +9.8 for Hatila rocks, and εNd(t) = +3.1 to +4.0 and εHf(t) = +8.6 to +10.0 for the Murgul VMS district, together with subduction-modified trace-element signatures, including elevated Th/Yb and Th/Nb ratios. These data indicate broadly similar mantle sources and slab contributions. In contrast, felsic rocks associated with VMS mineralization show restricted whole-rock εNd(t)–εHf(t) variability, with εNd(t) = +3.0 to +3.5 and εHf(t) = +8.3 to +9.2, limited intra-sample zircon εHf(t) dispersion, and coherent zircon trace-element arrays involving U, Th/U, and Nb/Ta versus Hf. Barren felsic suites show broader isotopic and geochemical dispersion, including whole-rock εNd(t) = −9.4 to +0.4, εHf(t) = −11.1 to +5.9, and zircon εHf(t) = −9.2 to +10.2. Zircon oxybarometry indicates broadly overlapping low- to moderately oxidized conditions in barren and fertile suites, with mean ΔFMQ values of +0.79 ± 0.87 and + 0.31 ± 0.34, respectively, suggesting that oxygen fugacity alone did not distinguish fertile from barren systems. Apatite compositions and Nd isotopes broadly parallel the zircon record, with Murgul apatite yielding εNd(t) = +1.6 to +3.6 compared with −1.0 to +2.2 in Hatila apatite. We interpret the fertile domain to reflect coherent juvenile felsic magma evolution, limited open-system crustal modification, and vertically connected magma transfer within a back-arc basin supplied by compositionally similar mafic magmas. These results highlight isotopic focusing, defined here as restricted isotopic dispersion expressed by limited whole-rock Nd-Hf variability and limited intra-sample zircon εHf(t) variation, together with accessory-mineral-scale geochemical coherence, as indicators of magmatic conditions favorable for VMS development in submarine felsic volcanic successions.

title: Evaluation of the minor elements and isotopic composition of bivalve ( Spisula sachalinensis ) shells as paleoenvironmental archives
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Yusuke Tamenori, Toshihiro Yoshimura, Saburo Sakai
abstract: Bivalve shells are valuable archives for paleoenvironmental reconstruction, as their chemical composition records environmental and biological signals during growth. In this study, we characterize minor element distributions (Na, Sr, P, S, and Cl) in Spisula sachalinensis shells collected from four localities along the Pacific coast of northern Japan, complemented by stable oxygen and carbon isotope analyses (δ18O and δ13C) of a representative specimen (Tomakomai_1). Micro-X-ray fluorescence mapping of hinge sections revealed distinct seasonal and age-dependent patterns in Sr, S, and Cl distributions. Sr and S broadly co-vary with δ18O, whereas Cl exhibits behavior more similar to δ13C. During early, rapid growth stages, elevated Cl concentrations indicated strong biological control on element incorporation, while increased Sr and S concentrations after growth stabilization displayed clearer annual cyclicity, reflecting a shift in the dominant controls on shell chemistry with ontogenetic development. The observed patterns were consistent among individuals and across sampling regions, suggesting characteristic features of this species. Reconstructed δ18O-based temperatures are consistent with bottom-water values during summer but show persistent positive offsets in winter, indicating that calcification ceases before the coldest conditions are reached. Despite parallel seasonal patterns in δ18O and Sr, the relationship between Sr concentration and sea surface temperature varies among individuals, indicating that Sr incorporation is influenced by biological factors in addition to environmental conditions. Overall, our results demonstrate that minor element distributions in S. sachalinensis shells reflect the combined influence of growth dynamics, physiology, and environment, underscoring the importance of a characterization-based approach when interpreting shell geochemical records.

title: Osmium isotope constraints on Mauna Loa–Kīlauea magmatic connectivity, Island of Hawai‘i
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Siddhartha Bharadwaj, Kendra J. Lynn, Aaron J. Pietruszka, Frank A. Trusdell, Mukul Sharma
abstract: The Hawaiian volcanic chain exhibits a long-recognized double track of volcanism defined by the Loa and Kea trends, which erupt chemically and isotopically distinct lavas. Mauna Loa and Kīlauea, the two most frequently active volcanoes of the Loa and Kea trends, produce distinct endmember compositions. However, historical periods of compositional convergence have prompted debate regarding a potential magmatic connection between the two adjacent volcanoes. Proposed links include a shallow edifice-level plumbing system, a common magma source at ∼40 km depth, or a deeper asthenospheric source. In the latter scenario, based on correlated Sr–Nd–Pb isotopes and trace-element systematics, a “shared” mantle source supplies melt alternately to both volcanoes on multi-decadal timescales. Here, we use Os isotopes to evaluate the proposed connections. We measured Os isotopes in eight historical Mauna Loa tholeiites along with three Kīlauea tholeiites (1832 summit eruption; Uēkahuna Bluff; 2000 Pu‘u‘ō‘ō eruption) previously identified as isotopically intermediate between Mauna Loa and Kīlauea endmembers. We found that the acidic bromide leachates of all samples yield more radiogenic 187Os/188Os than corresponding bulk residues, with the labile Os-bearing phase comprising ∼0.4–27% of bulk Os. Mauna Loa tholeiites display nearly constant 187Os/188Os over the past ∼200 years (0.134–0.136; mean = 0.1357 ± 0.0013, n = 8, 2SD), despite large variations in total [Os] ranging from ∼30 pg/g (2022 tholeiite) to ∼966 pg/g (1868 picrite). The Kīlauea 1832 sample has 187Os/188Os = 0.1302 ± 0.0008, slightly higher than the Kīlauea endmember (0.1285 ± 0.0008), whereas the Uēkahuna Bluff and Pu‘u‘ō‘ō samples exhibit more elevated ratios (0.1314 ± 0.0008 and 0.1327 ± 0.0008, respectively). We conclude that the “shared” mantle source exerts negligible control on Mauna Loa Os isotope systematics. In contrast, the Kīlauea mantle source is more heterogeneous, with contributions from small-scale recycled domains with variable time-integrated Re/Os ratios.

title: Progressive crustal melting during low-angle subduction to slab rollback: insights from late Mesozoic granitoids in the Liaodong Peninsula
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Jin-Feng Sun, Jin-Hui Yang, Ya-Dong Wu, Yu-Sheng Zhu, Lei Xu, Bao-Quan Zhou, Ji-Heng Zhang, Yan-Bin Zhang
abstract: Understanding how crustal melting responds to changes in subduction geometry is critical for reconstructing crustal evolution along convergent margins. In the eastern North China Craton, Late Mesozoic magmatism has been widely linked to the transition from low-angle subduction to rollback of the Paleo-Pacific plate, yet the geochemical response of crustal melting to this geodynamic shift remains incompletely constrained. Here we present new zircon UPb ages and HfO isotope data for nine Early Cretaceous granitic plutons from the Liaodong Peninsula and integrate them with previously published datasets. Four chronological stages are identified for the Late Mesozoic magmatism: Early−Middle Jurassic granitoids (182–165 Ma), Late Jurassic granitoids (159–155 Ma), Early Cretaceous syenitic rocks and A-type granites (129–123 Ma), and Early Cretaceous I-type granites (123–118 Ma). Jurassic granitoids were generated mainly by relatively high-pressure, low-temperature (ca. 756 °C), water-fluxed melting of lower crustal materials with garnet as a residual phase. Higher δ18O and strongly negative εHf(t) values of Late Jurassic granites indicate relatively more felsic source rocks than those of Early−Middle Jurassic granites. In contrast, the earliest Cretaceous syenitic rocks and A-type granites with variable La/Yb and Sr/Y ratios record high- temperature (ca. 822 °C), relatively dry crustal melting at deep and shallow crustal levels. The subsequent Early Cretaceous I-type granites formed by relatively lower-temperature (ca. 756 °C) melting of a more hydrous lower crust, with involvement of mantle-derived materials. Together, these stages define a progressive reorganization of crustal melting conditions, i.e., from Jurassic high-pressure, low-temperature and water-rich to earliest Cretaceous decreasing pressure, high-temperature and water-absent, and finally to Early Cretaceous low-temperature and hydrous conditions. This temporal progression can be interpreted as a response to the transition from continental thickening to thinning, related to the shift from low-angle subduction to slab rollback of the Paleo-Pacific plate, highlighting how the petrogenetic diversity of granitoids can be used to trace crustal evolution in response to subduction dynamics.

title: Hydrochemistry in the Gotthard Base Tunnel (Central Alps) – Composition and evolution of deep groundwater in continental crust
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Ingrid Stober, Federico Giovanoli, Kurt Bucher
abstract: Excavation of the Gotthard Rail Base Tunnel through the Central Alps opened fractured granite/gneiss and frequent fluid inflows provided access to the major water-rock-interactions (WRI) processes in orogenic crystalline upper crust. Construction of the 57 km long tunnel was divided into five different sections and was drilled from 1999 to 2010 (2011). Here we report data and observations from the long Faido- and Bodio sections of a combined length of 30 km. 152 water samples were collected at inflow points 550 to 2350 m below the surface. The exceptional samples and data provide a comprehension of the hydrochemical evolution and solute acquisition of deep groundwater in basement units. The Faido- and Bodio sections cut across a pile of nappes of granite, gneiss and schist of pre-Alpine age and across a narrow zone of Mesozoic meta-sediments. Rock temperature along the two sections varies from 20 °C to 47 °C depending on the thickness of the overburden. The fracture water is of meteoric origin and acquires its composition exclusively by chemical interaction with the surrounding rocks along the flow path. Total of dissolved solids (TDS) at inflow points, water-composition, and pH of fluids change dramatically along the two tunnel sections. Typically, TDS in granitic waters is low, waters are dominated by sodium (Na) and sulfate (SO4), fluoride (F) is high, and pH reaches values of 10 and more. Although plentiful in the rocks, calcium (Ca), potassium (K), and magnesium (Mg) are low to very low in the fracture waters. Along the tunnel sections two high-TDS zones (> 3000 mg L−1) occur, reflecting the occurrence of outcrops of Triassic metasediments (Röti-Formation, Rauwacke, cellular dolomite). These rocks contain gypsum (anhydrite) and dolomite and are strongly karstified at surface outcrops and to depth of some 100 m. Water in the tunnel arriving from these areas are typically Ca-SO4 dominated, have high TDS and a lower pH. They change the composition to a Na-Ca-SO4 dominated water type when passing through the granitic rocks below. High fluoride concentrations of up to 16.5 mg L−1 are characteristic for most waters. As a result of high pH dissolved silica (SiO2) reaches concentrations of up to c. 70 mg L−1, especially in the Faido section. The waters are typically strongly supersaturated with respect to quartz. Fluoride and dissolved silica result from alteration of biotite (micas) forming clay minerals and chlorite. The newly formed solids remove Mg, Fe, and K almost quantitatively from the water. The data show distinctly that at least up to depths of 2.5 km below surface infiltrating pristine meteoric water evolves to a low TDS, high pH solution by interaction with gneiss and granite. High-TDS Ca-SO4 waters in the tunnel result exclusively from waters that have passed through highly soluble and thus high permeable rocks near the surface.

title: Abiotic formation of 13 C-depleted graphitic carbon during serpentinization
description: Publication date: 20 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 719 Author(s): Long Zhang, Qiang Wang, Haiyang Xian, Yiping Yang, Xing Ding, Luhua Xie
abstract: Markedly light carbon isotope compositions (e.g., δ13C < −20‰) are often regarded as a sign of biological activity, yet certain abiotic processes can also cause similar carbon isotope fractionation. However, previous studies showing abiotic 13C depletion mostly focused on simple hydrocarbons, while generation of abiogenic 13C-depleted condensed carbonaceous matters remains poorly documented. This study investigates petrology and geochemistry of carbon species in variably serpentinized peridotite rocks from the north Qilian ophiolite, northern Tibet. It is revealed that poorly crystalline graphitic carbon, occurring as nanometer-sized veinlets included in secondary minerals, was generated by hydrogen-driven reduction of inorganic carbon during serpentinization. Moreover, the graphitic carbon probably has low δ13C (< −27‰) comparable to that of biogenic carbon. The finding indicates abiogenic graphitic carbon with biogenic-like δ13C may be produced during water-rock interactions, highlighting concerns about reliability of carbon isotopes as a standalone biosignature. Furthermore, such graphitic carbon may contribute significantly to the carbon budget of serpentinite, which may play a critical role in deep carbon cycling during serpentinite subduction.

title: Heavy silicon isotope and mass-independent mercury isotope fractionation signals of Archean TTGs: Insights into the recycling of the silicified oceanic crust in the source region
