These findings indicate the need for basin-specific nutrient management strategies to protect the integrity of freshwater ecosystems.

title: Data-driven simultaneous accounting of diverse agronomic and eco-hydro-climatological stressors for guiding targeted watershed restoration strategies
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 678 Author(s): Swetasree Nag, Ankur Sharma, Icy Trisha, Ravisha Gambhir, Srinivas Rallapalli
abstract: Watershed degradation-driven by land use transformation, climatic variability, and agro-ecological disturbances-poses severe threats to water security, agricultural productivity, and ecosystem resilience. Past studies often fail to simultaneously account for the interacting hydrological, climatological, agro-ecological, and terrain-related stressors that collectively determine watershed health. This study develops an integrated vulnerability assessment framework that systematically evaluates 98 sub-watersheds using 20 environmental indicators derived from satellite observations and process-based hydrological simulations. The methodology incorporates both beneficial and non-beneficial indicators—including sediment yield, water stress, drought intensity, vegetation condition, and topographic complexity—aggregated using the Complex Proportional Assessment (COPRAS) method. The key novelties of the approach are threefold: (i) indicators are treated in a sign-consistent manner, ensuring that protective and hazardous factors are evaluated without mutual masking; (ii) indicator weights are derived objectively using entropy, reducing subjectivity and emphasizing variables with higher discriminatory power; and (iii) a two-stage aggregation framework (domain-level followed by composite integration) preserves interpretability while capturing interactions among multiple stressor domains. Results indicate that watershed degradation emerges from the interaction of hydro-climatic variability, ecological condition, and terrain controls, rather than any single dominant factor. While the overall spatial prioritization pattern remains broadly consistent, noticeable sub-watershed-level variations highlight the influence of interannual variability on degradation dynamics. Domain-specific analysis further reveals the coexistence of structurally persistent and temporally sensitive vulnerability regimes, emphasizing the need for differentiated management strategies. The framework is scalable and transferable to other basins, particularly in data-scarce regions, and provides a foundation for prioritizing conservation investments and supporting adaptive watershed management.

title: Decoding flood hazard responses to reticular river network changes using interpretable machine learning
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shanheng Huang, Peng Wang, Zulin Hua, Yueyang Dong, Rongxu Chen, Yawei Hu, Shimin Tian
abstract: The structure of river networks critically governs flood propagation and hazard distribution, especially in reticular networks of low-lying delta plains where natural and engineered channels interweave. This study examines how structural changes in the Lixia River network—comprising both natural rivers and artificial canals—have influenced spatiotemporal flood hazard patterns from the 1960s to 2016. We developed a multi-index evaluation system based on complex network theory, representing river confluences and sources as nodes and channel segments as weighted edges characterized by length, width, and connectivity metrics. Hydrological-hydrodynamic modeling was employed to simulate water level dynamics under 100-year return period rainfall scenarios. Flood hazards were quantified using the Reliability-Resilience-Vulnerability framework, specifically measuring water level exceedance above warning thresholds. Interpretable machine learning methods were applied to identify key drivers of flood hazard distribution and their nonlinear relationships with network structure. Results demonstrate that river network restructuring significantly altered flood hazard patterns: hazards increased by 2.17%–5.01% from the 1960s to the 1980s, then declined but remained above 1960s baseline levels by 2016. Spatially, hazards concentrated in north-central regions with poor hydraulic connectivity, with centroids shifting westward by approximately 9.2 km. Network structural indices eccentricity and closeness centrality emerged as critical drivers comparable in importance to land use factors. Among topology‑based rehabilitation strategies, targeted dredging (capacity expansion) reduced flood hazards most effectively (mean improvement 7.95%), outperforming new channel construction (4.37%) and sluice‑gate optimization (1.74%). These findings provide quantitative guidance for structural rehabilitation in reticular river networks of low-lying plain regions.

title: Exogenous dust-induced snow albedo reduction and radiative forcing over the Third Pole
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Liang Li, Keqin Duan, Ting Yang, Yuhan Qi, Rong Chen, Peihong Shi
abstract: The evolution of snow over the Third Pole (TP) plays a critical role in amplifying changes in the Asian water tower. However, the quantitative contributions of exogenous dust to snow albedo reduction and radiative forcing over the TP remain largely unknown. Here, based on multi-source observations and numerical simulations of snow-darkening dynamic processes, this study systematically reveals the pronounced synchronicity and inverse coupling characteristics between dust and albedo changes over the TP, and quantifies the contributions of different exogenous dust to TP snow albedo reduction and radiative forcing. The results showed that exogenous dust-induced snow albedo reduction exhibited significant spatial heterogeneity, with core reduction regions concentrated in the northeastern TP and the southwestern slopes, where the regional mean albedo decrease exceeded 0.03 and locally surpassed 0.10. The dominant roles of different dust sources in snow darkening displayed significant spatiotemporal variability: dust from East Asia mainly affected regions below 3 km elevation of the north TP; dust from southwestern Asia and North Africa contributed 68.9% ± 22.2% and 20.9% ± 20.4%, respectively, to snow darkening in the central-western Himalayas, jointly dominating the snow darkening process in this region; whereas snow albedo reduction in the Pamir region was primarily influenced by dust from southwestern Asia and Central Asia, with Central Asian dust slightly prevailing during July–August. Exogenous dust deposition significantly enhanced the absorption of solar radiation by snow, generating total snow radiative forcing that generally exceeded 10 W m⁻2 in the major ice-snow covered regions. Among these effects, exogenous dust regulated the snow surface renewal process by altering snowfall frequency and snowfall amount, and the radiative forcing corresponding to this indirect regulatory pathway ranged from −7.6 to −1.3 W m⁻2. Meanwhile, exogenous dust also affected surface downward radiative fluxes by altering cloud-phase distribution, producing cloud-phase-related radiative forcing of approximately 0.3–0.69 W m⁻2. This study provides new quantitative perspectives and references for understanding the impacts of exogenous dust on the snow energy balance and hydrological processes over the TP.

title: Climate change and irrigation water demand: a review of modelling approaches and biophysical considerations
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shahin Solgi, Paul R. Petrie, Matthew J. Knowling, Ana Horta, Andrew Hall
abstract: Rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations are expected to influence future irrigation water demand (IWD) through complex interactions with crop growth and evapotranspiration processes. These biophysical dynamics are required for generating reliable seasonal and long-term projections under climate change. This systematic literature review analysed 80 peer-reviewed studies published between 2017 and 2024 to evaluate the methods used for projecting IWD under future climate scenarios. Due to differences in study design, model assumptions, and reporting formats, formal statistical comparison was not feasible. Instead, this review used evidence mapping to summarise the distribution and characteristics of the selected studies. Trends were identified for methodology, crop focus, and regional variation. maize, wheat, and rice dominated the research, collectively representing 70% of the studied crops. Although 40% of studies employed process-based simulation (PS) approaches, potential evapotranspiration (ET-P) methods were the most widely applied, used for 52% of the crops examined. Approximately 53% of studies projected an increase in IWD, 13% a decrease, and 28% reported mixed trends, depending on crop type, region, and scenario. Despite the relevance of CO2 fertilisation and climate-induced phenological changes, only 14% of studies accounted for both, with most incorporating either one or neither. The findings indicate that, despite the increasing complexity of PS models, simpler approaches such as ET-P and irrigation scheduling (Sch) continue to be widely used due to their lower data and resource demands. These methods potentially overlook crucial climate-sensitive processes, which may introduce bias into IWD projections. This review highlights how methodological choices can influence long-term projections of climate change impacts. The recommended research roadmap in this review would guide future studies to compare different IWD projection methodologies under identical climate, crop, soil, and crop/irrigation management conditions to achieve more robust and reliable projections and decision-making tools.

title: Setting the standard? Comparison of the implementation of decision-support modeling standards in Australia and the Netherlands
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): J.O.E. Remmers, J.H.A. Guillaume, L.A. Melsen
abstract: Choices during model development can substantially affect its outcomes, raising concerns about accountability when these outcomes inform decision-making. One way to address accountability is through modeling standards. Yet, standards may seem at odds with expert judgment and the specificity of modeling question, raising questions about who initiates the standards, and how they are established and enforced in practice. We examine the initiation, development and establishment of hydrological modeling standards in two contrasting cases: the development of standard software for the Murray-Darling Basin in Australia, and the formulation of modeling guidelines in the Netherlands. In both cases, standards were introduced with the aim to address elements of accountability. We found that consensus played a central role, which required flexibility in the standardization, diluting its effect. Moreover, standards tend to prioritize certain ways of working, risking that certain methods lose value without any apparent reason. Like models themselves, standardization is not neutral, demanding careful development, application, evolution, maintenance and reflection.

title: Future climate and land-use change reshape watershed best management practices portfolio for nutrient control
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yuanxin Ren, Hangzhen Zhang, Shuo Cheng, Bingqian Liu, Lin Ji, Jun Xia, Dandong Cheng
abstract: Understanding how hydrological and biogeochemical processes jointly regulate nutrient cycling in Earth’s Critical Zone is essential for adaptive watershed management under climate and land-use change. Here, Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (CMIP6-SSPs) climate and land-use scenarios were coupled with the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) to quantify future nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) losses in the Jialing River Basin, a major tributary of the upper Yangtze River. A fixing-changing scenario framework was used to separate the effects of climate change, land-use/land-cover change (LUCC) and their interaction, while an entropy-weighted assessment screened fertilizer reduction, no tillage, vegetative filter strips, grassed waterways and reforestation under nutrient-reduction, cost and yield-loss constraints. By 2055, all SSPs projected warmer and wetter conditions and a shift toward higher forest cover. These coupled changes produced divergent nutrient responses: N losses decreased by 1.90–3.50 × 106 kg yr−1, whereas P losses increased by 2.00–2.77 × 105 kg yr−1. LUCC dominated N-loss reduction under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5, contributing 60.28% and 58.48%, respectively, whereas climate change dominated P-loss increase across SSPs, contributing 44.21–69.15%. These results indicate that forest expansion enhanced N retention but did not fully offset runoff- and erosion-driven P mobilization. Historically, the preferred best management practice (BMP) portfolio required 80% fertilizer reduction and wider vegetative filter strips. Under future SSPs, however, all scenarios favored a less intensive 70% fertilizer-reduction portfolio with narrower filter strips, reducing TN by 67.211–71.356% and TP by 53.796–61.376% while lowering yield and cost pressure. Overall, BMP portfolios selected under historical conditions may become over-intensive or poorly targeted under future climate-LUCC settings. Adaptive nutrient management should therefore evaluate nutrient-specific drivers, implementation costs and yield-loss constraints simultaneously.

title: Three Gorges Reservoir operations regulate nitrogen transport and transformation via hydrology-sediment-carbon interactions
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Bei Nie, Yu Bai, Wei Zha, Shan Zhang, Miaomiao Chen
abstract: The global proliferation of reservoir construction has fundamentally altered nitrogen cycling across spatiotemporal scales. However, uncertainties persist regarding natural and anthropogenic regulation impacts on nitrogen transport-transformation processes in the reservoir, limiting the knowledge of accurately predicting different nitrogen components. Incorporating characteristics of sediment-mediated and drying-wetting process in the Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR), this study developed a novel Hydro-Sediment-Biogeochemical Model (HSBM) to systematically evaluate synergistic effects of reservoir operational schemes, sediment fluxes, and carbon inputs on nitrogen transport and transformation. The HSBM revealed that nitrogen dynamics in the TGR were engineered by three key drivers: reservoir operation, sediment load, and carbon input. Specifically, reservoir operation drove decreases in NH4 +-N and NO3 −-N concentrations that were inversely correlated with water level and impoundment duration, while nitrogen emissions scaled linearly with the drying-rewetting coefficient Kz , showing the strongest regulation during frequent fluctuating periods. Increased sediment loads suppressed nitrogen concentrations in water column while exponentially enhancing nitrogen emissions, with peak corresponding to low-water-level season. Similar to sediment load, regulation of carbon input on nitrogen transformation was stronger, especially with a linear growth relationship between the carbon augmentation coefficient (Kax) and nitrogen emissions (2–18% increase per Kax unit). Mechanistically, these dynamics are collectively regulated by reservoir-mediated nitrogen cycling, specifically via expansion of drying-rewetting zones, sediment-associated adsorption and nitrification–denitrification coupling, and carbon-stimulated denitrification. These findings provide a process-based framework to support adaptive nitrogen management strategies in reservoir systems.

title: Global cropland expansion amplifies the risk of compound dry and hot events under climate change
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Haiyang Tu, Guoyong Leng, Linfei Yu, Lei Yao, Jiali Qiu, Lubin Han
abstract: Compound Dry and Hot Events (CDHEs) pose significant threats to global food security, with their frequency and severity projected to escalate under future climate change. However, the combined impacts of climate change and cropland expansion on CDHEs exposure across varying severity levels remain underexplored globally. Using climate model projections from CMIP6 and dynamic cropland maps under four Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSPs), we assess global cropland exposure to CDHEs, categorized into mild, moderate, severe, extreme, and exceptional severities, and identify key drivers. Our findings reveal a consistent increase in global cropland exposure to CDHEs under all future warming scenarios, with exceptional CDHEs contributing the most significant rise (50.86% increase by 2070–2099), followed by moderate (15.23%), severe (14.43%), extreme (13.79%), and mild (5.69%) events. Northern South America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of Asia face the largest exposure increases, exacerbating vulnerabilities due to limited adaptation capacity. Attribution analysis indicates that climate change drives exposure increases under SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5, while cropland expansion is the primary driver under SSP2-4.5 (contributing 42.24% by 2070–2099). Crucially, the interaction term becomes increasingly important, contributing 15–25% by 2070–2099 and rising with CDHEs severity, as new cropland is expanding into areas where CDHEs are intensifying rapidly. These findings highlight the urgent need for targeted climate mitigation and adaptive land-use policies to reduce CDHEs risks, particularly in vulnerable regions, to safeguard global food production.

title: A mechanistic water erosion–carbon model integrating the soil aggregate fractal dimension
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Jinquan Huang, Yingtao Wu, Yi Zhu, Li Li, Wenjun Yang, Jigen Liu, Xiaolan Liu, Lu Zhang, Jiayu Liu, Jiapei Tian
abstract: Water erosion can serve as both a carbon source and a carbon sink in the global carbon cycle, but models often neglect soil structural dynamics, leading to biased soil organic carbon (SOC) transport predictions. We integrate soil aggregate fractal dimension (D) into water erosion–carbon model, combining controlled flume experiments with mechanistic simulations. The framework unifies aggregate protection, selective transport, threshold fragmentation, and dissolved organic carbon loss, with D as the key structural determinant of SOC dynamics. Under low-intensity erosion (0.16 m/s), runoff causes the selective removal of carbon-poor particles, resulting in a ∼ 9% enrichment in surface SOC concentration (g kg–1) (r = –0.86). However, mass balance consistency analysis reveals that this apparent increase is a concentration effect due to soil mass loss rather than a net carbon stock gain. In contrast, medium- to high-intensity erosion (≥ 0.24 m/s) causes aggregates breakdown and 25–30% SOC loss (r > 0.89). Our model delivers high prediction accuracy (R2 > 0.90), and sensitivity analysis confirms that D is the dominant parameter (S1 = 0.51; St = 0.83). Compared with empirical and process-based models, this approach greatly improves SOC prediction under dynamic erosion by explicitly distinguishes concentration effects from stock changes, providing a more credible interpretation of the system as a carbon source. We reveal that low-intensity erosion induces a transient enrichment of SOC concentration rather than a net carbon sink, whereas high-intensity erosion generates substantial carbon sources. Employing fractal dimension as a core predictor, our mechanistic model improves carbon cycle assessments and supports soil conservation and climate strategies.

title: Non-contact discharge estimation using physics-informed neural networks and CNN-enhanced image velocimetry
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yen-Cheng Lin, Cheng-Wei Wu, Hao-Che Ho
abstract: Accurate river discharge estimation using non-contact techniques remains a fundamental challenge in hydrology, particularly under complex field conditions. This study proposes a physics-informed framework for non-contact river discharge estimation by integrating CNN-enhanced Large-Scale Particle Image Velocimetry (CNN-LSPIV) with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). The shallow water continuity equation is incorporated into the loss function to enforce mass conservation during velocity refinement and water depth inversion. Two inversion strategies are developed: a velocity-refinement mode (PINN-VR), which refines CNN-LSPIV velocity fields prior to leapfrog-based depth integration, and a direct depth inversion mode (PINN-DDI), which simultaneously reconstructs velocity and depth fields through global physics-constrained optimization. The framework is validated using laboratory flume experiments under three bed configurations (smooth, lateral composite, and longitudinal composite beds) and further evaluated through unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based field observations with acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) validation. CNN-LSPIV substantially improves surface velocity measurement relative to conventional LSPIV. PINN-VR shows superior depth reconstruction under lateral bed configurations, whereas PINN-DDI performs best under longitudinal bed variations because its globally optimized formulation reduces sensitivity to directional error accumulation. Under composite bed conditions, both PINN-based strategies improve discharge estimation relative to CNN-LSPIV, with PINN-DDI yielding the lowest discharge errors. These results demonstrate that embedding physical constraints into image-based flow reconstruction improves the physical consistency and relative accuracy of non-contact discharge estimation, highlighting its potential for more reliable field-scale applications in complex natural river environments.

title: Mechanism-guided dynamic machine learning overcomes environmental non-stationarity in algal bloom prediction
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shujie Xu, Wenyu Zhang, Yong Tian, Shu-Chien Hsu, Chunmiao Zheng
abstract: Algal bloom prediction under environmental non-stationarity remains challenging, as historical regulatory thresholds frequently fail due to ecological concept drift. This study developed an integrated framework for Hong Kong rivers utilizing Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and Multiple Regression Trees (MRT) to extract complex structural associations and historical tipping points. However, rigorous generalization testing revealed threshold deactivation. Static MRT-guided discretization models collapsed (recall score = 0.32, ROC_AUC = 0.50) because long-term pollution baseline reductions drove phytoplankton adaptation. Permutation feature importance confirmed a mechanistic paradigm shift, transitioning from historical phosphorus constraints to complex nitrogenous limitations. To overcome this drift, we propose a novel dual-stage decision-support framework. While MRT is retained to establish interpretable, long-term policy baselines, continuous-variable Machine Learning is deployed to process the full environmental context, achieving highly adaptive, dynamic operational forecasting (recall score = 0.68, ROC_AUC = 0.89). Ultimately, this framework mitigates high-dimensional blind spots, providing a resilient blueprint for proactive watershed management under shifting ecological realities.

title: A novel high-resolution downscaling method for daily extreme precipitation using Sentinel-5P cloud parameters
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yuting Luo, Hongwei Zeng, Junbin Li, Yang Chen, Jiangyuan Zeng, Miao Zhang, Hantian Wu, Lu Sun, Bingfang Wu
abstract: Statistical downscaling of daily extreme precipitation remains challenging due to the limited availability of optical observations during rainfall events, delayed vegetation responses to precipitation, and the coarse resolution of soil moisture and reanalysis-based predictors. To address these limitations, this study proposed a cloud variable based DeepGeo Downscaler (DGD) framework for daily extreme precipitation downscaling. The DGD used daily cloud physical parameters derived from Sentinel-5P as physically meaningful and near real time predictors and employed a hybrid of convolutional neural network (CNN) and geographically weighted regression (GWR) to explore the complex nonlinear relationship between environmental variables and extreme precipitation. The DGD framework was applied to downscale the CHM_PRE V2 daily precipitation product from 0.1° to 0.01° for an extreme rainfall event from August 2 to 6, 2023 in the black soil region of Northeast China and an unprecedented extreme precipitation event in Zhengzhou from July 17 to 22, 2021. Compared with random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), artificial neural network (ANN), GWR, CNN, and hybrid models including GWR-RF (GWRF) and GWR-XGB (GXGB), DGD achieved the best overall performance. DGD reduced the overestimation of light precipitation and underestimation of heavy precipitation while substantially suppressing the “boxy” artifacts commonly observed in RF, XGB, GWRF, and GXGB based results. Compared with the original CHM_PRE V2 product, the final downscaled results from DGD substantially enhanced the spatial detail of the original CHM_PRE V2 product while maintaining similar accuracy against rain gauge daily precipitation observations. Overall, the results indicate that the DGD framework driven by Sentinel-5P cloud physical parameters provides an effective approach for daily extreme precipitation downscaling, with potential applications in flood forecasting, hydrological modeling, and agricultural risk assessment.

title: Causal structure and threshold characteristics of vapor pressure deficit regulation across different climate zones in China
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yang Han, Zhi-Gang Yan, Peng Zhou, Jia-Hui Qin, Chuan-Ye Hu, Yun-Cheng Jiang, Qing-Zhou Lv
abstract: Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) is a key indicator of atmospheric aridity and land–atmosphere interaction risk, yet its dominant processes, information structure, and threshold responses across China’s climate zones remain poorly understood. Using VPD and related meteorological and hydrological variables during 1980–2022, this study grouped the drivers into Circulation Background (CB), Non-local Moisture Transport (NMT), and Local Response and Feedback (LRF), and integrated directional causality detection, information decomposition, and threshold analysis to reveal the dominant mechanisms and nonlinear responses of VPD in China. Mean VPD was 0.54 kPa, with high values in the northwestern inland and low values over the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau and the northeastern semi-humid region. VPD was highest in Mt-A (0.98 kPa) and lowest in Pt-Sa (0.25 kPa). The dominant controls showed clear zonal differentiation, with humid and semi-humid regions mainly controlled by CB, Mg-H by NMT, and arid and plateau regions by LRF; precipitation exerted the strongest causal effect in both Mt-A and Pt-Sa, with peak ρ values of 0.918 and 0.695. Information decomposition showed that CB and NMT were dominated by synergistic information (88.52% and 79.27% of pixels, respectively), whereas LRF showed a lower proportion of synergistic dominance (64.25%) but higher unique and redundant contributions (0.236 and 0.148). A total of 21 robust threshold relationships were identified, with more consistent response directions for local hydrological factors and stronger regional divergence for CB- and NMT-related variables. Overall, VPD in China is regulated by climate-zone-dependent control pathways rather than a single uniform mechanism, and the identified causal pathways and threshold responses provide a process-based basis for assessing regional atmospheric drying risk, diagnosing water-limitation transitions, and developing climate-zone-specific adaptation strategies.

title: Three-dimensional reservoir characterization from hard and soft data based on latent diffusion model
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Ce Zhang, Gang Liu, Qiyu Chen, Zhesi Cui, Hongfeng Fang, Dajie Chen, Junping Xiong, Kaikai Zhang
abstract: The reliability of three-dimensional (3D) reservoir modeling directly influences the accuracy of subsurface resource evaluation and development decisions. Traditional modeling methods primarily rely on sparse borehole data. Consequently, they struggle to fully integrate multi-source information, such as seismic interpretations. This leads to significant uncertainty in the modeling results. To address this issue, this study proposes a Soft-Hard Constrained Latent Diffusion Model (SH-LDM). This method integrates the hard data from boreholes and soft data from seismic interpretations to provide global structural information. It effectively constrains the modeling process, thereby enhancing model reliability. The SH-LDM first maps high-dimensional geological models into a low-dimensional latent space for learning and generation. This significantly reduces the complexity of model training and inference. Building on this, a conditional fusion strategy with multi-level feature embeddings is constructed. It simultaneously introduces the exact matching constraints of hard data and the trend guidance of soft data within the latent space. This achieves both strict control over hard data points and a coherent representation of the overall structural morphology. This study validates the effectiveness of the SH-LDM on non-stationary 2D and 3D reservoir datasets. The consistency of the generated model with training images in both local and global features is evaluated using the minimum acceptance criterion. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons with various benchmark models demonstrate the superior performance of the SH-LDM in terms of modeling accuracy and statistical consistency. Ablation studies and sensitivity analyses demonstrate that incorporating soft data significantly enhances the reliability of modeling results. Furthermore, the SH-LDM exhibits a certain degree of robustness to noise present in the soft data.

title: Deep learning-enhanced sequential updating of hydraulic parameters and state variables in groundwater models
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Huiyang Qiu, Zejun Wang, Wanzhou Wang, Qi Li, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jiangjiang Zhang
abstract: As a fundamental component of the hydrological cycle, groundwater systems play a critical role in sustaining ecosystems, securing water resources, and supporting socio-economic development. However, substantial uncertainties remain in both parameter estimation and state prediction, limiting the reliability of groundwater models. Improving predictive accuracy therefore requires the sequential, real-time updating of model states and parameters using newly acquired observations. Although the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) has been widely applied for this purpose, its performance can degrade in non-Gaussian and strongly nonlinear systems, for which approaches based on transformations or multiple-point geostatistics have been proposed as effective remedies. In this study, we present an alternative strategy by introducing a deep learning (DL)-based update strategy into the EnKF framework, resulting in a hybrid ensemble filtering approach that integrates DL-based nonlinear updates with Kalman-type linear updates, termed EF(DL-K). The proposed method is designed to more effectively fuse information from numerical models and observations in complex groundwater systems. Compared with the conventional EnKF and a purely DL-based ensemble filter [EF(DL)], EF(DL-K) exhibits enhanced flexibility and robustness in the sequential updating of both hydraulic parameters and state variables in subsurface aquifer systems. The impact of the placement of the DL step within the EF(DL-K) framework is systematically investigated. The results show that EF(DL-K) yields assimilation performance comparable to that of the EnKF under Gaussian conditions, while achieving substantially improved joint state-parameter estimation under non-Gaussian conditions. Overall, EF(DL-K) provides a promising filtering-based data assimilation framework for real-time model-data integration and the dynamic updating of both parameters and state variables in groundwater systems.

title: Multi-resolution downscaling of inundation extents using deep learning
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Chanyu Yang, Fiachra O’Loughlin
abstract: The application of deep learning models for downscaling flood inundation extents has been brought into focus in recent years. Considered as an alternative to physics-based models, deep learning models have the advantage of faster computational efficiency with acceptable accuracy. However, recent approaches in downscaling flood inundation extents have either: (1) taken a considerable amount of computational effort for model training; (2) focused on large flood events or large flood extents; or (3) only considered downscaling using a small number of scenarios and often only one. Inspired by the hybrid modelling approach, this study uses a hydrodynamic model to generate a time-series of low-resolution flood inundation extents and depths. This series is then downscaled into high-resolution flood inundation extents using a generative deep learning model. The proposed method is applied to an urbanised area in Dublin, Ireland, which covers 16.3 km 2 . Ten combinations of low- and high-resolution flood maps are used to evaluate the models’ performance. The results show that: (1) there is no obvious relationship between model performance and the magnitude of downscaling; (2) a deeper model architecture can provide better predictions and is more robust in classifying deeper flood depths without increasing prediction computational cost; (3) 18 times downscaling (90 m to 5 m) was found to be the most efficient and accurate model tested. The proposed deep learning model offers potential for real-time flood inundation forecasting, where coarser, faster inundation models can be downscaled to useful inundation maps without a significant loss in accuracy and without real-time computational overhead.

title: Tracking long-term dynamics of soil salinization using a model combining convolutional neural network and Transformer
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Haohao Liu, Bin Guo, Xingchao Yang, Yilong Liu, Yujie Huo, Yuehua Zhong, Jianlin Wang
abstract: Accurately tracking long-term soil salinization dynamics remains challenging, particularly in highly heterogeneous regions. Here, we propose a novel approach based on the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-Transformer model for the spatiotemporal prediction of soil salinization using multi-source remote sensing data. The model adopts a cascaded structure that integrates the capabilities of CNN and Transformer to extract spatial contextual information and capture global spatiotemporal dependencies, enabling robust modeling of salinization dynamics. We compared the CNN-Transformer model with common machine learning and deep learning models in terms of soil salt content (SSC) prediction performance. To enhance model interpretability, we used SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to quantify the contributions of salinization-related features to SSC prediction. Using the proposed method, we achieved dynamic monitoring of soil salinization in the Yellow River Delta (YRD). The results indicate the following: (1) The CNN-Transformer model achieved the highest prediction accuracy (R2 = 0.71, RMSE = 3.36 g kg−1, RPIQ = 2.24) and demonstrated good spatial generalization under spatially independent validation, with spatial prediction results exhibiting fine-grained local details and accurately capturing the complex spatial distribution of soil salinity. (2) Vegetation type factors (VTFs) and the topographic factor contributed most to SSC prediction, followed by salinity indices, vegetation indices, and soil moisture-related indices. (3) Overall, from 2002 to 2022, soil salinization in the YRD was alleviated. Salinization intensity was markedly lower after autumn harvest than after spring plowing, primarily due to seasonal climatic-hydrological variations and the leaching effects of summer precipitation and irrigation. This study provides a paradigm combining deep learning with multi-source remote sensing data for the dynamic monitoring of soil salinization.

title: Seasonal controls, recharge thresholds, and hydrological memory in karst groundwater dynamics revealed by interpretable deep learning
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Linxian Huang, Henghua Zhu, Qichen Hao, Yong Xiao, Hao Liang, Zhenghe Xu, Chuanshun Zhi, Xiaonong Hu
abstract: Quantifying groundwater responses to climate forcing in karst systems remains difficult because recharge is nonlinear, threshold-dependent, and modulated by antecedent storage. We developed an interpretable deep learning framework to diagnose seasonal controls, threshold-like recharge behavior, and hydrological memory in the Baotu Spring karst watershed of northern China. A 66-year groundwater-level (GWL) record was segmented to isolate the period primarily controlled by meteorological forcing. Daily precipitation (P) and temperature (T) data from 2012 to 2024 were then used to train a long short-term memory model, and Expected Gradients together with Additive Decomposition quantified driver contributions and temporal memory. The model accurately reproduced groundwater dynamics in independent testing (Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) = 0.93, coefficient of determination (R2) = 0.95, and root mean square error (RMSE) = 0.155 m). Attribution analysis revealed a clear seasonal hierarchy: summer exerted the strongest model-attributed control on groundwater variability, whereas autumn contributed secondarily through delayed recharge transmission. At the annual scale, P attributions became more positive when annual P exceeded 620 mm and GWLs were above 28.5 m, suggesting a threshold-like shift toward stronger positive model-attributed GWL sensitivity. At the event scale, the strongest positive P-related attribution occurred for daily P of 11.4–41.3 mm; smaller events were consistent with vadose-zone replenishment, whereas larger events suggested reduced marginal recharge efficiency due to greater runoff partitioning. High-GWL events were dominated by rainfall forcing, with short memory in summer, whereas winter rainfall memory extended to approximately five months; low-GWL events were linked to persistent P deficits, elevated T, and unfavorable rainfall-intensity distributions. These model-derived indicators support recharge assessment and groundwater-drought early warning in heterogeneous karst systems.

title: Deep learning approaches for streamflow flash drought prediction across the contiguous United States
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Sophia Bakar, Hoang Hai Nguyen, Hyunglok Kim, Venkataraman Laskhmi
abstract: Reliable drought prediction is crucial for early warning and decision-making regarding drought-related disasters. Flash droughts, characterized by their rapid onset and severe impacts, are challenging to predict and present critical challenges to water resource management. Specifically, streamflow flash droughts (SFDs) are significant as they directly influence water supply for irrigation, industry, and domestic use. Traditional hydrologic models and drought early warning systems are primarily designed to capture slowly evolving drought conditions and often fail to represent rapid transitions in streamflow that characterize the onset of SFDs. Despite increasing attention to the identification and characterization of SFDs, their prediction remains unexplored. This study evaluates the ability of different deep learning architectures, especially the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), in comparison to the widespread baseline Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model and a two-source LSTM incorporating static catchment attributes, to predict SFDs based on streamflow percentiles. The model training and performance evaluation were conducted using hydroclimatic datasets from 671 Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies (CAMELS) catchments in the contiguous United States. Performance was evaluated using standard accuracy and event detection metrics. Results show that the TFT achieved the highest overall performance, with a median KGE of 0.87, RMSE of 0.13, MAE of 0.10, and a correlation coefficient of 0.91, outperforming the LSTM with static features (median KGE = 0.81) and the baseline LSTM (KGE = 0.78). In terms of detecting SFDs, the TFT showed the highest median detection rate and lowest miss rate across all models. These improvements were consistent across most catchments and hydroclimatic regions, indicating robust performance gains relative to LSTM-based approaches, although some regions with complex hydrologic behavior remained challenging for all models. While model performance varied across hydroclimatic regions, particularly in data-sparse or hydrologically complex areas, the integration of static attributes and attention-based mechanisms consistently improved predictive skill. These findings demonstrate that Transformer-based models can improve prediction of rapid streamflow changes associated with the onset of SFDs; however, the results are based on deterministic predictions and do not explicitly quantify predictive uncertainty. These findings contribute new insights into the spatial patterns and physical drivers of model performance under non-stationary climate conditions.

title: MvReNowcast: Disentangling radar product features for improved nowcasting of raincloud evolution
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Hongxu Zhu, Ji Chen, Xunlai Chen, Waikin Wong, Chao Tan, Hongyi Yao, Xianqi Jiang
abstract: Accurate radar echo extrapolation is fundamental for real-time monitoring and nowcasting severe rainfall events. However, most existing deep learning approaches tend to formulate this task in a simple manner, overlooking the physical mechanisms that govern radar echo evolution. This limitation restricts model interpretability and degrades nowcast reliability under dynamically evolving weather conditions. To this end, this study proposes a physics-informed deep learning framework that explicitly integrates prior hydrometeorological information into the radar echo extrapolation process. The evolution of radar reflectivity is decomposed into two distinct yet complementary components: advection and residual intensity evolution. By coupling both components within a unified neural architecture, the framework captures both large-scale displacement and small-scale intensity evolution of radar echoes. Numerical experiments conducted on multi-temporal radar datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the conventional data-driven benchmark model in both nowcasting accuracy and spatial consistency. The decomposition method not only reduces prediction errors but also enhances the physical interpretability of deep learning model outputs, allowing a more transparent attribution of echo evolution to dominant hydrometeorological processes. Quantitative verification confirms the MvReNowcast model’s systematic superiority over the Baseline. The performance gap widens significantly with time, reaching relative improvements exceeding 120.8 % on CSI30 and 52.9 % on CSI40 at the 120-minute forecast horizon. This study highlights the potential of physics-informed separation strategies in bridging the gap between data-driven and process-based modeling for rainfall nowcasting. The proposed approach provides a physically consistent and computationally efficient framework that can be extended to other hydrometeorological prediction tasks.

title: Progressive scale convolutional network for spatio-temporal downscaling of soil moisture: A case study over the Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Ziyu Zhou, Keyan Hu, Ling Zhang, Zhaohui Xue, Yutian Fang, Yusha Zheng
abstract: Soil moisture (SM) plays a critical role in hydrological and meteorological processes. High-resolution SM can be obtained by combining coarse passive microwave data with fine-scale auxiliary variables. However, the inversion of SM at the temporal scale is hindered by the incompleteness of surface auxiliary factors. To address this issue, first, we introduce validated high temporal resolution ERA5-Land variables into the downscaling process of the low-resolution SMAP SM product. Subsequently, we design a progressive scale convolutional network (PSCNet), at the core of which are two innovative components: a multi-frequency temporal fusion module (MFTF) for capturing temporal dynamics, and a bespoke squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block designed to preserve fine-grained spatial details. Using this approach, we obtained seamless SM products for the Tibetan Plateau (TP) from 2016 to 2018 at 10-km spatial and 3-hour temporal resolution. The experimental results on the TP demonstrated the following: 1) In the satellite product validation, the PSCNet exhibited comparable accuracy and lower error, with a mean R of 0.881, outperforming other methods. 2) In the in-situ site validation, PSCNet consistently ranked among the top three models in terms of the R metric across all sites, while also showing superior performance in overall error reduction. 3) In the temporal generalization validation, the feasibility of using high-temporal resolution ERA5-Land variables for downscaling was confirmed, as all methods maintained an average relative error within 6% and 2% in terms of R and ubRMSE, respectively. 4) In the temporal dynamics and visualization validation, PSCNet effectively captured temporal sensitivity and fine-grained spatial heterogeneity. Overall, PSCNet provides a promising solution for spatio-temporal downscaling by effectively modeling the intricate spatio-temporal relationships in SM data.

title: Deep learning-based downscaling of SMAP data for surface and root-zone soil moisture mapping
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Saman Rabiei, Ebrahim Babaeian, Sabine Grunwald
abstract: Accurate soil moisture (SM) information at sub-kilometer resolution is essential for hydrologic modeling, weather forecasting, precision irrigation, and drought monitoring. Satellite missions such as Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) have transformed global SM monitoring, but their coarse resolution, shallow sensing depth, and multi-day revisit cycle limit local-scale applications. Retrieval accuracy further declines over dense vegetation and complex terrain. This study presents a deep learning downscaling framework that integrates convolutional neural networks and long short-term memory networks (CNN-LSTM) to produce daily SM maps at 100 m resolution for surface (5 cm) and root-zone (20 cm) depths. The model was trained with seven years of SM data from ∼ 650 stations across the U.S., using dynamic predictors from SMAP and MODIS (i.e., brightness temperature, roughness coefficient, surface reflectance in red, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared) and static features predictors from elevation, land cover, and Soil Landscapes of the U.S. (SOLUS100) databases. Compared to SMAP level-3 SM, the CNN-LSTM improved surface SM accuracy, with median correlation coefficient (R) increasing from 0.61 to 0.82, unbiased root mean square error (ubRMSE) decreasing from 0.06 to 0.05 cm3 cm−3, and Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) increasing from 0.30 to 0.61. Root-zone SM achieved R ∼ 0.72, ubRMSE ∼ 0.05 cm3 cm−3 and KGE ∼ 0.53. The model also outperformed SMAP in forested and mountainous areas, capturing SMAP sub-pixel SM variability across the three well-instrumented watersheds and Florida. In Florida, where no training data was used, performance decreased but was still better than SMAP. These findings indicate that the CNN-LSTM framework bridges the spatial resolution gap in SM products and support small scale agricultural and hydrological applications.

title: Decoupled storm-phase source dynamics of dissolved and particulate organic matter in an agricultural watershed
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yun Kyung Lee, Ho-Yeon Park, Haeseong Oh, Seung-Hee Kim, Kyung-Hoon Shin, Jae-In Kim, Byung Joon Lee, Jin Hur
abstract: Storm events strongly regulate organic matter (OM) mobilization in agricultural watersheds, yet potential differences in the source evolution of dissolved and particulate OM (DOM and POM) across storm phases remain poorly constrained. Here, we conducted hydrograph phase-resolved storm sampling during two rainfall events and applied end-member mixing analysis (EMMA) to quantify phase-specific OM source dynamics. Source contributions were traced using δ13C–δ15N for POM and fluorescence indices for DOM. Bulk water-quality parameters and POM concentrations increased with discharge during the monitored events, closely tracking suspended solids and particulate nutrients, suggesting cumulative mobilization under event-specific hydrological conditions rather than a clear first-flush-like decline. EMMA results indicated highly dynamic POM source evolution, with leaf litter/riparian vegetation initially contributing 60–67% of POM during the early stage but declining to ∼29% near peak flow as soil-derived POM increased sharply to ∼51%, consistent with discharge-associated particulate mobilization and progressive source-area activation during storm progression. In contrast, DOM showed comparatively buffered dynamics and a strong manure/compost-like signature within the FI–BIX-based EMMA framework, contributing ∼37–58% across storm phases, suggesting persistent leaching and flushing from manure-amended areas once source areas became connected to active flow paths. Source-specific OC fluxes were concentrated in short high-flow windows, with sharp POC pulses near peak discharge and more persistent DOC export into recession. These findings indicate decoupled POM and DOM transport during the monitored storms and highlight the value of phase-resolved, OM-specific source apportionment for interpreting storm-driven carbon export and informing targeted watershed management.

title: The impact of seasonal hydroclimatic variability and vegetation dynamics on long-term nutrient trends − Evidence from an agriculture-dominated watershed draining to the Baltic Sea
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Beata Plutova, Carlos Gonzales-Inca, Elham Kakaei Lafdani, Iiro Seppä, Elina Kasvi, Maria Kämäri, Petteri Alho, Ville Kankare
abstract: Excess nutrient loads, particularly nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), play a significant role in the degradation of global water quality and aquatic ecosystems. The amount of these nutrients in rivers is significantly affected by the increasing hydroclimatic variability, coupled with changes in land use intensity. This study assessed trends over 30 years in total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) in the Aurajoki catchment, Southwest Finland, and evaluated how land use intensity and seasonal hydroclimatic variability influence nutrient dynamics. The utilized data consisted of long-term monitoring records of nutrient concentrations, discharge, temperature, precipitation, and the Landsat imagery series. Prior to the analyses, the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), Accumulated Winter Season Severity Index (AWSSI), and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) were used to characterize hydroclimatic variability and land use intensity. Data were analyzed using Mann-Kendall statistics to assess trends and generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) to evaluate the impact of land use intensity and hydroclimatic variability. Results showed a decrease in annual TN concentrations and TN loads, while TP trends remained stable. The seasonal trend test revealed significant TN and TP increases in fall and decreases in spring. The modelling results revealed that NDVI had a significant impact only on nutrient concentrations, whereas the effects of hydroclimatic class were limited to nutrient loads and varied according to different combinations of season and NDVI. These findings highlight the relevance of seasonal hydroclimatic variability and land use intensity when assessing nutrient dynamics, particularly in the context of climate change and water protection strategies.

title: Pre-monsoon flow-path switching regulates downstream dissolved organic carbon dynamics in a high-alpine river on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Dong Zhang, Yindong Tong, Xiaodong Li, Yanli Sun, Jiajun Han
abstract: High-altitude semi-arid rivers undergo rapid hydrological reorganization during the pre-monsoon season, yet the respective roles of antecedent warming, initial thaw, and changes in hydrological connectivity in regulating the downstream export of dissolved organic carbon remain poorly understood. To clarify these controls, we conducted high-frequency monitoring at 3-day intervals in the Lhasa River Basin on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau from March to early July 2024. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC), dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), major ions, and stable isotopes (δ13C-DOC, δ13C-DIC, δD, and δ18O) were measured to trace water sources and carbon dynamics. Our results reveal a pronounced pre-monsoon hydrochemical turning point, driven primarily by seasonal flow-path switching rather than by direct glacier meltwater inputs. During the early pre-monsoon period (March–mid-May), river discharge was dominated by groundwater, and DIC and major ions increased gradually while DOC remained relatively low. Distinct hydrochemical and isotopic shifts occurred around mid-May, coinciding more closely with sharp increases in air temperature. After mid-May, the river transitioned to a more mixed hydrological regime, as indicated by marked shifts in water isotopes (δ18O: −17.0‰ to −14.5‰; d-excess: 9.3‰ to 13.5‰), declining DIC and major ion concentrations, increasing DOC concentrations (0.7–2.0 mg C·L−1), and progressively more depleted δ13C-DOC (−25.8‰ to −28.5‰) and δ13C-DIC values (−4.5‰ to −6.9‰). These coupled patterns suggest that antecedent warming and initial thaw preconditioned near-surface hydrological connectivity and reorganized flow paths, thereby increasing the DOC mobilization from shallow organic-rich source areas while diluting groundwater-derived DIC and major ions with low-solute near-surface waters, including thaw and snowmelt contributions. Comparisons with glacier-fed streams further indicate that glacier meltwater contributes only marginally to downstream DOC in the Lhasa River. Overall, our findings show that pre-monsoon carbon dynamics in this high-alpine river are controlled primarily by thermally driven hydrological switching superimposed on early-season thaw, highlighting the sensitivity of alpine carbon export to short-lived connectivity pulses on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.

title: A four-decade satellite record of coupled lake area and water quality responses to climate changes and human activities in Northwest China
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Ming Shen, Yuan Liu, Tianci Qi, Changjiang Liu, Zhigang Cao, Zhenyu Tan, Juhua Luo, Hongtao Duan
abstract: Understanding the coupled dynamics of lake (including natural lakes and reservoirs) water quantity and quality remains scarce, both regionally and globally. This study establishes a novel remote sensing–based framework to assess coupled lake quantity–quality dynamics, represented by lake area and Secchi disk depth (SDD), and to classify lakes into four ecological–hydrological trajectories (Types I–IV). Applying this framework to Landsat imagery (1986–2023) across 729 lakes (>1 km2) in Xinjiang, China. We found that lakes generally experienced area expansion and improved clarity (Sen’s slope > 0, p 0, p 0.1). Partial least squares regression (PLSR) revealed that temperature and cropland area were the primary drivers in northern and southern Xinjiang, reflecting the joint impacts of climate change and human water use and management. Conversely, precipitation and the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) dominated in eastern Xinjiang, suggesting local hydroclimatic variability may offset the benefits of warming-induced glacier/snowmelt. This conceptual framework successfully links lake water quantity and quality, providing a scalable baseline for comprehensive lake assessments and sustainable water-resource management under climate change.

title: Incorporating variable source areas into rainfall-runoff pollutant export modeling for rural residential catchment
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Xuan Huang, Xu Yang, Yuhang Zhang, Man Lang, Ping Li, Kebing Chen, Dongli She, Yongqiu Xia
abstract: Rural non-point source pollution is primarily driven by rainfall runoff. The heterogeneous landscape of rural catchments, along with variable contributing source areas, result in complex pollutant export processes during rainfall events. Consequently, making accurate simulation of pollutant export during rainfall is both essential and challenging for effective water quality management. Existing Rainfall Runoff Model (RRM) assumes uniform contributing areas with exponential pollutant wash-off during rainfall, ignoring rural landscape complexity and dynamic expansion of contributing areas, leading to systematic errors during initial and peak rainfall periods. In this study, we propose a Modified Exponential Model (MEM) that integrates Variable Source Area (VSA) theory, using two parameters, α and β, which represent the maximum extent of VSA-contributing areas and their dynamic activation rates, respectively. The model was validated and applied to dissolved nitrogen (DN) and dissolved phosphorus (DP) modelling in rural residential catchments in the Yangtze River basin. We show that the MEM significantly outperformed RRM, particularly during medium and long-duration rainfall events (Regimes II and III), with Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) coefficients increasing by 0.15–0.24 for DN and 0.31–0.42 for DP. We also observed distinct parameter characteristics between pollutants: DN exhibited higher contributing area values (α: 0.076–0.924) than DP (α: 0.022–0.299). SHAP analysis demonstrated that runoff characteristics primarily modulate DN transport, while precipitation features more strongly influence DP dynamics. These findings not only deepen our understanding of rural pollutant export processes but also deliver a practical, interpretable modeling framework for water quality management in rural areas.

title: Trace element sources, migration and health risks associated with river-groundwater interaction: Insights from isotopes, fluorescence spectroscopy and Monte Carlo simulation
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Xu Yang, Muhan Li, Yiying Miao, Fuyang Huang, Zeyuan Liu, Hongli Ma, Ping Miao, Jigang Shi, Zengbao Zhang, Shen Qu, Ruihong Yu
abstract: The sources, migration pathways, and associated risks of trace elements (TEs) linked to river–groundwater interactions remain inadequately understood. This study integrated a Bayesian isotope mixing model (MixSIAR), a 222Rn mass balance model (RMBM), and Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) to elucidate TE dynamics in the Hangjin Section of the Yellow River, China. Groundwater exhibited markedly higher TE concentrations than surface water, accompanied by higher values of the entropy-weighted water quality index (EWQI) and heavy metal pollution index (HPI). The MixSIAR results indicated that dissolved Sr compositions were jointly controlled by natural and anthropogenic hydrogeochemical processes, including evaporite dissolution (15.53%), silicate weathering (14.10%), carbonate weathering (11.70%), irrigation water (15.98%), sewage (15.43%), municipal water (15.52%), and fertilizers (11.74%), thereby influencing TE occurrence and enrichment in the study area. Fluorescence indices indicated that dissolved organic matter, primarily derived from terrestrial and microbial sources, significantly influenced TE behavior through complexation and adsorption processes, particularly in groundwater. Groundwater discharge-mediated fluxes, particularly Li (0.0595–0.3114 × 10‒4 g/(s∙m)), Mn (0.0508–0.5994 × 10‒4 g/(s∙m)), and Sr (3.5427–12.4769 × 10‒4 g/(s∙m)), substantially affected water quality of the Yellow River. Health risk assessments indicated considerable hazards associated with TE-contaminated groundwater, with children being more vulnerable than adults. Spatially, TE enrichment and health risks were generally greater in the upper reaches than in the middle and lower reaches, while TE migration exhibited element-specific spatial variability. This integrated approach improves our understanding of TE cycling mechanisms mediated by river–groundwater interactions and provides scientific guidance for water resource protection and public health.

title: Time-series decomposition and stream metabolism reveal benthic control on particulate organic carbon transport from mixed-use Appalachian watersheds
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): William I. Ford, James Fox, Mindy Armstead, Andrea Erhardt
abstract: Algal carbon can be a significant energy source in stream ecosystems; however, knowledge is lacking regarding algal contributions to particulate organic carbon (POC) fluxes from mixed-use stream ecosystems and their potential implications for downstream waterways. We report a new four-year transported carbon elemental and isotopic dataset from a predominantly forested stream ecosystem in northwestern West Virginia, USA, carry out time series decomposition of the data, and compare our results to algae monitoring and ecosystem modelling to better understand the influence of algal carbon on these systems. Results show that variational mode decomposition (VMD) was more effective than empirical mode decomposition (EMD) for detecting in-stream process impacts on POC transport in the forested stream. Results from ecosystem modelling and significant modes from VMD point to benthic algal growth followed by heterotrophic stabilization resulting in residual algal C transport from the watershed during storm events as POC. The importance of the time lag and then carbon flux introduced by the algal stabilization process extends this paradigm to be inclusive of both open-canopied systems studied previously and predominantly closed-canopy systems, such as the one studied here. Contrary to results from open-canopy systems, the mixed-use Appalachian stream shows dual-peaks of algal carbon conveyance, starting in late winter-spring and again in late-summer to mid fall. Results provide evidence that mixed-use watersheds in Appalachia provide periodic contributions of labile POC enriched in algal C to the Ohio River, USA and thus merit further study regarding potential impacts on eutrophication and harmful algal blooms in the regulated rivers.

title: Modeling nutrient-driven water quality changes in Miyun Reservoir: An improved SWAT–Delft3D approach
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yan Jiang, Yiping Chen, Lijing Pang, Zhengfang Huang, Hongtao Zhao, Xuefeng Wu
abstract: Excessive nutrient input severely degrades reservoir water quality, yet reservoir responses to terrestrial pollution sources remain poorly quantified. This study developed an integrated watershed–reservoir simulation framework by coupling the SWAT model with the Delft3D model, where the Delft3D river module replaced SWAT’s channel routing module to better represent hydrological connectivity and nutrient transport across the overland–river–reservoir continuum. Following calibration and validation, the integrated model was applied to quantitatively evaluate the response of reservoir water quality under different hydrological year types (wet/normal/dry) to multi-source pollution control measures. The results revealed clear variations in the total nitrogen (TN) reduction efficacy of different pollution control measures. Among these, livestock manure recycling (utilization rate ≥ 90%) was the most effective, followed by township sewage treatment. In contrast, fertilizer reduction yielded limited benefits (TN reduction < 1%), while wastewater treatment upgrading had no significant effect under the tested scenarios. Hydrological conditions also influenced the effectiveness of these measures, with TN reductions of 2–6% in normal years but less than 1% in dry years. Spatially, inflow responses exhibited pronounced heterogeneity among tributaries. Analyses of tracer-based transport and mean residence time indicated that reservoir-scale buffering and transport delays constrain the rapid transmission of upstream load reductions to downstream outflows. These findings indicate that reservoir water-quality responses to watershed pollution-control measures are jointly influenced by pollution-source type, hydrological conditions, and variability among inflowing tributaries, highlighting the need to prioritize management strategies in drinking-water reservoir systems.

title: Catchment controls on nutrients at coastal outlets: a national typology for England and Wales
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Hassan Mohamed, Naomi Greenwood, Richard J. Cooper, Carolyn Graves, Yi He
abstract: Riverine nutrient concentrations at coastal outlets reflect upstream catchment controls and underpin nutrient flux estimates. Existing catchment classifications are not tailored to this scale, limiting their application for interpreting land-to-sea patterns and informing management of marine pressures. This study develops a data-driven typology for 178 coast-draining catchments across England and Wales, grouping them into eight types through geospatial characterisation and clustering. Nutrient concentrations (2000–2024) were retrieved from water quality archives at 271 near-tidal sites. The resulting typology is structured along a topographic gradient, further differentiated by dominant bedrock permeability. A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) confirmed significant differences between types for NH4 +, NO3 − and PO4 3− (p < 0.001), with a significant seasonal effect for NO3 − and PO4 3− only. NO3 − exhibited strong seasonality in arable lowland low- and high-permeability catchments where winter medians (8.8 and 8.4 mg N/L) exceeded summer values (5.1 and 6.4 mg N/L), reflecting enhanced leaching. NH4 + showed limited seasonality, with variability governed by point-source inputs. PO4 3− displayed an inverse seasonal pattern, with higher summer concentrations from reduced dilution of point-source inputs. Despite representing only 1% of the total catchment area, the urban type dominated NH4 + and PO4 3− concentrations, peaking in winter for NH4 + (0.176 mg N/L) and summer for PO4 3− (0.51 mg P/L), while NO3 − was controlled by arable types, with increasing urban influence in recent years. These results provide a framework for targeting nutrient management to the dominant controls of each type, supporting more effective nutrient reduction measures under the UK Marine Strategy and OSPAR commitments.

title: Hydroclimatic variability challenges apparent decadal improvements in riverine water quality across coastal watersheds
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shengyue Chen, Jinliang Huang, Ruping Zheng, Shijie Jiang
abstract: Coastal riverine environments face escalating degradation under dual climatic and anthropogenic pressures, yet high-resolution, systematic assessments remain constrained by spatiotemporally fragmented observations. Here we present a coupled deep-learning framework to robustly reconstruct daily runoff alongside multi-species pollutant concentrations and fluxes during 2010–2024 across 132 riverine sites in a representative coastal province of China. The reconstructed high-fidelity datasets reveal acute vulnerability in coastal regions and headwater systems, where intense anthropogenic stressors coincide with restricted dilution capacities. Over the past 15 years, riverine concentrations of total phosphorus, ammonia nitrogen, and permanganate index generally declined, whereas total nitrogen exhibited an upward trajectory; runoff reductions, concurrently, moderated downstream pollutant exports. Interpretable machine learning identifies urbanization, agriculture, runoff, and temperature as primary impacting factors of spatial variability in water quality baselines and trends. Critically, hydroclimatic shifts exert a stronger signature on long-term pollutant trends than human interventions alone, implying that the efficacy of current management interventions is likely overestimated due to natural climate variability over-amplification. This hydroclimatic non-stationarity is further manifested across interannual and event scales, where storm-induced pollutant pulses temporarily reverse decadal restoration gains. Our findings highlight the necessity of integrating hydroclimatic non-stationarity into watershed management, advocating for dynamic, targeted interventions in pollution hotspots and during high-flow periods to guarantee sustainable water security.

title: Urbanization is associated with changes in the sensitivity of water quality to drought
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Dongxin Tang, Pengcheng Sun, Shengzhi Huang, Xiaoting Wei, Yifei Li, Hao Cui, Dong Liu, Fuqiang Wang, Jingqing Gao
abstract: Rapid global urbanization has made water-quality degradation a core issue in assessing river health and aquatic ecosystem conditions. However, under a warming climate, the coupled relationships among urbanization, drought, and water quality remain unclear. In this study, we used regression analysis together with multiple statistical approaches to evaluate the sensitivity of two key water-quality indicators, specific conductance (SC) and water temperature (WT), to the relative discharge ratio (Q/MQ), which was used as a drought-related low-flow indicator. We also systematically analyzed how SC and WT varied with Q/MQ under different levels of urbanization. The results showed that SC followed a power-law response to Q/MQ and was significantly negatively correlated with the relative discharge ratio. WT showed clear seasonal contrasts in its response to Q/MQ: in the warm season, higher Q/MQ corresponded to lower WT, whereas in the cold season, higher Q/MQ corresponded to higher WT. We distinguished urbanization-related baseline shifts in water quality from drought-related low-flow sensitivity, defined as the response magnitude of SC or WT to changes in Q/MQ. The sensitivity of SC to relative discharge changes tended to be weaker at higher IMP levels. Based on the excess SC response, defined as P0.5 − 1, the SC response in low-urbanization basins was 23.48% and 129.03% higher than that in moderately and highly urbanized basins, respectively. In contrast, the response magnitude of WT to Q/MQ tended to be stronger at higher IMP levels. The WT response magnitude in highly urbanized basins was 47.89% and 70.34% higher than that in moderately and low-urbanization basins, respectively. Overall, urbanization was associated with changes in the sensitivity of water quality to relative discharge changes under drought-related low-flow conditions. This work characterized the response relationships between Q/MQ and SC and WT and documented how their sensitivities varied across urbanization levels. It provides scientific evidence to support watershed water-quality and river-health management for cities with different degrees of urban development.

title: Microplastics in karst groundwater: a review of current findings and methodological biases
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Syeda Maria Zainab, Dan Lapworth, Richard Cross, Katherine Pond, Monica Felipe-Sotelo, Louise Maurice
abstract: Karst aquifers are globally important yet highly vulnerable water resources. Their rapid recharge, limited natural filtration, and conduit-dominated flow make them susceptible to contamination, including by emerging pollutants such as microplastics (MPs). While MPs are well documented in marine, freshwater, and terrestrial systems, their occurrence and behaviour in karst groundwater remain poorly understood. This review synthesises 22 published studies on MPs in karst caves, springs, wells, and boreholes, assessing comparability using a widely applied quality assessment framework and a critical evaluation of methodological influences on reported MP concentrations and characteristics. Reported concentrations vary by several orders of magnitude (0.001–911 particles/L), which is likely to reflect both karst environmental variability and methodological differences in sampling design, detection limits, contamination control, and analytical specificity. Temporal datasets remain limited, but existing studies suggest high-flow events substantially increase MP loads. No single analytical technique is quantitative across the full diversity of MPs, each being inherently selective toward sizes, shapes, or polymers. Notably, stereomicroscopy appears to overrepresent fibres, while low-density separation, such as sodium chloride solutions, miss higher-density plastics. These findings highlight the need for clear reporting of the operational definition of MPs in each study to improve cross-study comparability. We propose a harmonised sampling and analytical workflow to support future karst MP research, alongside the continued need for robust quality assurance/quality control practices, broader geographic coverage, and higher temporal resolution sampling. More work beyond simple concentration reporting is needed to investigate mechanistic processes driving MP transport and fate.

title: Electrical conductivity and groundwater elevation as parameters for continuous infiltration and inflow detection in wastewater networks
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Behnam Motamedi, Elisangela Heiderscheidt, Axumawit Tesfamariam, Pekka M. Rossi
abstract: Extraneous groundwater infiltration and rainfall-derived inflow (I/I) undermine hydraulic capacity, raise energy costs, and dilute treatment performance in separate sewer networks. We evaluated electrical conductivity (EC) as a low-cost, conservative tracer for routine I/I diagnosis using yearlong monitoring with continuous EC sensors and groundwater elevation loggers in two Finnish catchments, a northern snow-dominated and a southern rainfall-dominated regime. Our analyses compared (I) commonly used hydrograph separation, (II) binary EC mixing (wastewater + groundwater), and (III) ternary EC–GW–SW mixing (wastewater +stormwater + groundwater). Relative to a volume-only split, incorporating EC increased the inferred infiltration share by up to ∼30 percentage points, while inflow remained secondary. Seasonal patterns aligned with meteorology; snowmelt dominated extraneous water in the north, whereas summer rainfall prevailed in the south. The binary EC-GW approach closely matched the ternary results but required no stormwater-EC sampling, favoring operational uptake. All diagnoses were cross-checked against precipitation, temperature, and snow-depth records to verify the link between weather and I/I dynamics. Pairing off-the-shelf EC and groundwater elevation sensors with simple mass-balance tools yielded accurate, season-resolved I/I budgets, targeting high-I/I zones, prioritizing rehabilitation, and building resilience under increasing freeze–thaw and rainfall variability.

title: A review of machine learning applications in inland and nearshore water color remote sensing: from preprocessing to object detection and parameter estimation
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Jiarui Shi, Zuchuan Li, Ge Liu, Chong Fang, Zhidan Wen, Yingxin Shang, Hui Tao, Sijia Li, Qiang Wang, Zijin Wang, Kaishan Song
abstract: A combination of Machine Learning (ML) techniques with satellite remote sensing has brought target objects and water-quality research into a new era. These emerging techniques and unprecedented opportunities have improved the accuracy of satellite data products, facilitated knowledge discovery, expanded the spatial domain of target objects and water-quality research to the globe, and extended the social, economic, and scientific impacts of water-quality research. This review provides the first systematic integration of machine learning (ML) across the full-chain workflow for inland and nearshore watercolor remote sensing, we examine recent progress in the application of ML across the full remote sensing workflow for inland and nearshore water color studies—from image preprocessing (including atmospheric correction, water body extraction, spectral simulation, spatiotemporal fusion and water extent extraction) to object detection and water quality parameter estimation. We also present a curated selection of valuable open-source resources and highlight key challenges—including data scarcity and label bias, limited model interpretability, insufficient uncertainty quantification, and the difficulties of multimodal data integration, long-term, large-scale, and multi-scale analysis, as well as the need for effective spatial relationship modeling—and discuss emerging trends such as multi-temporal data integration, and the incorporation of physical constraints. By providing a comprehensive overview of ML applications in this field, this review serves as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to enhance water quality monitoring and assessment.
