To this end, a few basic concepts which influence the climate on Earth will be discussed. The principal difficulty is the fact that in the long history of the Earth it is the first time that natural variations of the climate are influenced by human activities as well. And here, the problem arises that besides scientific issues of how these activities (e.g. fossil fuel burning) influence the climate, economic and political considerations are also drawn into the discussion. And this clearly has consequences on how to react to some of the observed changes (e.g. global warming). But emerging technologies to trace radionuclides in the environment at large may still help to get a better understanding of the climate on Earth.

title: Marine radionuclides in climate change studies: Pacific Ocean and marginal seas
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Pavel P. Povinec, Katsumi Hirose, Gi-Hoon Hong, Xiaolin Hou, Yayoi Inomata, Jakub Kaizer, Daisuke Tsumune, Xue Zhao
abstract: Observed global warming has profoundly affected the world's oceans, which are experiencing increasingly frequent marine heatwaves and a slowdown of the Global Meridional Overturning Circulation. These changes disrupt ocean circulation patterns, alter biogeochemical cycles, enhance surface ocean acidification, and drive poleward migration of marine organisms. Marine radionuclides (e.g., 3H, 14C, 90Sr, 129I, 134Cs, 137Cs, and Pu isotopes), released from nuclear activities since the 1940s, provide time-resolved tracers of oceanic processes owing to their well-documented input functions and distinct chemical behaviors. Their distributions in seawater, bottom sediments, and marine biota have recorded climate-driven modifications in ocean circulation and stratification. The Pacific Ocean, the largest ocean basin on Earth, has undergone changes in recent decades under ongoing climate forcing. Long-term radionuclide observations indicate a decline in vertical mixing in the upper North Pacific Ocean, likely associated with enhanced stratification. Variability linked to Asian monsoon systems and El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events is also clearly reflected in radionuclide records from the marginal seas of the Northwest Pacific. Radionuclide datasets provide essential reference benchmarks for calibrating and validating Ocean General Circulation Models and Earth System Models under future climate scenarios. To strengthen predictive capability, coordinated international, high-resolution sampling programs covering the entire world ocean are required, together with measurement campaigns employing newly developed ultra-sensitive analytical techniques. Particular attention should be given to the Southern, Arctic, and Subarctic Oceans because of their critical role in the global climate system and the current scarcity of comprehensive radionuclide data.

title: Environmental occurrence and empirical assessment of polonium-210 in freshwater environments
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Stephanie Walsh, Hailly Degagne, Jamie Carr, Dan Festarini, David J. Rowan, Jules M. Blais, Matthew J. Bond
abstract: Polonium-210 (210Po) is an important naturally occurring radionuclide in freshwater environments, yet large-scale datasets describing its occurrence and geochemical associations remain limited. Here we present a multi-compartment dataset of 210Po, and lead-210 (210Pb) activity concentrations compiled from Canadian freshwater systems, addressing longstanding gaps arising from the predominance of site-specific or marine focused studies. Activity concentrations varied widely among compartments and sites, reflecting broad spatial variability in hydrological and geochemical conditions. Simple linear regressions showed that 210Pb was strongly associated with 210Po across several abiotic compartments, with moderate to high explanatory power in surface waters, suspended particles, and sediment. For surface waters, multiple linear regression identified dissolved organic carbon (DOC), dissolved uranium (U), and calcium (Ca2+) as the strongest measured explanatory variables associated with 210Po activity concentrations. Complementary random-forest and generalized additive model analyses supported the recurring importance of these variables, although the models explained only a moderate proportion of total variability. These associations are interpreted as reflecting organic matter interactions, lithogenic source contributions, and cation-mediated particle processes. The resulting internally validated empirical models provide screening-level estimates of 210Po occurrence within the range of Canadian freshwater conditions represented in this dataset. Furthermore, observed activity concentration ranges provide comparative context for future monitoring and site-specific assessments.

title: A compact, platform-agnostic system for underwater radioactivity detection
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Christos Tsabaris, Efrossyni G. Androulakaki, Ioanna Kora, Stylianos Alexakis
abstract: This work presents the development and evaluation of a compact underwater radioactivity detection system, named Mini KATERINA, designed to be integrated in platform-agnostic mobile robotic vehicles operating in controlled aquatic environments to identify radioactive sources. It employs a 2″ × 2″ NaI(Tl) scintillation crystal coupled to a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), achieving reduced size, weight, and power consumption. The system was characterized in laboratory conditions using calibrated reference point sources and dedicated simulants (volume sources), enabling training and validation for the identification of suspicious objects. Initial performance assessment was conducted in a water tank to investigate detection capabilities as well as to perform calibrations in terms of energy, energy resolution and full energy peak efficiency. The calculated efficiency of the system for distances between source and detector surface at 4.5, 8.5 and 12.5 cm was 0.0038, 0.0016 and 0.00051, respectively. The limit of detection (LD) of the system at 662 keV for distances between source and detector surface at 4.5, 8.5 and 12.5 cm was 8, 17 and 54 Bq, respectively. Subsequently, field tests were performed in a marine environment to evaluate the limit of detection of a point source using a known radioactive simulant housed in a dedicated enclosure. The Limit of Detection of a point source (LD) of the system in this field configuration in the marine environment resulted a value of 43 Βq when the system is in a distance of 6 cm from the 137Cs point source. The results demonstrate the system's effectiveness for underwater radiation monitoring and its potential integration into diverse mobile underwater platforms.

title: Investigation of the migration behavior of 237 Np, 238 Pu, and 90 Sr in unsaturated silty loam sediment
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Chen Chao, Xu Cheng-Long, Liang Peng-Liang, Zhu Jun
abstract: Laboratory migration experiments investigating 237Np, 238Pu, and 90Sr were conducted over a period of 1073 days (approximately 3 years), corresponding to the predetermined duration of the study project, using large-scale undisturbed unsaturated silty loam soil columns to compare their migration behaviors under identical conditions. Results revealed distinct patterns: after 1073 days, 237Np and 90Sr exhibited single, symmetrical concentration peaks without tailing, with peak concentrations of 1688 Bq·g−1 and 398 Bq·g−1 migrating downward by 3.25 cm and 9.75 cm, respectively. The significant difference in migration distance between these nuclides primarily stems from variations in their chemical speciation, adsorption characteristics, and interaction mechanisms within the soil. Conversely, 238Pu displayed a distinct bimodal distribution, with a high-concentration peak (423 Bq·g−1) retained near the surface at 0.25 cm due to strong initial adsorption, and a secondary lower-concentration peak (408 Bq·g−1) formed at 4.04 cm. This pattern indicates partial desorption of 238Pu under leaching conditions, leading to accelerated downward migration and subsequent re-adsorption deeper in the profile. Numerical simulations using HYDRUS-1D, incorporating colloidal effects, showed that both equilibrium and non-equilibrium adsorption models adequately described 237Np and 90Sr transport. For 238Pu, a non-equilibrium model featuring a first-order adsorption-desorption rate constant (β) effectively captured the leading-edge tailing of the secondary peak. However, reproducing the full bimodal distribution required a more sophisticated conceptualization using a two-region or dual-porosity model.

title: Radiological dose assessment of waterborne radon and Monte Carlo–based evaluation of lifetime excess cancer risk in uranium mining regions of South Africa
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Abubakar Adekunle Muritala, Idowu Richard Akomolafe, JJ van Zyl, Naven Chetty
abstract: Radon (222Rn) is a naturally occurring radioactive noble gas found in groundwater, particularly in regions with uranium-rich geology and extensive mining, such as South Africa. This study presents a multi-site comparative assessment using a unified methodology and represents one of the first South African investigations to explicitly integrate ingestion and water-to-air inhalation pathways within a probabilistic lifetime excess cancer risk (LECR) framework. Using a RAD7 radon monitor, we measured radon concentrations in 80 boreholes across Carletonville, Wedela, Mokopane, Beaufort West, and Sutherland to calculate the total effective dose and lifetime excess cancer risk. Radon concentrations ranged from 18 ± 2 to 369 ± 96 B q L − 1 , with an overall mean of 127 ± 32 B q L − 1 , resulting in total effective doses (ingestion + inhalation of waterborne radon released into indoor air) ranging from 0.09 ± 0.02 to 1.87 ± 0.50 m S v y − 1 . The calculated mean radon concentration exceeds the World Health Organization (WHO) reference level of 100 B q L − 1 . Although the mean total effective dose remains below the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) public dose limit of 1 m S v y − 1 , the result indicates a non-negligible public health concern that warrants mitigation. Monte Carlo simulation (100,000 iterations, water-only pathway) yielded a mean lifetime excess cancer risk (LECR) of 2.58 × 1 0 − 3 and a median of 2.36 × 1 0 − 3 , both above the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) acceptable risk threshold of 1 × 1 0 − 4 . These translate to approximately 2580 and 2360 additional cancer cases per million people exposed over a 70-year lifetime, respectively, with 100 % of simulated iterations exceeding the USEPA threshold. The reported risk reflects only the waterborne pathway; soil-gas and building-material contributions, which typically dominate total indoor inhalation dose, were not measured. Even so, the waterborne component alone exceeds international risk benchmarks across the entire simulated distribution and at every site sampled, supporting the case for explicit national radon-in-water regulation, systematic monitoring, and complementary indoor-air radon assessment.

title: Artificial radionuclide levels in land cover of radiological warfare agent test site ‘4’
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): N.V. Larionova, V.V. Bozhko, A.V. Panitskiy, P. Ye Krivitskiy, M.V. Skripnikov, A.V. Toporova, V.N. Monayenko, A. Ye Kunduzbayeva, A.O. Aidarkhanov, V.V. Baklanov
abstract: Assessing the environmental legacy of historical test sites for nuclear weapons and radiological warfare agents (RWAs) is critical for understanding long-term isotopic evolution and evaluating land safety. This study evaluates artificial radionuclide levels (241Am, 137Cs, 90Sr and 239+240Pu) in the land cover of Site ‘4’, a historic RWA testing ground in the Republic of Kazakhstan. Within the 37 km2 area analysed via pedestrian and discrete gamma spectrometric surveys, 14 radioactively contaminated locations with gross gamma count rates exceeding the experimentally established baseline of 180 cps were identified, totalling ∼0.37 km2. Soil analysis revealed 90Sr activity concentrations exceeding those of other artificial radionuclides by several orders of magnitude, with the highest values at all sampling points recorded in the upper soil layer (0–10 cm). From the vertical 90Sr distribution within the soil profile, two distribution patterns were identified: (1) high migration into the 10–20-cm layer and below, and (2) high activity concentrations in the 0–10-cm layer, followed by a sharp decrease in the 10–20-cm layer. This differing distribution pattern is attributed to the use of liquid vs. powdered RWA formulations. The maximum total dose rate of the investigated artificial radionuclides to herbaceous vegetation reached 220 μGy/day, driven primarily by 90Sr exposure. This study fills a critical research gap in the radioecological monitoring of this area and provides precise geographical and radioecological data necessary for the rehabilitation of these lands.

title: Up-scaling of radon migration in rock media based on multi-resolution CT pore modeling and volume averaging method
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Yuan-Chao Chen, Dong Xie, Zhong-Luo Liao, Jun Zeng, Qian-Ran Jia
abstract: The macroscopic radon migration behavior in rock media is inherently dominated by its microscopic pore structure and transport properties. However, the lack of accurate correlation methods between microscopic transport characteristics and macroscopic parameters has long been a bottleneck in revealing radon migration mechanisms. To address this issue, this study proposes an integrated approach combining multi-resolution CT pore modeling and the Volume Averaging Method. 3D pore models of rock specimens were constructed at resolutions of 48.9 μm/voxel, 7.3 μm/voxel, and 1.1 μm/voxel using CT scanning and 3D visualization and analysis software. Through thresholding, connectivity analysis and REV analysis, key pore structure parameters (porosity and connectivity) and optimal REV sizes were determined. The results indicated that connected pore channels in the Z direction were only formed at the highest resolution (1.1 μm/voxel) with a connected porosity of 1.92%. On this basis, radon diffusion and seepage simulations were performed on the identified REVs to obtain the radon migration parameters. The Volume Averaging Method was innovatively adopted to realize the up-scaling of REV parameters to macroscopic ones, yielding the up-scaling diffusion coefficient (9.57 × 10−9 m2/s) and permeability (2.19 × 10−15 m2) in the Z direction, while parameters in disconnected directions were close to 0. Furthermore, the up-scaling parameters were extended to unsaturated and non-isothermal conditions by coupling the unsaturated non-isothermal radon diffusion coefficient model and Brooks-Corey model. Experimental verification showed that the deviation between the up-scaling radon diffusion coefficient and the experimental value was only 1.83% at 20 °C, and the deviation between the simulated radon exhalation rate (based on the up-scaling parameters) and the experimental value ranged from 10.38% to 31.12% when water saturation varied from 0% to 70%. This study presents a feasible technical approach for the accurate up-scaling of radon migration parameters in rocks, which helps to narrow the disconnect between microscopic and macroscopic research.

title: Recent advances in radioisotope geochronology for quaternary environmental and paleoclimate reconstruction
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Azhagu Madhavan Sivalingam
abstract: Reliable chronological frameworks are fundamental for reconstructing Quaternary environmental change, paleoclimate evolution, landscape development, and human history. Recent advances in radioisotope geochronology have substantially improved the accuracy, precision, and temporal resolution of dating across diverse geological and environmental archives. This review synthesizes developments in major Quaternary dating methods radiocarbon (14C), lead-210 (210 Pb), cesium-137 (137Cs), uranium-series, potassium–argon (K–Ar), argon–argon (40Ar/39Ar), and cosmogenic radionuclide techniques (10Be, 26Al, 36Cl, 81Kr) and highlights emerging analytical technologies including accelerator mass spectrometry, multi-collector ICP-MS, atom trap trace analysis, Bayesian age–depth modelling, and integrated multi-proxy approaches. Applications spanning terrestrial, marine, lacustrine, archaeological, and glacial settings demonstrate the value of combining complementary methods to build robust chronologies for sedimentation, tectonics, landscape evolution, paleoclimate reconstruction, and groundwater studies. Improvements in calibration datasets, uncertainty quantification, computational modelling, and high-resolution analytics have expanded the applicability of radioisotope geochronology to more complex systems. Persistent challenges contamination, open-system behaviour, reservoir effects, inheritance, and post-depositional alteration necessitate rigorous sample selection and methodological validation. We recommend prioritizing standardized analytical protocols, enhanced calibration frameworks, interdisciplinary integration, and adoption of machine-learning-assisted chronological modelling to further improve precision and reproducibility. Continued innovation in radioisotope geochronology promises more reliable chronological frameworks for investigating Quaternary environmental change and for reconstructing Earth's climatic, geological, and ecological conservation.

title: Treatment of barium-contaminated wastewaters using adsorption: a review
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Nathan Vinícius Martins da Silva, Amanda Magliano Pontes, Clascídia Aparecida Furtado, Ana Cláudia Queiroz Ladeira
abstract: Barium-containing wastewaters are produced on a large scale by various industries, including electronics, pigment, and ceramics manufacturing. They are also generated by the nuclear industry, where barium chloride is used to precipitate and remove Ra-226. Improper disposal of these wastes can potentially cause various adverse effects on the biosphere because the metal can be toxic to humans and other life forms, depending on the dosage. Therefore, choosing the best available treatment technology that is economically achievable is essential to ensure the safety of both the environment and human health. Among the various methods available for this purpose, adsorption is considered one of the most promising because it offers benefits like low cost, simple design, and high efficiency. This review discusses the use of adsorption for decontaminating industrial wastewaters containing barium. It highlights the adsorptive performance of various materials and explores key factors influencing adsorption, including optimal pH, contact time, and the impact of competing species. The adsorption capacities of various adsorbents ranged from less than 5 mg/g to over 500 mg/g. Adsorption mechanisms such as ion exchange and complexation were described. Surface modifications have been found to significantly improve the performance of some adsorbents. Similarly, nanotechnology has enabled the design of materials with enhanced properties, such as increased surface area and porosity, as well as the ability to be functionalized. Nature-derived adsorbents, in turn, offer the advantages of high environmental compatibility and wide availability, although some of these exhibited poor adsorptive performances. Finally, suggestions for future work include the incorporation of the adsorbents into macrostructures to facilitate their removal after adsorption.

title: Indoor radon exposure in Serbia – A critical review
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Predrag Kuzmanović
abstract: The aim of this study was to provide the first comprehensive assessment of indoor radon levels in Serbia based on long-term monitoring data and available studies, including a critical review of methodological limitations. The analysis, conducted using activated charcoal canisters, includes 875 buildings (2011–2024) across seven cities in Serbia, with radon concentrations ranging from 5 to 1609 Bq/m3, an arithmetic mean value of 119 ± 149 Bq/m3, and a geometric mean value of 76 ± 3 Bq/m3. About 38% of buildings exceed 100 Bq/m3, while 7% exceed 300 Bq/m3. Comparison with other national studies shows a much wider range (1–13,400 Bq/m3 in residential and commercial buildings and 10–1130 Bq/m3 in schools and kindergartens), depending on building type, geology, and measurement methodology. Higher values were observed in southern Serbia and in Kosovo and Metohija, with a log-normal distribution and pronounced local variability. Effective dose estimates indicate moderate average exposure, but also localized areas of elevated risk (average < 4 mSv/y, maximum up to 40 mSv/y). The critical analysis highlights key limitations, including data heterogeneity, dominance of short-term measurements within monitoring campaigns, inconsistent national criteria compared with WHO guidelines, and insufficient spatial coverage. In particular, there is a lack of epidemiological studies and insufficient integration of radon data with geological and building material sources. The conclusion is that Serbia exhibits moderate average indoor radon levels, but with pronounced local radiation risks. Standardization of measurement methods, long-term monitoring aimed at developing a more comprehensive radon map compared to the current one, expansion of the monitoring network, and development of epidemiological studies are necessary to improve public health protection.

title: Analytical determination of radium isotopes in water: current capabilities, challenges and future directions
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): M. Gongora, J. Martínez, A. Peñalver, C. Aguilar, F. Borrull
abstract: Radium isotopes in water remain a significant analytical challenge due to their low environmental activity concentrations, chemical similarity to alkaline-earth elements, and strict regulatory limits. Accurate determination of 226Ra and 228Ra requires efficient preconcentration and selective radiochemical separation prior to detection. This review evaluates contemporary methodologies for radium isotope determination in water, with particular emphasis on developments reported since 2014. Special attention is given to preconcentration strategies, radiochemical isolation procedures, source preparation and measurement techniques, as well as to how these steps influence analytical performance in terms of ingrowth time, counting time, recovery and minimum detectable activity concentration. Overall, this review provides a critical framework for selecting appropriate analytical methods for environmental monitoring and regulatory applications, by critically comparing complete analytical workflows and highlighting the parameters which control analytical performance.

title: Evaluation of radon progeny mitigation techniques (HEPA filtration, ionization, electrostatic deposition) and their potential use in caves
description: Publication date: June 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 297 Author(s): J.E. Martínez, B. Juste, G. Verdú
abstract: Radon and its short-lived progeny are recognized as significant contributors to the radiological dose received indoors and are associated with increased lung cancer risk. This study evaluates the effectiveness of various air purification technologies—including HEPA filtration, ionization, electrostatic deposition, and combined systems—in reducing airborne concentrations of radon progeny (PAEC, 218Po, and 214Po) in a controlled, non-ventilated environment. Measurements were carried out using active and passive detectors over multiple campaigns with and without air purifiers. Statistically significant reductions were observed for all purification methods tested, with the greatest decrease found for 214Po and PAEC, and more moderate reductions for 218Po. The combination of HEPA filtration and ionization proved most effective, achieving reductions exceeding 40% in PAEC. The results confirm that air purification systems, particularly those using ionization and electrostatic principles, can play a crucial role in mitigating radon progeny exposure in enclosed spaces. These findings support the practical implementation of air purification strategies in high-risk environments such as underground workplaces, shelters, and laboratories.

title: Gamma emissions from NORM in building materials: A position paper on national transposition of the Euratom basic safety standard
description: Publication date: June 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 297 Author(s): M. Dodek, R.E. Djabou, C. Sainz, I. Fuente, L.L. Vintró, O. Hanley, J. Goggins, M. Foley
abstract: This position paper examines how the Euratom Basic Safety Standards (EU-BSS), Council Directive 2013/59/Euratom) on gamma radiation from building materials have been transposed into national regulation across selected EU Member States. It focuses on Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Netherlands, Spain, and Sweden. Drawing on national legislation, technical guidance and direct correspondence with regulators and researchers, the paper compares who is responsible for characterising Naturally Occurring Radioactive Material (NORM) in building materials, and how compliance with the 1 mSv/year reference level is demonstrated. Across the countries studied, regulation is broadly convergent with the Gamma Index being widely used as a screening tool. Responsibility for measurements generally lies with manufacturers or suppliers using accredited laboratories with regulatory attention primarily focused on natural igneous and pozzolanic stones, alum-shale–related products, and construction materials containing industrial residues such as fly ash, phosphogypsum, slags and red mud. At the same time, there are notable differences in the existence of long-term national datasets, the degree of integration with construction-product approval systems, and whether NORM above exemption levels is treated as radioactive waste or managed under a more flexible “existing exposure” regime. The paper provides a current snapshot of this evolving European regulatory landscape and is intended to inform the further development of proportionate NORM regulation and monitoring strategies for building materials and recycled building materials in Europe. Its added value lies in bringing dispersed national sources into a single comparative framework and in identifying recurring implementation models, practical divergences and emerging issues for recycled and secondary materials.

title: Seasonal patterns in the relationship between gamma emitters in the ground-level atmospheric layer and total atmospheric precipitation in southern Poland (Kraków), 2022 - 2025
description: Publication date: June 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 297 Author(s): Sylwia Błażej, Jerzy W. Mietelski, Renata Kierepko, Mikołaj Wielgat
abstract: Atmospheric physical and chemical processes significantly influence the presence of radionuclides, affecting their production (for cosmogenic isotopes), horizontal and vertical transport, and resuspension. This study presents weekly gamma-spectrometric measurements of aerosol and monthly measurements of atmospheric precipitation collected in Krakow (southern Poland) during the years 2022-2025, which is a continuation of studies initiated in 1990. For both types of samples, time series and correlations between observed activity concentrations of 40K, 210Pb, 7Be, 22Na and 137Cs for the whole period and in sub-sets of four seasons. Most observed trends correspond to seasonal patterns characteristic of temperate climate zones and to prevailing atmospheric phenomena during the study period. Due to increasing solar activity during the 25th solar cycle a decreasing trend for both cosmogenic radionuclides is observed, however with a strong seasonal variation. No traces of 131I were found either in aerosol form or in gaseous form.

title: From zonal containment to spot recovery: Multi-platform geostatistical reassessment of radiation risk boundaries in Fukushima (2019–2024)
description: Publication date: June 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 297 Author(s): Imam Ghazali Yasmint, Yo Ishigaki, Kayoko Yamamoto
abstract: This study provides a spatiotemporal reassessment of the radiological landscape within the Difficult-to-Return Zone (DTRZ) surrounding the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant (FDNPP), integrating airborne, car-borne, and walk-borne survey data from 2019 to 2024 through Empirical Bayesian Kriging (EBK) to generate high-resolution (50-m) dose-rate surfaces. Applying the official Japanese government occupancy threshold of 3.8 μSv·h−1 (equivalent to 20 mSv·y−1), the 2019 DTRZ boundary demonstrated complete radiological containment, with all threshold-exceeding grid cells located within the zone boundaries in both monitoring years, but exhibited pronounced internal over-restriction: 96.2% of the 337.34 km2 DTRZ area comprised grid cells that did not exceed the threshold in 2019, rising to 98.4% by 2024 as the threshold-exceeding area contracted by 56.8% from 12.74 km2 to 5.50 km2. Radiological assessment of the seven Specified Reconstruction and Revitalization Base Areas (SRRBA) (digitized from published cartography) revealed that mean dose rates across all patches declined from 6.45 mSv·y−1 to 3.08 mSv·y−1 (−52.2%), with all patches recording doses below the 20 mSv·y−1 policy threshold and threshold-exceeding area contracting by 86.1%. Forest classes (Deciduous Broadleaf Forest [DBF], Deciduous Needleleaf Forest [DNF], Evergreen Broadleaf Forest [EBF], Evergreen Needleleaf Forest [ENF], and Bamboo forest) accounted for 60.2% of threshold-exceeding cells in 2019, declining to 56.5% in 2024, with a notable compositional shift from DBF (39.6% to 25.8%) toward ENF (15.1% to 22.8%) reflecting differential radioecological recovery rates. These findings empirically validate the radiological justification for the SRRBA designation and the broader transition from broad zonal restriction toward spot-based recovery management.

title: Snow cover over the Iberian mountains in km-scale global climate simulations: Evaluation and projected changes
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Diego García-Maroto, Elsa Mohino, Luis Durán, Álvaro González-Cervera, Xabier Pedruzo-Bagazgoitia
abstract: Study region We focus on the four main mountain ranges of the Iberian Peninsula. In such Mediterranean mountains, complex topography and high climate variability make snowpacks a crucial natural resource, highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Study focus Due to their coarse resolution, traditional climate models cannot properly represent the complexity of orographic processes. In this work, we assess the performance of the global km-scale IFS-FESOM model in simulating seasonal snow cover and projecting climate change effects in Iberian mountains. This approach provides high-quality regional information directly from global simulations, bypassing the need for traditional regional downscaling. The model is evaluated against high-resolution reanalysis-based products, satellite retrievals, and in situ observations. Furthermore, future snow cover trends are assessed under the SSP3-7.0 emission scenario. New hydrological insights for the region Despite a positive bias in snowfall days, the model successfully represents key features of the snow climatology, such as the elevation dependency, the seasonal cycle, and the mean covered area. The projection shows a marked reduction of the snow season across Iberia, with low- to mid-elevations and the southernmost ranges showing the greatest reductions. These changes are linked to reduced snowfall days, caused primarily by rising temperatures but also by decreasing precipitation. The results demonstrate that global km-scale simulations can provide physically consistent local climate projections in complex terrain as a simpler and robust alternative to traditional regionalization.

title: Climate-induced changes in flow seasonality and peak discharge with socio-hydrologic consequences in the Hunza River Basin, Upper Indus
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Muhammad Ahsan Mukhtar, Donghui Shangguan, Muhammad Adnan, Abhishek Banerjee, Amjad Ali Khan, Qin Ji, Ali Muhammad, Muhammad Naveed Anjum, Asim Qayyum Butt
abstract: In the glacier-fed Hunza basin of the Karakoram, traditional irrigation channels (kuls) are increasingly damaged by floods even as farmers advance their cropping calendars by weeks. Does warming threaten this basin through scarcity or through a timing crisis? To address this question, we couple a calibrated daily hydrological model (UBCWM) with a stratified survey of 491 households across 20 villages. The model is calibrated on 1995–2015 daily discharge at Danyore and validated independently on 2016–2023 (NSE = 0.85, KGE = 0.89), over a baseline in which glacier melt supplies 70% of annual runoff. Under a five-member CMIP6 ensemble (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP5–8.5) to 2100, the hydrograph reorganises robustly: the peak advances by twelve days, late-winter flow rises sharply, and both high-flow days (Q80 = 609 m³ s⁻¹) and extreme-flow days (Q90 = 895 m³ s⁻¹) rise by a median of nine per year, with the May to June signal emerging from internal variability around 2038. Although total spring discharge increases, 86% of households report worsening spring shortages because the earlier, sharper melt pulse arrives before the main cropping demand and in flows that damage the intakes responsible for distributing it. Consistent with this, 75% have advanced irrigation onset by 2 or more weeks, and 67% report flood or landslide damage within 5 years. The modelled physical advance and the surveyed operational strain are two readings of one shift, in which water arrives earlier and more intensely than the infrastructure was built to receive. Water security here turns on timing and channel resilience rather than absolute scarcity, so we prioritise intake protection and channel reinforcement over reservoir-scale supply augmentation.

title: Assessment of meteorological drought in Thailand: Historical and future projections under CMIP6 climate change scenarios
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Teerawat Ram-Indra, Nantawoot Inseeyong, Zhenxing Zhang, Supattra Visessri
abstract: Study region Thailand. Study focus This study assesses historical and future meteorological drought hazard across Thailand using the NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 dataset. Thirty-five Global Climate Models (GCMs) were evaluated against observations using the modified Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE′), and 19 models were retained. The selected models with relatively high performance were bias-corrected using Empirical Quantile Mapping (EQM) for the baseline period and Equiratio CDF Matching (EQCDF) for future projections. They were then used to calculate the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Drought event, duration, severity, and intensity were then combined into a composite Drought Hazard Index (DHI) to evaluate drought hazard under the baseline period and future SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5 scenarios. New hydrological insights for the region The selected GCMs reproduced historical climate conditions reasonably well after bias correction, providing a reliable basis for drought projection. SPI and SPEI showed broadly similar historical drought patterns. However, their future projections diverged, particularly at longer timescales. Future SPEI projections generally indicate more severe and prolonged drought conditions compared to SPI, reflecting the increasing influence of atmospheric evaporative demand represented through potential evapotranspiration (PET) in SPEI. This divergence becomes more pronounced with increasing accumulation periods, suggesting the growing importance of cumulative evaporative-demand-related processes in long-term drought assessment. Regional analyses reveal substantial spatial heterogeneity, with certain areas exhibiting stronger sensitivity to temperature effects. Compared with SPI, SPEI indicated stronger evaporative-demand-driven shifts in drought hazard under future scenarios, particularly under SSP5–8.5. Regional analyses showed that northeastern Thailand is likely to remain the most drought-prone region, with consistently high variability in drought hazard. The central and eastern regions showed greater uncertainty and stronger future shifts, whereas the southern region remained relatively less vulnerable with more stable mean hazard levels. These results suggest that precipitation-only indices may underestimate future drought risk in a warming climate and highlight the need to incorporate temperature-sensitive drought indices into national drought monitoring, regional adaptation planning, and water resources management in Thailand.

title: Development and assessment of a bimodal synthetic design storm using observed rainfall data from eThekwini, South Africa
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Joshua David Spooner, Ione Loots, Jeff Smithers
abstract: Study region eThekwini metropolitan region, humid subtropical coastal environment, South Africa. Study focus Urban stormwater design commonly relies on single-peaked synthetic rainfall events, despite evidence that multi-peaked storms occur frequently and can strongly influence runoff response. This study investigates the occurrence and temporal characteristics of bimodal rainfall events using long-term observed records from eThekwini. An objective, reproducible method was developed to identify bimodal storm events and quantify their frequency, duration, and peak structure. Based on these characteristics, two synthetic triangular bimodal design storms were developed. The performance of the proposed storms was evaluated against conventional single-peak design storm approaches in reproducing observed bimodal rainfall structure. New hydrological insights from the region Bimodal rainfall events constitute approximately 12% of major storms in the study region and are typically longer and more extreme than single-peaked storms. Because the second rainfall peak occurs before catchment recovery, it produces substantially greater runoff volumes and peak flow rates due to antecedent saturation. Conventional single-peaked design storms do not adequately represent peak sequencing and inter-peak rainfall characteristics of these events. The Bimodal-Split Rainfall design storm most effectively reproduces observed events, providing a data-driven representation of regional rainfall structure and improvement over conventional approaches. While demonstrated for a humid subtropical coastal catchment, the methodology is transferable to other regions where double-peaked rainfall occurs, supporting improved characterisation of rainfall structure and hydrological implications.

title: National-scale patterns and controls of hydrological drought recovery in Poland
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Paweł Marcinkowski
abstract: Study region Poland, Central Europe. Study focus Hydrological drought recovery remains much less studied than drought onset, duration, and severity, despite its importance for understanding river-system resilience. This study investigates the recovery phase of hydrological drought in Poland using a daily variable-threshold approach. Drought events were identified and characterized in terms of recovery duration. Geographical variation in recovery behaviour was assessed at the station scale, and catchment controls on median recovery duration were examined using descriptors of topography, land cover, and soils. The aim was to determine whether recovery represents a distinct hydrological phase and to identify the basin characteristics associated with slower or faster return above drought-threshold conditions. New hydrological insights for the region Hydrological drought recovery in Poland was generally short, but highly variable across events and catchments. Recovery was often faster than drought development, although substantial asymmetry occurred and slow-recovery events were widespread. Recovery metrics showed marked geographical variation across the national gauging network. Catchment-level analyses identified statistical associations between median recovery duration and soil-profile properties, terrain steepness, and surface-water share. Steeper catchments tended to recover more rapidly, whereas catchments with a greater proportion of water surfaces tended to recover more slowly. However, the reduced multivariable model explained only part of the observed variability, indicating that these static catchment descriptors provide an incomplete representation of the factors associated with hydrological drought recovery.

title: Assessing future flood risks to cropland under climate change in the Second Songhua River Basin, China: A depth-duration framework for adaptive management
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Yifei Zheng, Zhihui Li, Jie Zeng
abstract: Study region The Second Songhua River Basin (SSRB), a representative mid-latitude agricultural basin in Jilin Province, northeastern China. Study focus To overcome the limitations of traditional single-indicator flood hazard assessments that overlook agricultural waterlogging stress, this study develops a process-oriented, depth-duration dual-factor risk assessment framework. We couple a bias-corrected CMIP6 multi-model ensemble with a calibrated distributed Rainfall-Runoff-Inundation (RRI) model. Future cropland inundation extent, depth, and duration are simulated under multiple emission scenarios (SSP245/SSP585), future horizons, and return periods (50/100-year). A dual-factor decision matrix is constructed to classify cropland into four risk quadrants to guide differentiated drainage planning. New hydrological insights for the region Future flood hazards show a shifting trend from localized ponding to contiguous deep waterlogging belts. Under the far-future SSP585 scenario, inundated cropland reaches 3,107.33 km2 (uncertainty range: 2249.50–3830.13 km2) for a 50-year flood and peaks at 3287.41 km2 for a 100-year event (uncertainty range: 2364.96–4179.78 km2). By deploying the proposed depth–duration framework, we successfully decoupled and interconnected the compound hazard components: within the 100-year footprint, a critical 931.34 km2 (uncertainty range: 654.72–1174.25 km2) of the affected cropland is identified as the highest-risk zone, suffering from concurrent severe submersion (>2.0 m) and prolonged waterlogging (>3 days). The resulting risk matrix effectively categorizes the basin into four distinct adaptive management zones, providing a scientific baseline for implementing differentiated farmland governance and supporting climate-adaptive risk management.

title: Future climate–driven earlier shifts and reductions in streamflow extremes in Vakhsh River, Amu Darya Basin
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Amirkhamza Murodov, Xingcai Liu, Murodkhudzha Murodov, Farhod Nasrulloev, Qiuhong Tang, Ying Yi, Gulfam Hussain, Firdavs Vosidov
abstract: Study region The Vakhsh River Basin, a major tributary of Amu Darya River Basin (ADRB), an essential source of irrigation and hydropower, has experienced substantial alterations in streamflow under climate change. Understanding how glacier– and snow–fed streamflow will evolve under continued warming is critical for ensuring future water security. Study focus This study assesses historical and future changes in high-flow extremes using the Spatial Processes in Hydrology model and downscaled bias-corrected CMIP6 data. New hydrological insights High-flow extremes exhibited declining magnitude and progressively earlier timing during the baseline period (2000–2023). Future projections show consistent declines in annual mean high-flow extreme, with relative decreases of 11–13% in far future (2076–2100) across the scenarios. High-flow extreme events are likely to occur earlier, advancing by 2–3.5 weeks for central date of event occurrences in the far future. Early-season high flow extremes remain dominated by snowmelt (77–96%), with glacier melt as a secondary contributor. The projected advance in high-flow extreme timing is primarily driven by earlier snowmelt peak, shifting from June in baseline (with ∼50% snowmelt contribution) to May in future periods (70–80% snowmelt contribution), along with the compression of glacier-melt-driven extremes into late summer. Overall, the results indicate an earlier, shorter, and weaker melt–driven flood season. These changes have important implications for hydropower operations, irrigation planning, and downstream climate adaptation in the Amu Darya River system.

title: Meteorological-to-hydrological drought propagation and its drivers in the Upper Indus Basin, Pakistan: A multiscale analysis using explainable machine learning
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Khalil Ahmad, Shahbaz Ali, Adil Dilawar, Muhammad Farhan, Saidur Rahaman, Fazli Hameed, Anis Ur Rehman Khalil
abstract: Study region The Upper Indus Basin of Pakistan is a critical headwater region for the country’s water supply. Study focus This study investigated meteorological and hydrological drought characteristics and the propagation of meteorological drought into hydrological drought in the Upper Indus Basin of Pakistan during 1982–2022. Meteorological drought was quantified using the Standardized Precipitation Index at 1-, 3-, 6-, 9-, and 12-month scales, and hydrological drought using the one-month Standardized Runoff Index. Drought propagation time was estimated using the maximum Pearson correlation coefficient method, while rate, counts, and intensity were derived from event-based analysis, and an explainable machine-learning framework (XGBoost-SHAP) was used to identify the dominant drivers. New hydrological insights for the region Meteorological drought was most frequent at short time scales, whereas hydrological drought was less frequent but more persistent. Mean propagation time was 5.84 months, with 31.61% of the basin showing a one-month response. Mean propagation counts and rate were 18.25 and 0.32, respectively. The model performed well, with a mean R² of 0.75 and a maximum of 0.84 for propagation intensity. Vegetation condition, temperature, and runoff were the dominant drivers of propagation time, whereas temperature, runoff, and potential evapotranspiration mainly controlled propagation counts and intensity. By integrating multiscale drought propagation metrics with explainable machine learning, this study provides new regional evidence to support drought monitoring and climate adaptation.

title: Effects and mechanisms of moss cover reducing surface runoff and soil erosion compared to pine needle litter on karst slopes
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Jiaqi Yang, Ya Yang, Juan Jiang, Lulu Che, Dongdong Liu
abstract: Study region Huaxi District, Guiyang City, Guizhou Province, southwestern China. Study focus Karst regions have experienced severe rocky desertification from intense weathering and soil erosion, threatening regional ecological security. However, systematic comparisons of soil and water conservation effects of different surface covers (moss and pine needle) on karst slopes remain insufficient. The study established runoff plots on karst slopes in Guizhou. It monitored soil water content dynamics at 5 cm and 15 cm depths under moss cover and pine needle litter across different rainfall types and slope gradients. We also recorded runoff and sediment loss during erosive rainfall events. New hydrological insights for the region Moss cover exhibited more stable and higher soil water retention at 15 cm depth, pine needle cover showed greater sensitivity to moisture changes at 5 cm depth. Moss achieved significantly better runoff and sediment reduction than pine needles, with average reductions of 27.176% in runoff coefficient and 58.840% in soil erosion. Heavy rainfall and steeper slopes intensified runoff and sediment loss, moss maintained effective soil and water conservation performance. Predictions based on XGBoost and RUSLE models indicated high accuracy in runoff, sediment loss prediction was unstable due to multiple influencing factors. These included rainfall, slope, cover type, and antecedent moisture, as well as complex nonlinear processes by these factors. Moss cover has significant advantages for ecological restoration in karst regions.

title: Evaluating morphological quality and scale effects in a Mediterranean river using IDRAIM methodology: The Jerte river (Spain)
description: Publication date: October 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 67 Author(s): Viviana Bellomo, Manuel Sánchez-Fernández, Edoardo Rotigliano, Alvaro Gómez-Gutiérrez
abstract: Study region The upper-middle section of the Jerte River (39.4 km, Tagus River Basin, Spain), a mountain water body with a Mediterranean pluvio-nival regime. The primary disturbances to the river’s natural regime are driven by intense agricultural activity (specifically terraced cherry cultivation), recurrent wildfires, and seasonal recreational river uses. Study focus The research addresses the need for standardized tools to evaluate fluvial systems under the Water Framework Directive in Europe. Specifically, we examine the applicability of the Italian IDRAIM framework and its core tool, the Morphological Quality Index (MQI) in an Iberian-Mediterranean environment. The Jerte river was segmented into 21 reaches to assess geomorphological functionality, artificiality, and channel adjustments. Additionally, a statistical sensitivity analysis was carried out at both reach and water body scales to evaluate MQI stability to indicator variations and expose local critical conditions. New hydrological insights for the region While the length-weighted water body assessment shows an overall moderate morphological quality (MQI = 0.67), the multiscale approach reveals high spatial heterogeneity, demonstrating that aggregated estimations mask localized degradation. For instance, reaches near towns exhibit constraints on lateral mobility, deficient riparian vegetation, and extensive riverbed modifications. Reaches with poor quality account for 52% of the river length. Integrating IDRAIM with sensitivity analysis successfully identified unstable reaches and indicators driving perturbation, providing an objective tool for regional river management and restoration prioritization.

title: Managing the Nile under climate change: A systematic review of hydrological shifts and adaptive strategies for transboundary water security
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Nahom Mena, Joseph Awange, Xiaolong Mi
abstract: Study Region: The Nile River Basin (NRB), spanning 11 countries in East Africa and supporting over 300 million people. Study Focus: This study synthesizes three decades of research using an AI-enhanced PRISMA review to assess impacts of climate change, land-use change, and infrastructure on water availability and risks across the basin. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: The review reveals pronounced spatial heterogeneity in hydrological responses. In the Blue Nile, discharge trends are mixed and often statistically insignificant, with recent changes increasingly linked to land-use dynamics rather than climate alone. In the White Nile, hydrology shows multi-decadal variability rather than consistent long-term trends. A major regime shift in 1961, associated with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), raised Lake Victoria by about 2 m and increased baseline outflows. Flows declined through the 1990s, dropped sharply in the early 2000s due to dam operations, and reached record highs in 2020 following IOD-driven extreme rainfall. Attribution studies indicate climate change has likely contributed to increased White Nile flows in recent decades, although uncertainties remain regarding the roles of climate, land use, and human interventions. Future rainfall and river flow projections show wide divergence, ranging from − 10 % to + 25 % for rainfall and − 20 % to + 40 % for discharge by late century, highlighting uncertainty in future water availability and increasing pressure on transboundary water management.

title: Increased soil moisture dominates the prolongation of leaf longevity for alpine grasslands in the Three-River-Source Region
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Yuxi Wang, Lin Zhang
abstract: Study regions The Three-River-Source Region Study focus This study integrated multi-source remote sensing and flux data from 2003 to 2022 to analyze the spatiotemporal dynamics of grassland leaf longevity (LL) and moisture conditions in the Three-River-Source Region. By applying a binning-based decoupling approach, we successfully isolated the independent impacts of soil moisture (SM) and vapor pressure deficit (VPD). New hydrological insights for the region Nearly half the region experienced intensified water stress, expanding warm-season compound droughts. Initially, LL correlated positively with SM and negatively with VPD in most regions, masking their distinct roles. Decoupling revealed SM as the dominant regulatory factor for LL, contributing approximately threefold more than VPD. The widely reported inhibitory effect of atmospheric dryness on grassland phenology was strongly amplified by its collinearity with soil aridity, with the role of VPD became more prominent when SM exceeded the non-restrictive threshold. Spatially, cold-region LL was more sensitive to soil-atmosphere moisture shifts, while in semi-humid regions, SM change still dominated, but VPD stress grew. These findings clarify the distinct mechanisms of soil-atmosphere moisture impacts, highlighting the importance of decoupling methods for ecological regulation analysis and guide adaptive ecological management.

title: Responses of streamflow extremes under solar radiation modification in the Muda River Basin, Malaysia
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Puteri Nur Atiqah Bandira, Mou Leong Tan, Igor Gómez, Zaher Mundher Yaseen, Zhongli Chen, Ying Shao
abstract: Study Region This study focuses on the Muda River Basin (MRB) in Malaysia, a tropical basin that is important for water supply and paddy irrigation in northern Peninsular Malaysia. Study Focus The impacts of Solar Radiation Modification (SRM) on tropical river basins remain largely underexplored. This study employed a calibrated SWAT + model driven by bias-corrected precipitation and temperature from GeoMIP6 projections under four scenarios, SSP2–4.5, SSP5–8.5, G6solar and G6sulfur, to evaluate the impacts of SRM on streamflow extremes and dry-wet abrupt alternation (DWAA) in the MRB. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Future hydrological responses are primarily characterised by intensified streamflow extremes and seasonal redistribution, while annual streamflow exhibits contrasting responses across climate scenarios. Streamflow generally decreases during the Northeast Monsoon and increases during the Southwest Monsoon. High-flow frequency and maximum streamflow are projected to increase under all scenarios, with the greatest increases under SSP5–8.5. Although SRM scenarios moderate changes in mean streamflow relative to SSP5–8.5, they do not consistently weaken hydrological extremes. Furthermore, DWAA analysis reveals relatively stable transition lags but considerable spatial variability in wet-phase intensity, with more abrupt post-drought responses projected in downstream areas. Overall, the SRM scenarios reflect complex, spatially heterogeneous hydrological responses in the MRB. Future research should consider different SRM deployment strategies and extend these assessments to include multi-hazard disaster risks and compound events.

title: Important contributions of winter and spring precipitation to the water sources of a montane shrub community in the Tianshan Mountains of China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Bahejiayinaer Tiemuerbieke, Linjia Li, Shunli Chang, Yutao Zhang
abstract: Study region Tianshan Mountains (Xinjiang, China). Study Focus Precipitation exhibits distinct spatiotemporal variability in arid-region temperate forests, and the contributions of summer and winter precipitation to the plant water supply throughout the growing season are not well understood. Clarifying the seasonal water sources utilized by forest species is essential for accurately predicting ecosystem responses to future climate change. This study examined seasonal soil moisture dynamics in montane shrub communities on the northern slopes of the Tianshan Mountains, using soil water content, isotopic signatures of soil water and precipitation, and the seasonal origin index (SOI) method to trace water sources for two dominant shrubs (Cotoneaster melanocarpus and Berberis heteropoda) during the growing season. Soil water SOI values reached their minimum (near −1) at 0–40 cm in April, partly exceeded 0 in August–September, and fluctuated between −0.5 and 0 from May to July. These patterns indicate that snowmelt-derived winter precipitation dominated soil moisture in April, which was subsequently mixed with spring rainfall by May. Summer precipitation had limited influence, penetrating only the surface layer (0–20 cm) and mixing with pre-existing soil water. Xylem water SOI values followed similar seasonal trends. B. heteropoda showed lower SOI values in May–June, indicating strong dependence on winter and spring precipitation during early summer. In contrast, C. melanocarpus maintained SOI values between −0.6 and 0 throughout the growing season, reflecting consistent use of mixed water sources. New Hydrological Insights for the Region These results underscore the ecological importance of spring and winter precipitation in enhancing plant water availability in this region. Under future climate scenarios, shifts in seasonal precipitation and increased winter snowfall and increased winter snowfall may play a critical role in sustaining arid temperate forest ecosystems.

title: Evaluation and prediction of water resource carrying capacity in Bortala Mongolian Autonomous Prefecture based on the GRA-TOPSIS-PSONN model
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Feifei Sheng, Jianjun Yang, Wenli Xing, Ninglu Zhang, Zhiguang Zhang, Wanqing Zhao
abstract: Study region Bortala Mongolian Autonomous Prefecture in Xinjiang. Study focus To support water management in water-stressed regions, this study developed an integrated “assessment-diagnosis-prediction” framework for evaluating Water Resources Carrying Capacity (WRCC) in Bortala Prefecture. A water resource-society-economy-ecology indicator system was constructed, and indicator weights were determined by combining the Entropy Weight Method and CRITIC method through game theory. The GRA-TOPSIS model was used to assess WRCC from 2013 to 2022 and diagnose key obstacle factors, while a two-stage neural network model was employed to predict WRCC trends during 2023–2030. This study fills a gap in WRCC research for arid inland regions by linking historical assessment, obstacle diagnosis, and future prediction within a unified framework. New hydrological insights for the region WRCC in Bortala Prefecture increased from 0.40 in 2013–0.49 in 2022, but remained mostly at the Critical Carrying Capacity level, indicating limited room for further water-resource development. Water production modulus, ecological water-use proportion, and per capita water resources were the most frequent limiting indicators. Forecast results show that WRCC will fluctuate between 0.371 and 0.509 during 2023–2030, with clear regional differentiation, suggesting that future water security depends more on adaptive allocation and demand regulation than on water-supply expansion alone.

title: Pixel-level flood loss assessment driven by a consistent high-resolution land-cover base map: Integrating semantic segmentation, hydrodynamic simulation, and ecosystem service valuation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Lai Yishu, Zhang Sherong, Cheng Xiaoliang, Wang Chao, Wang Xiaohua, Zhang Jiabin
abstract: Study region This study examines a typical piedmont depression in Xushui District, Baoding City, on the North China Plain, where fragmented land cover and mixed exposed elements require refined regional flood loss assessment. Study focus Regional flood loss assessment is often limited by inconsistent land cover datasets used for hydrodynamic parameterization, exposure mapping, and loss estimation. We propose a pixel-level framework driven by a consistent 0.8 m, 16-class land cover base map. Four EfficientNetV2-S-enhanced semantic segmentation models generated the map and supported unified assignment of roughness, economic value, ecosystem service value, and vulnerability, ensuring semantic, parametric, and scale consistency. Coupled with two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations, the framework estimates flood intensity, exposure, direct economic losses, and environmental damage. E-UNet performed best, with mIoU of 76.83% and mPA of 89.64%. New hydrological insights for the region Land cover resolution, class definition, and temporal consistency affect inundation patterns, exposed assets, and direct economic loss and environmental damage estimates, while amplifying the influence of built-up areas and small water bodies on loss composition. Under two extreme flood scenarios, inundated areas from the proposed map differed from contemporaneous Esri-LC24 by 3.0%–5.0%. In Case 1, direct economic losses reached CNY 1.147–1.684 billion, and monetized environmental damage reached CNY 123–177 million, accounting for 8%–10% of total losses under the adopted ESV coefficients and Fusion map assumptions. The framework provides an updatable, transferable, and spatially consistent method for regional flood risk assessment.

title: Interaction of soil water and shallow groundwater in a hillslope in the Ordos Basin: Insights from transient 2D flow system analysis
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Jia-Xin Shi, Xiao-Wei Jiang, Peng-Fei Han, Xue-Kai Jiang, Zhenbin Zhang, Xu-Sheng Wang, Li Wan
abstract: Study region A semi-arid region with shallow groundwater and distinct topographic relief in the Ordos Plateau, China. Study focus This study aimed to investigate the interaction between soil water with groundwater and the transient two-dimensional unsaturated–saturated water flow systems. Particular attention was given to the effects of rapid infiltration and strong evapotranspiration in the lowland and their role in driving lateral groundwater flow (LGF) between the upland and lowland positions. New hydrogeological insights from the region The results reveals the occurrence of transient 2D unsaturated-saturated water flow systems induced by rapid infiltration and strong evapotranspiration in the lowlands. The former causes lateral groundwater flow (LGF) from the lowland to the upland, whereas the latter generates LGF with an opposite direction. In unsaturated zone of the upland, there are convergent or divergent zero flux planes separating upward or downward soil water flow. In drought period, the proportion of water loss caused by downward flux in the profile in the upland ranges from 33% to 72%, demonstrating that a large proportion of soil water loss is contributed by ex situ evapotranspiration (water from topographic highs is consumed by evapotranspiration in topographic lows) via LGF, not by in situ evapotranspiration. Therefore, in regions with shallow groundwater, analyzing transient 2D unsaturated-saturated water flow systems can be useful in interpreting soil water flow as long as there is topographic relief.

title: Propagation of precipitation errors to streamflow: A large-sample evaluation of IMERG V06 and V07 in southern China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Wen Liu, Naili Zhao, Yonghua Zhu, Haishen Lü, Qingyi Yang, Jianbin Su
abstract: Study region 312 small- and medium-sized watersheds across humid southern China. Study focus Using the Xinanjiang (XAJ) model together with an effective automatic calibration algorithm, this study systematically evaluates the streamflow simulation performance of the Integrated MultisatellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG) Version 06 (V06) and Version 07 (V07) Final Run products across 312 small- and medium-sized watersheds (SMWs). Hydrological impacts of two types of IMERG precipitation error characteristics are quantified through parallel experiments and sensitivity analyses. New hydrological insights for the region Simulation skill varied markedly among products and regions. The calibrated IMERG V07 product achieved the highest median Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) during calibration, but its validation performance deteriorated because of the anomalous overestimation associated with the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) after 2019. After removal of this temporal anomaly, the calibrated IMERG V07 and V06 products achieved median NSE values of 0.61 and 0.58, respectively, over the full period. Recalibrating the XAJ model accommodated the modest underestimation of the uncalibrated IMERG V07 product in eastern watersheds, whereas severe underestimation in western high-elevation watersheds still resulted in substantial streamflow-volume underestimation and degraded simulation skill. This study provides baseline streamflow simulation performance for IMERG precipitation in humid southern China. More broadly, it demonstrates that precipitation-error magnitude and temporal anomalies can constrain streamflow simulation under model recalibration.

title: Transient bidirectional flow in Yangtze River Estuary: Driving mechanisms and spatiotemporal variations
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Chi Zhang, Jicai Zhang, Guansuo Wang
abstract: Study region The Yangtze River Estuary, China, located at the confluence of the Yangtze River and the East China Sea. Study focus This study combined observations and numerical modeling to investigate the occurrence, driving mechanisms, impacts, and spatiotemporal characteristics of transient bidirectional flow (TBF) events in the Yangtze River Estuary. New hydrological insights for the region In the Yangtze River Estuary, we identified TBF events characterized by instantaneous surface-seaward and bottom-landward currents that persisted over multiple tidal cycles. This differs from classical estuarine exchange flow, whose instantaneous flow field is usually vertically unidirectional under tidal dominance. Although similar instantaneous bidirectional flow structures have been observed previously in estuaries, their impacts, governing mechanisms, and spatiotemporal characteristics remain insufficiently understood. Our results show that TBF significantly influenced water column stratification and enhanced the net transport of water and salt. Momentum analysis and sensitivity experiments revealed its driving mechanisms: during ebb tides, strong northerly winds enhanced saltwater intrusion, generating a persistent landward baroclinic pressure gradient that reversed the bottom ebb current landward; during flood tides, the combined effect of river discharge and the salt wedge raised the upstream water level, producing a strong seaward barotropic pressure gradient that reversed the surface flood current seaward.

title: Investigating climate change-induced extreme floods: Insights from super-high-resolution climate datasets using Rainfall-Runoff-Inundation (RRI) model
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Sophal Try, Jackson Hian-Wui Chang, Sovannara Uk, Mengshan Lee, Huan-Yu Shiu, Carlos García Castro, Yong Jie Wong
abstract: Study region Characterized by steep mountainous terrain, short river systems, and frequent typhoon-induced rainfall, the river basins of Taiwan are highly susceptible to flooding. Despite the expected intensification of extreme precipitation under climate change, regional hydrological assessments using super-high-resolution climate projections remain limited. Study focus This study investigates the impacts of future climate change on extreme streamflow and flood hazards across 15 hydrological stations representing major river basins in Taiwan. Super-high-resolution climate projections from the Meteorological Research Institute Atmospheric General Circulation Model (MRI-AGCM3.2S HighResMIP) and the Database for Policy Decision Making for Future Climate Change (d4PDF) under the 4°C warming experiment were coupled with a Rainfall-Runoff-Inundation (RRI) model to simulate flood responses. Annual peak discharges were estimated for near-future (2020–2040), mid-future (2050–2070), and far-future (2080–2100) periods under 10-, 100-, and 1000-year return periods. New hydrological insights for the region The simulations indicate that projected annual peak discharges under the 4°C warming scenario consistently exceed those under the present climate across all return periods, indicating an increased probability of extreme flood events throughout Taiwan. The magnitude of change varies among river basins, demonstrating strong regional heterogeneity in hydrological responses to climate change. These findings provide new evidence that super-high-resolution climate projections improve the representation of future flood extremes and offer valuable regional-scale information for flood risk assessment, climate adaptation planning, and the design of resilient water resources and flood management strategies in Taiwan.

title: Spatiotemporal changes and flow–sediment associations of planform adjustment in the wandering reaches of the upper Tarim River
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Bo Feng, Xuewei Fan, Zhexin Zhang, Wenhong Dai
abstract: Study regions The wandering reaches of the upper Tarim River. Study focus Under the combined effects of mountain meltwater recharge, changing flow and sediment conditions, and human activities, planform adjustment in the upper Tarim River poses risks to bank stability and water conveyance. Using multi-temporal remote sensing images from 2005 to 2023, this study delineated channel water boundaries and centerlines, and quantified channel width, sinuosity, lateral migration rate, and water-boundary expansion and contraction. Hydrological and sediment records were further used to construct high-flow metrics, and hierarchical clustering and correlation analysis were applied to identify interannual adjustment types and their associated flow and sediment conditions. New hydrological insights for the region Planform evolution showed clear downstream differences. Reach R1 exhibited slowly increasing sinuosity and persistent bend-scale centerline oscillation. Reach R2 was wide, shallow, and relatively stable, with limited sinuosity variation. Reach R3 showed increasing sinuosity, bend development, and stronger local main-channel oscillation. Interannual adjustment was classified into three types, including strong migration with main-channel oscillation, expansion and widening with bank retreat, and contraction adjustment with bend development. These types corresponded to different high-flow and sediment conditions. Multi-stage water-boundary overlay analysis identified persistently expanding and contracting active bank sections, which were further assigned to the three adjustment types. The results provide a basis for risk identification and segmented, type-specific management of wandering reaches in arid inland rivers.

title: Coupled hydrological–hydrodynamic modelling of GLOFs triggered by extreme precipitation in the Western Himalayas
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Deepali Gaikwad, Daishisha Iawphniaw, Vikas Singh Jadoun, Reet Kamal Tiwari, Biswajeet Pradhan
abstract: Study region Western Himalayas (Himachal Pradesh). Study focus Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) are increasingly recognized as a major cryosphere-related hazard in the western Himalayas, where accelerated glacier retreat, elevation-dependent warming, and intensifying extreme hydro-meteorological events collectively amplify downstream flood risk to settlements and infrastructure. Most existing GLOF hazard assessments treat lake outburst processes and extreme rainfall-induced flooding independently, potentially underestimating worst-case flood magnitudes and inundation extents. To address this critical gap, the present study integrates Extreme Rainfall Events (EREs), including Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP), into a coupled hydrological–hydrodynamic modelling framework to assess compound GLOF–flood hazards in glacier-fed Himalayan basins. New hydrologic insights Two high-risk glacial lakes in the Beas and Sutlej river basins were analysed using coupled HEC-HMS and HEC-RAS models under multi-return-period flood scenarios (2–100 years) and the Probable Maximum Flood (PMF). PMF discharges peaked at 17,086 m³ /s at Pandoh Dam and 23,478 m³ /s at Bhakra Dam, with model validation showing strong performance (Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency > 0.65 and > 0.75). Incorporating PMP-based discharges into GLOF simulations enabled worst-case combined GLOF-PMF modelling, yielding peak flows of 17, 356 m³ /s (Beas) and 24,723 m³ /s (Sutlej). Inundation mapping revealed major risks to hydropower projects, religious sites, and over 680 structures. Given the projected intensification of extreme precipitation under climate change, this integrated approach is readily transferable to other glacierized basins across the Himalayas.

title: Hydrological controls on seasonal nitrate reduction and microbial community dynamics in the hyporheic zone of Songjiho lagoon, South Korea
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Chanyoung Jeong, Soo Min Song, Woo-Hyun Jeon, Soo Young Cho, Sung Pil Hyun, Hee Sun Moon
abstract: Study region Songjiho lagoon, located on the east coast of Korea, is a coastal freshwater-seawater transition system in which seasonal water-level fluctuations shape hyporheic biogeochemical conditions. Study focus We investigated how seasonal changes in water level and salinity affect nitrate reduction and microbial community structure in the hyporheic zone of Songjiho Lagoon, South Korea. New hydrological insights for the region Managed sandbar breaching during the wet season maintained relatively saline conditions, whereas subsequent water-level decline increased groundwater influence and freshened the upper sediments. This hydrological shift altered porewater salinity profiles and coincided with elevated organic carbon and nitrogen concentrations, particularly at 20 cm depth, where potential denitrification was also highest. Potential denitrification rates were consistently greater under saline than freshwater conditions, reaching 85.1 ng N₂O-N g⁻¹ h⁻¹ . Putative nitrate-reducing taxa also varied with salinity, with genus Shewanella associated with saline conditions and genus Pseudomonas more abundant under fresher conditions. These results indicate that seasonal hydrological variability regulates nitrate-reduction potential by modifying salinity gradients, groundwater-surface water interactions, and associated microbial assemblages. Under drawdown-driven freshening, nitrate-reduction potential may decline, increasing the likelihood of nitrogen retention in lagoon sediments.

title: Influences of meteorological factors on stable isotopic fractionation of evaporating water bodies: Insights from experiments and simulations of the evaporation pans
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Xiong Xiao, Yong Zhang, Xinping Zhang, Jinzhao Liu, Zhu Liu
abstract: Study region A typical subtropical monsoon region. Study focus Parallel evaporation pan experiments under rain-excluded and rain-included conditions were conducted. The Rayleigh fractionation (RL), Craig-Gordon (C-G), and Isotope and Water Mass Balance (IWB) models were used to simulate residual water isotopes (δL), aiming to reveal how meteorological factors control isotopic fractionation. New hydrological insights for the region The δL were negatively correlated with the residual water fraction (f), with larger amplitude variations in f induced correspondingly larger fluctuations in δL. The C-G model showed better performance than the RL model in the δL simulation, with RMSE values of only 1.6‰ for δ2H and 0.7‰ for δ18O, and the integration of the IWB model on rainy days improved the simulation accuracy of both models; High temperature and low relative humidity decreased the slope of the evaporation line systematically, which was attributed to the asymmetric reduction of kinetic fractionation coefficients for 18O and 2H and the preferential depletion of 2H in evaporative vapor, with relative humidity acting as the dominant controlling factor; Simulation accuracy was highly sensitive to parameterization schemes rather than merely depending on model structure, and arithmetic averages of meteorological factors yielded better δL series than weighted averages in high-humidity environments of our evaporation pan experiment.
